div.p: put*. KLSSED HIS MOTHER. She sat on the porch in the sunshine • k, As I went down the street— t A woman whose hair was silver, But whose face was blossom sweet, Making me think of a garden, When,lin spite of the frost and snow b Of bleak November weather, Late, fragrant lilies blow:i I beard a footstep behind me' . And the sound of a merry laugh, And I knew the heart it came from Would be like a comforting staff In the time and hour of trouble, Hopeful and brave and strong, • One ofithe'llearts to lean on When we think all things go wrong. I turn at the click of the gate-latch, ; fv• And meet his manly look; A face like his gives me pleasure, Like the page of a pleasant book. It told of a steadfast purpose, Of a brave and daring will; EY; A face with a promise in it, That, God.grant, the years fulfil. 7 Be went up the pathway, singing, • I saw the woman's eyes Grow bright with a worldless welcome, As sunshine warms the skies. "Back again, sweetheart mother 7 EW cried, and bent to kiss That loving face that was lifted For what some mothers miss. - That boy will do to depend on ; I hold that this is true— From lads in love with their mothers, Our bravest heroes grew. Earth's grandest hearts have been loving hearts Since time and earth began; ' And the boy who kissed his mother Is every inch a man. •

- If a small boy is called a lad, is it not proper to call a bigger boy a ladder? Do not lose courage by *considering your own imper- fections, but instantly set about to remedy them. Never fear to bring the sublimest motive to the small- est duty, and the most infinite comfort to theismallest trouble. An employer of labour concludes his advertisement for assistants with the significant note—" None need apply who are in the habit of being poorly on Monday morning." An Irishman put up the following notice :—" Whoever is caught trespassing upon these grounds will be given forty lashes on the bare back. Half the penalty will be paid to the informer." The minister (reproachfully): " Ah, James, I'm sorry to see this! I thought you were a steadfast teetotaller !" James (who is too full to walk) : "Sho I am, slur; but I'm no a bigoted ane !" "A woman, whose husband was blind, being asked, "Gin her husband widna feel it dull, no' bein' able to read?" "Na, na," she answered, "he disna feel that. I read the Scriptures to him every day, an' mony's the bit I put i,n for his guid." In Whately's time .the great circulating library of Dublin was Morrow's, and the most popular preacher was a Mr. Day. "How inconsistent,' said the arch- bishop, "is the piety of certain ladies here! They go to ' Day for a sermon and to Morrow for a novel." The Emperor of Morocco, having subscribed for newspaper, reads all the advertisements first. They tried to get him to read the editorial page first, but he remarked that he had been a monarch too long not to know what was interesting, reading. - Judge Jeffreys, taking a dislike to a man who had a long beard, he told him "that if his conscience was as long as his beard, he had a swinging one." To which j the fellow replied—" My Lord, if you measure conscience ' by beards, you will have none at all." See here, my friend, that dog of yours killed three' sheep of mine last night, and I want to know what youl propose to do about it." "Are you sure it was my dog ?" "Yes." "Well, i hardly know what to do. I guess I had better sell him. You don't want to buy a good dog, do you ?" "Tell me, Murphy, how came you by that black eye? Were you fighting, eh ?" Murphy-0 Well, indade, I won't decaive yer riverence. Mick O'Flaherty and me- self had a little difference; but shure if yer riverence only seen .Mick's eye now, troth you'd say there was I nothinlwrong with mine at all, at all." J A tradesman who is in the habit of wearing knicker- bockers in the summer was accosted by one of his d •btors (who had a friend with him) in this manner:— ' Well, Mr. D--- how is it that your breeks are getting j so short,?" "Just, sir," said Mr. D—, "because youl and, the like of you take bits off them." Collapse of the debtor, to the merriment of his friend. "Say that you will be mine, dearest Angelina." "I 'will, upon one condition." "Name it, my adored, and if it were to get you the moon—" "It is easier than that; in brief, simply this—that you will, invite me to spend a month in your father's house previous to our marriage." "Of course, certainly; but why make such a strange quest?"/ 0 "Well, I wish to learn to cook like Your mother." In a small Texas town a cow-boy was on trial for maliciously shooting a dog. The principal witness for the prosecution, an aged negro, was asked if he had not testified at the preliminary examination that the defend- ant had shot the dog in self-defence. The cad fellow, rolled his eyes for a moment, as he laboriously searched his memory, and then exclaimed, "Oh, no, boss! I tes- tified dat he shot de dog in de back, and den jumped de fence." • Pivmsarr nz Manx—Payment to singers has sometimes taken an odd form When Mademoiselle Zelie. a vocalist from the Theetre Lyrique at Paris, was making a pro- fessional tour round the world, sore years since she gave a concert at the Society Islands. She agreed to sing an air from " Norma " and a 'few other songs, and was to receive in exchange a third part of the re- ceipts. When counted, the prima donna's share was found to consist of three pigs, twenty-three turkeys, forty-four chickens, five thousand cocoa-nuts, besides considerable quantities of bananas, lemons, and oranges. A gentleman who had been at a missionary collection was met the next day by a man of opposite habits who began to chide him with the folly of sending out such sums abroad, when there was so much to be done at home. The gentleman calmly replied, "I will give yeti five pounds for our poor at home if you will give the same." "Oh, I didn't mean that," said the objector; "but if you must go from home, why so far? Think of the poor in Ireland." "I will give five pounds for the poor in Ireland," said the gentleman," if you will give the . same." "No. I don't mean that either,' said the man. A Scotch subaltern at Gibraltar was one day on guard with another officer, who unluckily fell down a precipice • 400 feet, and was killed. Non-military readers should understand that in the guard reports there is a small addendum, viz. :—" N.B.—Nothing extraordinary since ,guard-mounting.", Our friend, however, said nothing about the accident, and some hours after, the brigade- major came down to his quarters on the part of the officer commanding, with the report in his hand, to de- mand an explanation. "You say, 'N.B.—Nothing ex- traordinary since guard mounting,' when your brother officer on duty has fallen down a precipice 400 feet, and been killed." "Wee!, sir," replied he, "I dinna think there's onything extraordinary in that; if he'd faun doon a precipice 400 feet, and no been killed, I should hae thought it very extraordinary indeed, and wad hae put it doon in my report." • A YOUNG ROMAN'S SACRIFICE.—A TRITE STOUT.-011C0 upon a time, many hundred years ago, when Rome was mistress of the world, and the Romans were braver and .Bronger than anyone else, there lived a boy of thirteen whose name is still remembered. Lucius Valerius was fond of his lessons, but most of all did he love poetry; so, although he was only thirteen years old, he made up his mind that he would try to win the gold. medal and ivory lyre which were given every five years to the boy who should write the best poem. Lucius not only tried, but he succeeded, and one day, before all the schools and a number of visitors, the prizes were presented te him. Now besides the medal and lyre which every one who gained them valued very much, there was something else which they thoughtlar grander. A statue of thnprize-win- ner was placed in the skhool and crowned with laurel. You may imagine how the boy's heart beat with joy as he saw the judge step f6rward to crown his statue, but just at that moment Lucius caught sight of a young man who had also tried for the prize, and who looked most downcast and miserable) Lucius sprang forward, siezed the laurel crown, and put it on the head of the poor fel- low who had been unsuccessful. "You are more deserv- ing of it than I am," he said; "I obtained it more on ac- count of my youth than my merit, and rather as an en- couragement than as a reward." Then the people set up a great shout of joy, for they knew that a noble heart was worth more than all the poems in the world, and they gave a new name to Lucius Valerius in memory of that day. So Lucius was always called Pudens, which means Modest, and you may be sure he valued his new title as much as he deserved it, for " Sind hearts are more than coronets."

The driver, fireman, and guard were seriously hut, and a portion of the line was torn up. Great delay was caused by the accident, the cause of which is unknown. COTTAGE GARDENING

Swum RUNNER BEANS.—These are growing apace and if they are not provided with support about 61 t. high they should have the tops of the shoots pricked off before they quite reach the top of the stake placed for them. This will stop their upward progress and cause them to become more bushy. Beans intended to be treated in this way should be sown much thinner than those that are allowed to run up uninterrupted. STRAWBERRY Ruxienns.—lf the best of these are layered at once they will make good plants and bear a heavy crop of fruit next year. Fortunately, the best runners are to be found round the outer edges of the bed, which is really the only place where they can be conveniently layered. The work should be proceeded with in the following manner :—The gravid will now be naturally firm, and it should be well loosened with the fork. On the top of it place three inches of rich mellow soil, not all over the ground, but in patches, just where most of the runners can be directed. Spaces must be left for the feet, so that the fruit may be conveniently gathered. The runners must be three inches diatant Ifrom each other, and a stone, the size of a hen's egg, placed on each, just at the back of the embryo plant The portion ahead of the future plant must be pinched off, or it will:continue growing and rob the other of its sustenance. If after this they are sprinkled over with water, so as to settle the soil, they will soon root, and in about three weeks will be fit to plant out in their per- manent quarters. LEEKS are now large enough to plant out, which should be done in rich soil, or, what is better still, in shallow trenches, with a few inches of manure dug in. The dis- tance between the plants should be about six inches, and if the trench system is selected the plants should be earthed as they make progress. This will double the bulk of the white or blanched portion, which is by many cooked and served as a vegetable, the green portion being reserved for broths, &c. CELERY needs constant attention as to water, and the earliest should have an inch or two of soil placed round it, after receiving a good soaking, which will encourage surface roots as well as intercept rapid evaporation. All small leaves at the base of the plants, as well as suckers, should, however, be moved before any soil is added to them. THE FRONT GARDEN.—Rose budding may now be pro- ceeded with, as the bark rises well at this time of the year, if the ground has not been too dr3% and so checked the supply of sap. Should there on this account be any difficulty, it is as well not to proceed till matters change. Budding is a very simple process if all goes on smoothly, but no one can conduct it effectually if the bark of the stock, or that attached to the bud, refuses to part freely. The budder must be provided with a small sharp knife, with which he will make a longitudinal cut about an inch and a half long, extending from the base of the shoot, by drawing the knife on its upper side towards its point. Here he will make a transverse section ex- tending a quarter of an inch on either side of the previous cut. These incisions must not penetrate any deeper than the bark. In the ab- sence of a proper budding knife the operator may use a hard piece of wood not unlike the blade of a knife with rounded point, but with an edge on both sides. This he will thrust down the longitudinal cut, pressing slightly to each side as he proceeds and he will soo a perceive the bark rising. Cut then the piece of Wo3l to which the selected bud is attached. The length of the longitudinal cut, split it with the knife in half and make the end at the back of the bud bevelled by a sloping cut with the knife so as to give it the appearance of that portion of the writing pen we thrust in the holder. By bending back the piece of wood the bark will slip off and the bud attached to it. The bevelled end must now be inserted into the cut at the orifice and gradually pushed downwards. The object of the bevel- ling is to enable it to pass on more readily than if square, as the upper end must necessarily be. It frequently occurs that the bud or the bark which carries it is longer than the cut, which is a very good fault, for we have only to place the knife in the transverse cut and press it on to the bark so as to snip it off, and it will settle in its place a perfect fit. t THE WINDOW.—AII plants of the Cactus tribe require plenty of water from now till they have completed their growth. This rule applies to other succulents, such as Aloes, Crassulas, and Mesembryanthimums. It is sur- prising that these plants are not more patronised, as they are really easily grown, and there is something so grotesque in`their appearance that they attract atten- tion even when out of flower. They are as well suited for window culture as any plant we are acquainted with.

"AS I WENT SAILING." BY THOMAS GIBBONS. Author of "Boxing the Compass," "Naval Songs and Song Writers,"" The Way to Ichang," &c. No. V.—ON THE GREAT RIVER OF CHINA. "I have voyaged—and voyaged—and voyaged; but I declare to you, Master Jack, I had rather he here, with you and Nature, than play spaniel to the finest dame in the city."—Two Travellers. The Yang-tsze Kiang (ocean-child river) is the great waterway of China. Its source is in Tibet; and, follow-- ing a sinuous course through the heart of China, the river extends over 3,000 miles from the headwaters to the mouth, where the sediment of its muddy stream dis- colours the Pacific for nearly 300 miles seaward. Many important cities stand on the banks of the lower branch of the Yang-tsze ; Chin-kiany, Nanking, Kiukiang,s, and Hankow, all teeming with life and interest to the traveller. The lower part of the river has often been described, for excursions thereon are frequent; a fleet of large and comfortable steamers ply to and fro from Shanghai; shooting parties visit the game-infested locality of Nanking, porcelain hunters go to Kinkiang, and tea buyers rush to Hankow; but the pper Yang-tsze, trending through the country beyond Hankow, was until a few years ago an almost unknown tegion, visited only occasionally by adventurous missionaries, trade pioneers in Chinese costume, and consular officials, pro- tected by native authority. Poor Augustus Raymond Margery, of the Shanghai Consulate, went the journey to his cost, and his head was spiked on the gates of Man- wyne in 1875. His murder resulted in trouble between the English and Chinese Governments not far removed from actual warfare; an imposing British fleet visited Chinese waters, and remained at anchor below Shanghai; Sir Thomas Wade, the English Minister in China, and the famous Chinese Secretary, Li Hung-chang, met at Che- foo ; weary negotiations followed, and a new treaty with China was the result. A money indemnity for the mur- der, sinking of past quarrels, and the opening of addi- tional Chinese ports to foreign vessels, were the principal concessions; and Ichang, an important city in the pro- vince of Hupeh,about 1,000 miles in the interior of China, was one of the ports opened to Western commerce by the Treaty of Chefoo. In 1877, the writer joined in an important excursion to the city of ichang ; was present at the official opening of the port, when the roar of cannon proclaimed the advent of the "Western ocean men," and enjoyed the opportunity of meeting and speak- ing with Chinese, whose sight had never before rested upon the face of a foreigner. We then decided that China improved on a closer acquaintance, and time has not shaken our belief, however distant the people of that country be removed from us in the essentials of human sympathy. Certainly a river voyage into the heart of China has many attractions; an excellent opportunity is afforled to view the changeful scenery of the land; and one so inclined may study somewhat the characteristics of an interesting people. We can merely glance at the features of the country between Hankow and Ichang, presented to view while rapidly navigating the waters of the great river. Throughout the distance the course of the river is very tortuous, and rushing currents and shoal waters are alternate serious obstacles to speedy and successful navigation in the spring season of the year. In the summer months, until June, the water often rises 15 and 20 feet, the current proportionately increasing with the greater volume of the stream. Hankow was opened to foreign trade in 1861; until the opening of Ichang, in 1877, Hankow was the limit of navigation for merchant vessels on the Yang-tsze, and it certainly may be regarded as the most important trading mart to which foreigners have atcess in the interior of China. It is distant from the coast-line about 600 mites; large tea steamers can reach it in safety; and its com- mercial prosp6rity has been greatly influenced by the ready proximity of Shanghai. It stands at the mouth of the Han, where that river joins the Yang-tsze. On the other shore of the Han stands the city of Hang-yang,and on the opposite bank of the large river, facing the mouth of the Han, rises the ancient and famous provincial capi- tal of Wu-ehang, with its massive pagoda, and a part of the walls of the city extending along the waterside. Wu- chang and Hang-yang are walled-cities, while Hankow is a great un-walled town, the trade centre of the three. A Chinese proverb refers to the prosperity of Hankow : "In the streets every inch of ground supports a man, and the square feet of ground are more valuable than a cubic inch of pure gold." Without doubt, since the port was opened to foreign commerce, there has been an immense influx of Chinese merchants, who have carried trade with them thereby, greatly increasing all other classes of the native population. The foreign settlement—a considerable area of land, well laid out, and containing some fine residences—is built on the north side of the Chinese town, but the forei n com- munity is not a large one, and is almost confined to consuls, merchants, and foreigners in the Imperial Cus- toms service. Leaving Hankow, ascending the b°Teat river, the course of the Yang-tsze trends through a flat and uninteresting country for a distance of 150 miles. At that distance from Hankow the waters of the Tung-ting, the largest lake in China, join the river; but, thus far, there is little to invite attention. The land is low, the depression covering a vast area, and consequently the inundations in the summer season are severely destructive. From Tung-ting to Shi-show, the Nan-tsuin hills, a bold moun- tainous chain rising 1,500 feet, are occasionally seen in the distance, and at Shi-sho ar the hills dip down and touch the riverbank. This is the only high land conti- guous to the river for nearly 200 miles, and is an agree- able break in the monotonous level. The little walled town of Shi-show nestles between the hills, on the right bank, at a sharp bend of the stream, and some temples on the hill tops, fringed around with trees, give a pleas- ing effect to the view. Sha-sze is the first port of particular importance on the Upper Yang-tsze ;it is 285 miles above Hankow. The town struggles along the left embankment for nearly two miles. It presents all the usual characteristics of Chinese industry; junks crowd the port, receiving and discharg- ing their cargoes; and the restless crowd of motley natives, coming and going, would bewilder the Western stranger. The junks trade from above and below Sha-sze, making that port the end of their voyage, transferring their cargoes to craft suitable to the changeful navigation of the river. The trade covers opium, tobacco, drugs, silk, wax, and small quantities of gold from the province of Sze-chuen. Viewing the resources of the country, as they are hastily presented while voyaging on the Yang-tsze, one is at little loss to understand somewhat of the reasons hitherto inducing the Chinese to remain an iso- lated nation. The land yields everything for the ordinary purposes of life; and the great plains are carefully cul- tivated. Rice and wheat, thus far are extensivelpgrown, forming a Large trade with distant parts of the empire. We remember an incident at Sha-sze, which will serve as an example held by high Chinese officials, though we have no reason to believe that similar summary dealings with offenders are common. A junk sailor, impressed with a wish to see the foreigners, failed to hasten out of the way of the sedans carrying the Tautai, (lieutenant- governor of the district), and his suite, and s'everal of our party on a visit of ceremony; the Tautai stopped his chair-bearers, stepped into the roadway, and had the man seized. In spite of the poor fellow's cries, the atten- dants threw the man on the ground, face downwards, stripped the few rags of clothing off his body, held his arms and legs spread out, and belaboured him most savagely with bamboo staves, evidently carried by the guard for such an emergency. Atter witnessing the in- fliction of the punishment, the Tautai entered his chair, and called fbr the procession to move on. A few miles above' Sha-sze the land becomes undula- ting, and more varied in picturesque effect. The trees thicken; and the lilac and fruit blossoms interlace with full green foliage. Gray and grim old habitations, showing their dilapidated gables in all manner of odd ways, are dotted over the landscape; and on the elevated ground are the earth mounds wherein the "forefathers of the hamlet" are gathered to rest. Pagodas and Budd- hist temples—the latter fantastic and gaudy enough in all outward seeming—with the usual accompaniment of grotesque images, crown the hill tops. The village of Yang-chi (about thirty-five miles beyond Sha-sze) is the prettiest view on the upper river; it nestles in greenery and blossoms. Directly north of the town is an exten- sive quarry, where limestone is burned and made into tiles. At other similar places on the river the industry of the people is evident, junks' and sampan g (small row- boats) throng the beach, and hundreds of men, women, and children gather at every available point to watch us as we glide along within ten yards of the shore. Again the open country ; again the same rich cultivation; vege- tation trailing down the sloping hills, kissing the water of the great river; and so this vest panorama of culti- vated grandeur keeps on unfolding itself for miles and miles. The choicest of rural scenery is presented to the voyager. This wide region is certainly one of the most lovely in China ; so unlike the sparse cultivation and sameness on the seaboard of the northern provinces, or the severe sterility of the coast scenery of the south. No pen can fully describe it; portions might be selected and placed under the lens for examination, but it would all teem with beauty. Twelve miles above Yang-chi, the Chin-kiang, which flows from the westward, joins the waters of the Yang-tsze. The walled city of Itu stands at the junction of the two rivers, on the right bank; the river front has no signs of trade, the only prominent feature about the city walls being the roofs of the temples. A high mountainous country fills the view to the westward. The- river bank now rises in huge bold masses of sandstone, one and two hundred feet high. The acclivities of the hills and the occasional clefts, which- form long sweeping valleys, teem with cultivation; every ridge and slope, wherever prac- ticable, is carpeted with green. The country retains this same bold character, more or less beautiful, until Ichang is reached. Three miles below Ichang, about a mile backward from the river, a monastery is perched on the summit of an isolated mountain _peak, 1,230 feet high; the view is very romantic. •

QUALIFICATIONS OF ELECTORS. 80. • Freeholders having a clear 40s. value arising out of lands or houses which have been in their possession—if by purchase, since January 15 of this year; if by will, no term is required. Owners of freeholds in a Parlia- mentary borough may vote Tor a county, providing they do not occupy the property; and if any name is °bitted or not correctly described a claim should be at once made.

COPYHOLDERS.—CopyhoId property requires to be of the clear yearly value of Z, and to have been in possession of its present owner prior to January, 15, 1885. Copy- hold in a borough does not give a county vote. LEASEHOLDERS.—LeasehoId property must be of the clear yearly value of £5, and have been in the hands of the present holder 12 months prior to July 15th of this year. A sub-lessee cannot vote as an owner for his property unless he resides upon it. Leasehold in boroughs does not give a vote for a county. The property lists are now on the church and chapel doors, and should be examined at once. Persons claim- ing for property must send in their claims to the over- seer of the township in which their property is situated prior to July 20th this year. Occur/Bats of houses, shops, offices, premises, land, &c., are entitled 1,0 be placed upon the new lists, which are published lit the Overseers on the Ist August, without notice of claim , that is, if they have occupied the pre- mises 12 months previous to the 15th July, and all poor rates, due before the sth January, paid before the 20th July. Should any occupiers be in any way wrongly described or omitted from the list of voters published on the Ist of August, they should make a claim at once. The occupation qualification is a house, with a residence in the same or other houses in succession for 12 months prior to July 15th of this year • such house or houses to be rated to the poor; the rate;s, due Jan. sth, whether paid by the landlord or tenant, to be paid before July 20. LODGERS must have occupied for twelve months prior to July 15th rooms of the annual value—if let un- furnished—of £lO a year, and they inust claim each year. Joint Lodgers, occupying rooms of the clear an- nual value (unfurnished) of £2O can claim but not more than two can claim. Lodgers who change their rooms in the same house must claim for such rooms in succession. Lodgers who are on the register must send in their claim on or before the 25th July. Lodgers who are not on the register must send in a claim on or before the 20th August. BOROUGHS.

In boroughs, the household occupation and service franchise are the same as those named for the counties; lodgers are also on the same basis. SERVICE OCCUPIERS.—This is a new qualification in county and borough, and affects the same class in both kinds of constituency. A person who is qualified to be put on the list of voters as a service occupier is a man who lives in a house attached to works, or offices, or mill, or bank, or other building, as caretaker, and where the tenant of the several classes of premises named does not:reside on such premiss°. Persons entitled to this franchise should see the lists published by the overseers in church, chapel, and Post Office notice boards on Aug. Ist. If their names are omitted, they should at once make claims. In this case, a twelve months' occupa- tion of the same premises is required. SUMMARY.

Forty-shilling freeholders, copyholders, and lease- holders of the value of £5, who are not on the present register, must claim before the 20th July next. Occu- piers who are omitted from the lists published on the Ist Aug. must claim before the 24th Aug. Lodgers must claim before the 25th July, if they are on the present register. Lodgers not on present register must claim before the 20th August. Claim forms can be obtained from the Liberal agents in every constituency.

Ichang, in latitude 30 degrees 42 seconds N., longitude 111 degrees 30 seconds E., is a walled city in the pro- vince of Hupeh, 355 miles above Hankow, and about one thousand miles from the sea; it stands on the left bank of the river, within twelve to fifteen miles of the Ichang gorge and rapids, terminating the present steam naviga- tion of the Yang-tsze. About four miles above Ichang, near the small village of Tung-yan Tung, is the Mi-Tan gorge, revelling in magnificent and picturesque effect; where peak dips to peak, almost forming natural archways. Elsewhere the sides of the gorge rise vertically four and five hun- dred feet; and in the face of a steep cliff, about one hun- dred feet from the summit, overhung with a great Sagged mass of sandstone, is a large cavern, or grotto, where a shrine has been raised to the memory of some deified Christian female; and, combining art with nature, a temple has been constructed for the worshippers of Bud- dha. The temple is gained by ascending several hundred rude stone steps, takin., a zig-zag course up a steep cleft in the mountain, the saes of which revel in wild luxu- riousness. The temple is in charge of four or five priests, who, in addition to their devotional exercises, serve tea: to the pilgrims and visitors. The priests of China, in all 'parts of the country, gain a share of their Income by entertaining travellers; for ,the temples are often used as taverns, and spacious apartments are set aside for visitors. A deep chasm, running through a Last year of Tory rule £75 809.994 range of high mountains to the west, marks the windings Last year of Liberal rule 86,755 931 of the Yang-tsze in its course to Sze-chuen ; undulating land fills the view to the east; and a beauteous country, rich and ripe in variegated splendour, presents itself to the north and the south. Trouble had been anticipated on the part of foreign officials by the opening of Ichang, owing to the generally supposed aversion to foreigners at that port, and the native authorities somewhat favoured the rumour. It is just to remember, during a very excited period we ex- perienced no unfriendly demonstration on the part of the Chinese at Ichang; yet at the time we knew of several instances where the same people had displayed a decidedly hostile disposition towards foreigners. While preserving intact all their customs and traditions, the Chinese have adapted themselves to Western settlers at other ports in the Far East, and we may reasonably expect the same adaptability of the people of Ichang. The benefit derived by the opening of Ichang is a problem which time shall answer. Perhaps a peaceful way through China to India was the object most to be desired; but we cannot help asking—What shall be the end of all this greed and acquisition?

FREE TRADE V. FAIR TRADE. Several leading Conservatives have recently pro- posed a duty on corn. It is urged that the higher wages of the operatives will compensate them for an increase in the price of the quartem loaf. An old fable describes how a dog witn a bone in its mouth was crossing a stream, when he saw the reflection of the bone in the water. The foolish animal snapped at the shadow and dropped the substance. Moral : The English working-classes have now a substantial advantage in the. shape of cheap food, which they should not part with merely on the very shadowy promise of increased wages. Even the American tariff, which is almost prohibitive, has failed to main- tain high wages in the United States during the year 1884, in spite of the good corps of wheat, corn, &c., there. Trade has been bad here, but is improv- ing. Witness the great change at Bradford, which is busier now than it has ever been before. In the meanwhile let us not be deluded by the fallacious cry of ," Protection" in any form. Stick to the sub- stance; and never mind the shadow. A.B.P. PROTECTION IN GERMANY.

The report of the German Chamber of after one year's experience of the new tariff, is as follows: "The high duties have greatly enhanced the cost of the necessities of life' while instead of wages rising, as was predicted, they have either re- mained stationary or decllne3, and the condition of the German workman has consequently materially deteriorated. Nor has the trade of Germany beneficed any more than the workman by the new policy. A small number of large industries and joint-stock com- panies may have derived some advantage from the new duties, but in the great majority of trades the tariff has proved not a protection but a burden ; the Germans have found that import duties fall upon the consumers and not upon the foreign sellers." Bcononsist.

THE COTTON TRADE.—GREAT STRIKE AT OLDHAM:- -As a matter of form the mills in Oldham and the district, at which the notices of the reduction of 10 per cent, in the wages of the employes expired on Saturday were opened at the usual hour on Monday morning, but in no case did the operatives put in an appearance. The object of the masters in opening the works was to afford their hands an opportu• nity of returning to work if they thought proper to do so at the reduced rate of wages, but it was hardly expected, in view of the advice given by their leaders, that they would return to work. The masters hold that they are perfectly justified in enforcing the proposal, and the fact that they gave their hands an opportunity of working at the reduced rate puts the operatives in the position of being on strike absolutely, and they are not idle as the result of being looked out. The day passed over very quietly. Many of the operatives who have been saving for the wakes, which commence shortly, will, it is believed, make use of their money at once, and not wait for the holiday season to come round. There has been nothing in the way of angry feel- ing manifested on either side up to the present, and there is an evident desire on the part of the employers' committee and the leaders of the operatives that the struggle may be waged quietly. THE MUNSTER Bastx.—A deputation on Monday waited on the Lord-Lieutenant of Ireland at the Viceregal Lodge, stating that the assets of the Munster Bank over the liabil- ities were £850,000, that its closing would cause widespread dimster amongst the farming classes, and they applied for a Government guarantee to open a current account with the Bank of Ireland or of England to the extent of .8500,000. His Excellency said it was outside the province of the Government to giva a guarantee of the kind asked, although they might do so such a panic were created as was threatened last week in order to prevent a public calamity. This had now been averted to some extent, and he did not see why, after the favourable statement submitted to him and the well•known ability and energy of the company, they should not be able to resuscitate the bank without Government aid. In any case they would hardly expect him to express an opinion on the proposition brought before him at such short notice. Whatever might happen they could reckon on the sympathy of himself and his colleagues. It is proposed to double the nominal capital of the bank, making it £3,000,000. The existing £1,500,000 will be represented by giving the shareholders 10 shares taken to have £2 paid up, instead of as ' now £3 with £8 to call, while the additional £1,500,000 will be issued in £lO shares onimyment of 30s, with £8 10s to call.

MODERN BABYLON. CHARGE AGAINST A BARONET. —At Bow-street Police Court, on Saturday, Mr. W. Doveton Smyth, solicitor, of 21, Bow-street, attended before Sir James Ingham, accompanied by a lady, named Wilkinson, for the purpose of making a com- plaint against a baronet, and to seek magisterial advice as to the best course the lady should pursue with reference to the abduction and seduction of her daughter, aged twelve years.—Mr. Smyth said that he Bad been consulted on ,the matter, and he bad thought it advisable to introduce Mrs. Wilkinson to the presiding magistrate, in order that she might relate her story berself.—Mrs. Wilkinson, a ladylike person, and a widow, then stepped into the witness box. She addressed the magistrates in a low tone, and her re- marks were scarcely audible; but she was understood to say that four years ago her step-daughter, then a child under twelve years of age, was a pupil at a boarding-school in the Life-road, Brixton. While there a well-anown baronet, after watching the school for some time, obtained an inter- view with the young child, and eventually induced her to go away with him, and, it was alleged, succeeded in effect- ing her ruin. She had ever sinco remained under his pro- tection. The sad fate of the child had caused the death of applicant's husband, who, at the time of her daughter's seduction, was in a very weak state of health. Applicant complained that she had also suffered great personal annoy- ance at the hands of the baronet. She had gone to Hastings for the benefit of her health, and while there she was still persecuted.—Mr. W. Doveton Smyth banded up the name of the baronet, but this was done privately.—Sir James Ing- ham, having been informed of the above facts, said that as , the alleged offences occurred at Brixton that would be withho the jurisdiction of the Lambeth Police Court, and therefore referred applicant to the Lambeth Police Court. BANK PARK AND GARDENS,

WARRINGTON. An old writer, Thomas Fuller, in one of those delightful discourses which go far to justify the estimate of Coleridge, who places him second only to Shakespeare amongst English writers, says that "Home wonders lack nothing but distance to make them admired," and he satirises the English of his day who could give "a better account of Fontainbleau than Hampton Court, of the Spa than of Bath, of Arras in ' Spain than Mole in Surrey." That this fashionable weakness of the seventeenth century has not yet dis- appeared we all know. There are plenty of English- men of to-day who could give a better account of the Rhine than of the Thames, of the Alps and Apennines than of the mountains of Wales and Scotland, and of the Pyramids of Egypt than the Druidic remains of ' Stonehenge. Nor is this little failing confined to those favoured mortals who can include a course of foreign travel in their education. It is the same weakness which often draws the humbler excursionist from his snug couch at unearthly hours, and which hurries hlia off to distant places in stuffy carriages, often in uncongenial company, to spend a day of listless and aimless wandering among sights and scenes which are not unfrequently less worthy of notice than those left behind. There are no doubt many in Warrington who have not heeded the sage , advice to know the rooms of their own house before they go over the threshold thereof, and who could give a better account of what is to be seen in North Wales, in Blackpool, or in Southport, than of their own town, and this not so much because that town lacked " observables " as because those " observa- bles " lacked distance. The philosophy of the old school-book story of the traveller who, after telling to an admiring and astonished circle the marvels he had seen in one of the countries he had visited, concluded his narrative by informing his enraptured listeners that he had simply been describing to them the cus- toms and scenes of their own country, things which took place beneath their eyes every day in the year, is as applicable to localities as to countries. Were any one, for instance, to expatiate eloquently on the subjects .of parks and gardens—to talk of smooth- shaven laws, of flowers "all red and white," of shady grottoes and arbours and ornamental waters enlivened with rare fowl, of bands discoursing mush,—

With many a winding bout Of liuk“l sweetness long drawn out, and of devotees of Terpsichore tripping it "on the light fantastic toe" on summers eve, it is certain that there would be many War- ringtonians who would never think that all this had any reference to a place to which they had free access at almost any time. Yet all this and something more might be said of Bank Park and Gardens. Our public park and gardens are not so extensive, nor have they so great a variety of attrac- tion, as those of some other towns; there have been no ill- advised attempts made to convert them into a feeble copy of a zoological garden by locating in them a few evil-smelling wild beasts or a cage full of chattering monkeys, which would be altogether out of congruity with their surroundings; nor are the gardens stocked with objects of antiquarian or artistic interest, which are better fitted for museums and art galleries; but for design and floriculture those who have frequented them during the present summer will feel disposed to maintain that they could not easily be improved upon. Since, to quote the quaint lines of ''Dan" Chaucer, " Apzilis, with his showers sweet," Bathed every vein in such licour, Of which virtue engender'd is the flower, the eye has been pleased on every side by irregular clumps of fresh green foliage and a bright succession of delicately tinted flowers. In the laying out and management of the gardens the happy mess between unkempt wildness in the name of natural beauty, and excessive refinement has been well served. Nature and art have been judiciously commingled to make an effect which must be delightful and refresh- ing in the highest degree to those who spend the better part of their lives in narrow streets, and in factories and workshops. in which the practical and useful is certainly more obvious than the iesthetic. In these gardens we see none of that Chinese and Dutch artificiality whioh has captivated some horti- culturists ; we see no trees and shrubs which have been clipped and backed into the rude semblances of men and animals, or into shapes which are those of neither men nor animals. Nor do we see amongst the flowers any of those abnormal and in a sense un- natural developments which the selective skill of the gardener enables him to produce. The "modesty of nature" has been carefully preserved throughout, and although there Fe none of those scenic effects which more extensive grounds permit of, there are many features of the gardens which strike one as very fair imitations of nature's handiwork. Of some of the rock-work this may be said, and the luxuriant growth of shrubs and creepers which encircles the pond is suggestive of mountain, stream, and lake. The arbours and covered seats, so useful as shelters from the hot sun or inclement weather, have been very tastefully designed, and if it Gannet be said of them, as of Titania's bower, that they are " Quite over-canopied with lush woodbine, With sweet musk-loses and with eglantine," it can at least be said that when they are at their best they almost deserve the poetical description of the favourite resting-place of the Queen of the Fairies. The sight of such appropriate types of rural beauty and grace as the fox-glove among the flowers and the mountain-ash among the trees and shrubs will also call up in many minds pleasing memories of wood- land and mountain rambles. Side by side and as a kind of complement of these natural beauties Mr. Green, the skilful head gardener, gives us what may not inappropriately be called the embellishments of art, such as mathematically shaped parterres planted with the choicest and prettiest flowers both oxotic and indigenous; smooth well-kept lawns, and green- houses filled with the rarer and more delicate kinds of flowers. On the whole it may safely be augured that so long as Warrington possesses a park and gardens so well-situated and so attractive it will never, to again quote quaint old Thomas Fuller, want its " obeervables.' That they are fairly appreciated by people of all grades and ages it only needs a walk through the grounds on a fine afternoon or evening to prove. It is therefore satisfactory to see that the Town Council seems disposed to be generous in its dealings with this part of the town's property, and probably not even the most captions critic of muni- cipal expenditure would deny that it was acting in the best interests of the ratepayers in voting at its last meeting a very small subsidy to the bands which play in the Park; and certainly Mr. F. Monks and those other gentlemen who are assisting him to en- hance the musical attractions of the people's pleasure grounds could not readily have hit upon a more un- exceptionable way of benefitting their fellow-towns- men.

Packets ONE PENNY and Unwards.—ildrt LORD CARNARVON AND IRISH TRADE DEPRESSION.—A deputation from the Dublin Chamber of Commerce, headed by Sir Richard Martin, presented a congratulatory address to Lord Carnarvon, who, in replying, expressed his regret at the depression in Irish trade, and said while there were cases where the Government might grant loans, in others it would be against the interests of the community. Trade had suffered from English policy in former days, and conse- quently had strong claims, and he trusted some temedies would he applied.

SIR C. DILKE ON THE FRANCHISE ACTS—OiI Saturday night, at the Reform Club, London, a banquet was given to Sir C. Mike, who has belonged to the club for many years. Mr. S. Morley, M.P., presided.—Sir Charles Dilke, in re- sponding to the toast of his health, referred to the Redistri- bution of Seats Bill. He did not wish to reopen controver- sies which had come to an end, but he thought it only right to say that he did not reeard with uniform suspicion the plan of treating any question of agreement between the two•sides. The essential point which should be had in view was that of the country's gain. They should all re- joice that the agreement entered into on this occasion gave I rise to no hot controversy, and was by universal admission carried into effect not only in the letter but in the spirit. The only personal remark upon the transfer of power effected by the bill which he would make was that it had greatly increased the Parliamostary weight of four parts of the United Kingdom, which contained a large share of the intelligence and enterprise of the country—he meant the metropolis, the South of Scotland, the West Riding of Yorkshire, and the county of Lancashire. (Hear, hear.) One of the most amusing historical facts connected with English representation had to do with the last county which he had named. How strange it seemed to think of the days when Sussex was the iron comity and Lancashire was a sort of sleepy Hollow. He once saw it stated in a little journal which deals with antiquarian matters that for five whole reigns the sheriffs of Lancashire reported that there were in the whole county of Lancashire no cities or boroughs which were wealthy enough to afford the cost of two shillings a day which was then involved by representa- tion in rarliament. The present Parliament and Mr. Glad- stone's seeond Administration were not likely to be forgot- ten in the history of this country when it was remembered that they had increased the electorate by two fifths, that they had trebled the weight in Parliament of Lancashire, of the West Riding, and of the metropolis. (Cheers.) div.p: dition, could not read or write, but he was only employed temporarily, and the aocident did not take place when he was en duty. The Inspector of Mines had visited thp col- liery in order to ensure the future use of safety lamps, and in deference to his opinions safety lamps are in future to be exclusively used instead of naked lights ; indeed, they are now being used, and regulations against smoking were being enforced. He would rather say nothing more on the sub- ject until he had received the report of the counsel who had attended the inquest. Lrerecy.—ln reply to Lord Algernon Percy, Mr. A. J. BALFOuIt saki that as the Lunecy Act Amendment Bill was not being proceeded with, he proposed to bring in a short bill to amend the existing state of the law as to the detentionin workhouses of persons supposed to be insane, pending the confirmation of their mental condition and their removal to certified lunatic asylums. M. O'BRIEN'S CONTEMPT OF COURT.—Mr. MCCOAN, on rising to ask a question as to the non-enforcement of the order of the Queen's Bench Division of the High Court of Justice in Ireland imposing a fine of £5OO on Mr. William O'Brien, M.P., for contempt of court, was received with a storm of derisive cheers from the Parnellite members.—Mr. SEXTON, amidst lead cheers from the same quarter, asked whether it was in order for the hon, member to repeat a question which he had asked before and to which he had re- ceived an answer that the Government were not responsible for a matter which lay entirely within the jurisdiction of the court ?—The SPEAKER said that probably the Minister to whom the cuestion was put would say whether it had already bees put and answered. (Laughter.)—Sir WM. HART DYKE said that this was not the first question the hon. member had asked on the subject. In answer to it ha had only to say that there was no record of the matter in his office, and therefore he was not able to say whether the facts were as suggested by the hon, member in his question. (Cheers.) " FILTHY " LITERATURE A LITTLE SCENE. Mr. STAvELEY HILL, in putting his question in reference to the sale of certain literature in the streets of London, repu- diated the use of the namby-pamby word "indelicate," which had been substituted for the word "filthy," which he used in giving notice of his question. He preferred to speak of the obscene literature. (Hear, hear.)—Sir R. CROSS said if this question referred to what appeared in a newspaper a short time ago he had nothing to add to the answer he had already given. If obscene literature was being spread abroad, those who spread it abroad would do so at their peril.—Mr. STAVELEY HILL: Is the right hon. gentleman aware that illustrated copies of the articles are now selling? —Mr. ONSLOW : If the right hon. gentleman is not aware of that, then I beg to hand him a copy of the publication. (The hon. member handed a paper across the bench, but ithe Home Secretary, shaking his bead, declined to touch it. Mr. Onslow then dropped it on the front bench by the side of the right hon. gentleman, and went on to invite him to say whether it was not against order and decency in the streets to allow such foul prints to be sold. Sir R. Cross made no I reply, and handed back the paper. Mr. Onslow would not take it, and it was flung en the floor by Sir Michael Hicks- Beach amid laughter.) MEDICAL RELIEF DISQUALIFICATION BILL.—On the motion to go into Committee en this Bill, Mr. COURTNEY moved that the House could not approve of a measure which removed an incentive to independence and fundamentally changed the principle of the Poor Law, under which pauper- ism had steadily diminished since 1834.—Mr. C. S. READ seconded the amendment, because he regarded the bill as a direct attack on one of the essential principles of the poor law. He pointed out that there would be great difficulty in giving practical effect to the clauses by which it was pro- posed to make the measure applicable to the registration list of the present year, and expressed great doubt as to the large number of the new electorate who, according to its promoters, would, but for this bill, be disqualified under the operation of the exising law. He cared little for a few thousand paupers, more or less, being added to the fran- chise, but he entertained very.strongly the opinion that no pauper ought to be regarded as a capable citizen.— Mr. RATHBONE hoped the Government would limit the operation of the bill to one or two years, and next session appoint a strong Committee to inquire thoroughly how the beneficial arrangements which existed in some parts of the country might be carried out generally.—The debate was continued by Sir F. Milner. Mr. Bryce, Sir H. James, Mr. H. Davey, and other bon. members.—Mr. COLLINGS wanted to know ehy gratuitous medical assistance in country places should be more reprehensible than the assistaece in town hospitals, which were often supported out of the rates.—Mr LABOUCHERE could not help expressing his re- spectful sympathy with the Government. They might be good men or not, but they were certainly struggling with adversity. There was no other instance of a Government having been so utterly discredited within a fortnight after entering office. (Cheers.) The country ought to understand that whenever a Liberal Government passed a good measure in the House of Commons the Tory majority in the other Chamber threw it out, but adopted it afterwards when their own party came into office. Then they were able to say, " Look how good we are, and what a deep interest we have in the country." (Laughter.) Of course the present Government would pass the measure in any case, but it was only in order to retain their position as " dummy " Ministere. ("Oh, oh," and cheers.)— The CHANCELLOR of the EXCHEQUER said the Government had introduced the bill because they thought it necessary. (Ironical cheers from the Opposition).—Mr. HILL explained his reasons for supporting the bill, instead of opposing it as he had done previously.—The House divided—for Mr. Courtney's amendment, 22; aga flat, 226-204.--The House then went into Committee on the bill.—A long discussion ensued on various amendments, in which several members took part. The House continued sitting until a late hour. HOUSE OF LORDS.—WEDNESDAY.

Their Lordships met at half .past four o'clock. ROYAL ASSENT—The Royal assent was given by commis- sion to 34 public and private bills, including the East India Loan Bill, Northwich Local Board Bill, St. Helens and Wigan Junction Railway Bill, Southport Improvement Bill, Bradford Waterworks and Improvement Bill, Manches- ter City Extension Bill, and the Whitehaven Town and Harbour (Incorporation) Bill. The Lord Commissioners were the Lord Chancellor, the Marquis of Exeter, and Lord Bar- rington. The only other peers present were the Earl of Wemyse and Lord Herries. The House adjourned at a quarter to 5 o'clock. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—WEDNESDAY. The Speaker took the chair at twenty minutes past 'twelve o'clock. . .

THE DOCNTY FORCE IN IRELAND.—MT. PEAS?, in the absence of Mr. Parnell. asked for details of the new distri- bution of the County Force in Ireland.—Sir W. Thar- DYSE was unable to give the details asked for. The late Government bad not entirely disposed of the matter, and the great pressure of public business bad prevented Lord Carnarvon dealing with it. THE SALE OF OBSCENE LITERATITRE.—Mr. ONSLONY called the attention of the Home Secretary to the sale of indecent prints under the heading " The Pall Mall Illustrated," and asked was there no power in the Executive to step /such sale 7—Sir R. CROSS repeated what he said yesterday, that the publishers of obscene publications acted at their peril. Whatever motives mighttite pleaded for the articles pub- lished in the first instance, nothing but evil could result front these pictorial publications, and special orders had ben given the police to watch these publications with a view to taking such proceedings as proper legal opinion might ad- ,vise. (Hear, hear.) SUPPLY : THE TUBBERCLURRY CASE.—In Committee of Suppply on the Civil Service Estimates, upon the vote to complete the sum of £89,206 for law charges and criminal prosecutions in Ireland, Mr. SEXTON asked whether the Government would instruct the law officers of the Crown to institute a prosecution for perjury against John Moran, the approver in the Tabberciurry case, and one for conspiracy against Mr. Randall Paton, solicitor, the resident magistrate, and the police detective engaged in the magisterial investi- gation. The horn gentleman went once more and at great length into all the details of this case, asserting that it fur- nished evidence that the system of government in Ireland was e vast conspiracy from the Viceroy in Dublin Castle down to the lowest policeman.—Mr. SULLIVAN. who fol- lowed, also complained of the system of government which had appeared under the regime of the late Government, and urged that the new Adminiettation should inaugurate a new and better era, which, while not requiring that jastic, should be set aside, would tend to produce greater respect for the law and a more contented and peaceful state of i things throughout the whole of Ireland.—After some re- marks from Mr. P. J. Power and Mr. Marum Mr. Deasy spoke in terms strongly condemnatory of the system of jury packing. After a few observations from Mr. Corbett, the ATTORNEY GENERAL for IRELAND, replying generally to the speecbes of the Irish members who had initiated and taken part in the debate, expressed his be- lief that as far as both judges and juries were concerned in the various cases that had afforded matter for unfayourable comment, they had done their duty honestly and to the ,beat of their ability. With reference to the prosecution asked for in the Tabberourry case, he was unable to promise such a procedure, is he was of opinion that no indictment either for perjury Or conspiracy could be sustained on the information supplied to hon. members as brought forward In that debate.—Mr. WeracEE, the late Attorney-General for Ireland, justified the action of the late Irish Executive, . and endorsed the view biked by the present law officers of the Crewn asi to the futility and inexpediency of any such f''°urtrerads w greed to.—On the vote to seaus. saisoknedthfeorviontetbweaTsaabbercurry cum.—After some complete the sum of £78,677 for the Irish Land Commis- sion, Colonel Covrannsr complained that the provision for the erection and repair of labourers' cottages in Ireland had been greatly neglected by the local bodies to whom the duty of seeing to the execution of the work was entrusted.— The debate was continued by Mr. Wearthy, M.P., Mr. P. J. Power, and Sir P. O'Brien, the latter of whom was inter- rupted by the entrance of the Black Rod, who desired the attendance of the Speaker (who in the meantime bad re- sumed the chair) and the members of the House in the • House of Lords, to hear the Ittyal assent given to certain • Acts.
