there was no confirmation of the news of the death of the Mandi.

Ihe House adjourned at 5-58. HOUSE OF LORDS.—THIIRSDAY. The Lord Chancellor took his seat on the woolsack at twenty minutes after four o'clock. MISCELLLNEOUS.—Tbe Stalybridge and Mossley Gas Bill was read a third time and passed, with amendments. In committee on the Submarine Telegraph Cables Bill the Marquis of Tweedale protested against the measure, which, he said, was introduced without consulting the owners of the various cables. The Duke of Richmond proposed an amendment to provide that the owners of a telegraph cable should not be liable ander the bill tot damages to the cable of another company whilst endeavoutini; to repair their own. The proposal was agreed to, and the bill passed through committee. The Lord Chancellor of Ireland submitted ad- ditional clauses to the Land Purchase (Ireland) Bill on the measure coming up on report, and the report was adopted. _ _ . . . .
Their Lordships adjourned at twenty minutes past seven,
HOUSE OF COMMONS.-TRUSSDAY.

The speaker took the chair at four o'clock. QUESTIONS.—Mr. BOURKE confirmed the report that nego- tiations are in progress for the issue of the new Egyptian loan. He added that the statement that the whole of the Great Powers had given their consent to the raising of the loaa was substantially correct.—Tbe CHANCELLOR of the EXCHEQI7ER, who was questioned as to the mission of Sir H. D. Wolf, said he had no information to give to the House, as the matter was not yet complete.—Mr. BOURKE stated that a telegram had reached the Foreign Office from Cairo mentioning that Brigadier General Grenfell, who was on the Nile, telegraphed that the report of the MandPs death seemed to be generally confirmed, and a shiek, who had ar- rived at Assouan, had spoken of having attended the MandPs funeral. The news of his death was universally believed in and around DOngOla.—The CHANCELLOR of the EXCHEQUER moved a resolution expressing the just sense the House entertained of the exemplary manner in whioh Captain Gossett had discharged the duties of Sergeant-att. Arms for nearly fifty years.—Sir W. HancounT seconded the motion, which was supported by Mr. PARNELL, and tarried non. con.

An inquest was opened on board H.M.S. Heck at Ply- mouth on Wednesday on the bodies et David Jones, aged 50, second mate ; and Miss Minnie Houldbrook. of Hendon, passenger on board the Cheerful. David Houghton, able seaman, stated that he was on deck at the time of the col- lision, having relieved the middle watch at eight belts (4 a.m.) The weather woe foggy, but slightly clearing, and it was possible to see a ship's length ahead. The Cheerful's whistle was blowing just before the collision, but he heard no other whistle or foghorn—Jacob Greer, who was at the helm, said be was warned by the look-ont man af the Recta's approach, and ported his helm, but the Hecla'a helm was at the same time starboarded, thus causing the collision.—The inquest was adjourned. The two bodies were afterwards brought ashore in coffins which had been made by the ship's carpenter of the Hecla. All the pas- sengers lost everything they had no board. Late on Tuesday afternoon the owners in Liverpool of the steamer Cheerful received a telegram from the captain of the vessel at Plymouth, stating that the number of lives lost by the disaster was twelve, viz., nine of the passengers and three of the crew. This telegram gave the names of the unfortunate people as under :—Passengers: Miss Hol- brook, Daniel A. Harrison, P. Bernard, Mr. and Mrs. Chad- wick, of Manchester; Mr. Stevens and Mr. Neal, London ; Mr. Hartiese, Falmouth; and Mr. Jones. Crew: David Jones, second mate, belonging to Llauelly ; Walter Long, boy, London ; and Miss Connolly, stewardess, Liver- pool. The number of passengers who sailed in the steamer from London was 35, and of these 13 landed at Plymouth and did not again join the vessel. Two others embarked at Falmouth, but the owners have not had the record of those who went on board at Plymouth.

the good feeling displayed by the United States Go- vernment in watching the frontier during the rising. The new Governor-General estimated the total expen- diture for the year for all departments at 37,000,000 dollars. Before rising the House passed 95 bills, including the Franchise Bill and a bill for the relief of the Canadian Psicific Railway from the statutory mortgage of 30,000,030 dollars. • IHE CHOLERA IN SPAIN.—ALARMING INCREASE. MADRID, SATURDAY —The official bulletin issued this morning shows that 1,328 cases and 621 deaths occurred in Spain yesterday. MADRID, SLINDAY.—Tbere were 1,886 cases and 718 deaths yesterday. MADRID, Moirnmr.—There were 1,850 cases and 761 deaths! yesterday. Details :—Alicante (province), 141, 51; Valencia .(capital), 101, 34, (province), 538, 253; Toledo (capital), 1 death, (province), 89, 35; Teruel (province). 58, 18; Castellan (capital), 6,4, (province), 212, 65 : Cuenca (capital), 33, 20, (province), 26, 18 ' • Murcia (capital), 5,3, (province), 206,81 ; Jean (province), 53, 31; Saragossa (province), 356, 133; Aranjaez (province), 1. 3; Ciempazuelas, 4 cases; Madrid (neighbouring villages), 9,3, (capital), 12,8. Some cares are reported from the provinces of Granada and Palencia.
MADRID, TIIESDAY.— The official bulletin yesterday morning showed that there were 2,243 cases and 876 deaths in Spain yesterday. .

M;SDRI-D, WEDSESDAY.—The official cholera bulletin issued this mornine reports that there were 1,752 cases and 685 deaths in Spain yesterday. A Central News telegram, dated Madrid, Thursday morn- ing, states :—During the past twenty-four boars there were throughout Spain 2,262 fresh cases of cholera and 960 deaths. The official returns, for the first time, admit the existence ef cholera in the city of Barcelona, although it has been suspected for some time past. Two cases occurred there yesterday. DEATH OF GENERAL GRANT.

NEw Yong, WEDNESDAY, i a.m.—General Grent is rapidly sinking ; it is feared be will hardly survive 24 hours. It is thought the end has come at last. All his re- lations have been summoned to his bedside, those at a dis- tance being telegraphed for. Dr. Douglas has called in additional medical aid. Crowds surround the General's house. Tne bulletins are wired te the newspapers directly they are posted outside. The injecticn of morphia has had little good effect. NEW Yong, THURSDAY MouNtxn.—General Grant suc- cumbed at eight o'clock this morning. p easing away after a night of exhaustion. All his relatives were with him at the time. Although his death was fully expected, yet the news has caused a general shock among the public. The city bells are tolling and the flags are flying at half- mast. Universal sorrow is expressed at the death of the General.

THE POPE AND THE ARCHBISHOP OF DUBLIN. BOME, WEDNESDAY.-Dr. Walsh, the newly-appointed Archbishop of Dublin, had a private audience of the Pope to-day. His Holiness conferred with Dr. Walsh regarding the political situation in Ireland, and, while recognising the difficult position of the Archbishop, recommended him to exercise prudence. ENGLAND AND TURKEY.

CONSTANTINOPLE, TOESDAS.—The Grand Vizier had an interview to-day with Horsart Pasha, in the course of which the former declared that he recognised the necessity for Turkey of an alliance with England, and that the conclusion of such an alliance was now easier than before.

div.head: 'DeIi—Dia—I...RELIEF BILL—DEFEAT OF THE GOVERNMENT.
div.p: 'DeIi—Dia—I...RELIEF BILL—DEFEAT OF THE GOVERNMENT.

On consideration of the Medical Relief Disqualification Removal Bill, Mr. Montessori contended that persons re- ceiving medical relief from friendly and provident societies should not be placed on the same level as those who made no provision for themselves whatever.—Mr. COLLINGS moved a new clause to the effect that the term medical or surgical assistance should include all medical and surgical attendance and all matters and things supplied by or on the recommendation of the medical officer having authority to give such attendance and recommendation at the expense of any poor ratt.—Mr. BALFOUR, on behalf of the Government, urged that if the House carried the amendment they would make the relieving officer a political agent, with immense power either to strike a man off or put him on the register of voters. The right hon. gentleman stated that it was the intention of the Government to exclude Scotland and Ireland from the operation of the bill. If the bon. gentleman forced the amend- ment on the Houser then if any serious accident happened to the farther progress of the bill en him and his friends alone would rest the responsibility.—Sir W. HARCOURT said it was the opinion of the great majority of the House that persons who received medical relief when sick ought net to be disfranchised, and therefore they ought to act upon that principle and not interpose fine-drawn distinctions of this character. He contended that without the proposed clause the bill would be practically inoperative.—Mr. MACAUTNEY remarked that apparently the principle of action was that whatever was loudly advocated by one party should be adopted by the otner.—Mr. E. CLARKE said if ever there was a bill over which the front bench had no right of con- trol it was this, and therefore the Government were not at liberty to threaten the House that they would abandon the bill if the House adopted a view different from theirs of the interpretation to be placed upon one phrase in the bill. —Mr. HENEAGE ob- served that if the Government threw out the bill they would not make much further progress with their other business.—Mr. BELL announced that the only course he could pursue was to walk out when the division was taken, and in accordance with this intimaton the hon. member, with Mr. C. S. Read and other Conservative members left the House. Upon a division being taken the proposed new clause was carried by 180 to 130, showing a majority of 50 against the Government—The CHANCELLOR of the EXCHEQUER then stated that the matter was one of great importance, and the Government could not uader the circumstances take any responsibility with regard to the measure. Sir W. HARCOURT rejoined that under the circumstances he supposed that the responsibility rested with the majority of the House, whose property this bill was. He asked the House to allow the bill now to be read a third time.—The new clause having been added to the bill, Mr. J. COLLINS pro- ceeded to move the amendments standing in the name of Mr. BeaForrn..—At the suggestion of Mr. HEALY a clause was added to secure that the bill should have no disqualify- ing effect in Ireland.—Mr. RAMSAY moved the recommittal of the bill in order that the hon. member for Dumbarton might move an amendment.—The motion was agreed to.— , The House having gone into committee, Mr. ORR EWING moved an amendment to the second clause intended to ex- clude Scotland from the bill.—Sir W. Hesicouar supported the inclusion of Scotland.—Upon a division the amendment to exclude Scotland was rejected by 125 to 30 votes, and the bill as amended was reported to the House.—Mr. J. Coaarnos then moved that the bill be read a third time.—As there were several dissentients, the Speaker ruled that a day must be fixed for the third read- ing.—Sir W. Haucounr wished to know what facilities the Government intended to give.—The CHANCELLOR of the EXCHEQUER replied that the Government could not put the bill before Sepply.—Mr. LABOUCHERE asked if the Govern- ment regarded this as a Ministerial crisis, and, if so, whether they would follow the precedent of a few weeks ago, and having gone through the orders adjourn.—Mr. CHAMBERLAIN pressed for information as to whether the Government would oppose the third reading.— Lord R. CuuscuraL replied that the bill would take its place with the other orders, and come on in the ordinary course; and the CHANCELLOR of the EXCHEQUER, upon being further pressed, said he really had not had time to consult his colleagues on the matter.—Mr. HENEACIE moved the adjournment of the debate in order to give the Govern- ment time to make up their minds.—Sir M. HICKS•BEACH said he must consult with his colleagues, aad would be pre- pared to make a statement at half-past four o'clock next day. The motion for adjournment having been withdrawn to-day was fixed for the third reading. The House then went into Committee on the Customs and Inland Revenue Bill.

div.head: COLLISION WPM A WAR SHIP. A LIVERPOOL STEAMER BUNK: 12 LIVES
div.p: COLLISION WPM A WAR SHIP. A LIVERPOOL STEAMER BUNK: 12 LIVES

At a late hour on Tuesday evening her Majesty's torpedo ship Fleela arrived in Plyenouth Sound from Ireland, having on board several of the passengers of the steamship Cheer- ful, of Liverpool, with which she had been in collision at four o'clack that morning off the Land's End. The Cheer- ful, which had a large number of passengers on Board, was on the voyage from Plymouth to Liverpool, and after get- ting round the Land's End on Tuesday morning she ran into a fog so dense that her speed was reduced. The cap- tain states that he had his fog signals constantly sounding. Suddenly he was struck amidships by the Llecla with such terrific force that the ship was cut nearly in two. In about five minutes the Cheerful went down, carrying with her twelve or thirteen of the crew and passevgers in spite of the splendid efforts which were madeefrom the Heels to save all hands. Two persons died on board the Hec Houldbrook, of Hendon, and David Jones. the second mate. The surviving passengers were landed late at night at Plymouth, and they all express their deep gratitude to officers and crew of'the Ilecla for the efforts made to save their lives. The list of passengers saved from the Cheerful, who are now staying at Parley's Hotel, Plymouth, is as follows L. Beckhofer. 3, Red Gross-street, London; Herbert Dove, 230, St. Paul's Road, Highbury, London ; A. H. Wood, 16, Redcliffe Road, London; Edgar Percy Carter, 61, Basing- hall-street, London; John Trueman, Lower Broughton-road, Manchester; W. T. Cotton, New Romney; Mr. and Mrs. Metcalf, London; Mr. D. A. Harrison, jun.; Dr. and Master Houldlerook, Hendon, Middlesex; Mr. A. Needham, Church. street, Manchester ; W. E. Simpson, Tamworth-street, Hulme, Manchester; Mr. J. B. Choc! ton, Upper Brook- street, Manchester ; and Herbert White, Ditton, near Widnes. Thirteen other passengers of the Cheerful left the steamer at Plymouth on Monday morning, having ex- perienced an unpleasant run from London. An elderly gentleman and his two daughters went aboard at Plymouth and left at Falmouth. Mr. Needham' of Manchester, had his nose broken and his eye contused through coming in contact with wreckage. Both ML Needham and Mr. True- man went down with the vessel. The latter had gone on deck on hearing the crash, but had returned below for his watch and msnev. He was drawn down with the sinking ship, and had, with Mr. Needham, to swim about until picked up. Mr. Wood was drawn down with the Cheer( al, but, although unable to swim, he drifted towards the Reda and was rescued. Mr. Chorlton was in his berth at the time of the collision, and, having got on deck, be returned for a valuable pair of opera glasses which after all, he was oblised to leave. He then jumped overhbard and swans about until picked up by the Hecla's boats. Mrs. Metcalf was saved by securing a barrel and a cow's hide which were floating about And by which she supported herself until picked up. The Cheerful was about 640 tons register, and about 1,300 tons gross. The list of efficers and crew saved ices follows: Ciptain Stevens, Liverpool; Mr. Crosby, chief officer, Dublin ; Mr. Drake, first engineer, Liverpool ; Edwin Venables, second engineer, Liverpool ; John Matthews, second steward, London ; John Stookeley. fireman,. Liverpool ; John Farkey, able seaman, Liverpool; John Connelly, don- keyman, Liverpool • T. Hughes, able seaman, Liverpool ; W. Dorman, cook, itranraer ; Green, able seaman, Liver- pool ; D. Houghton, able seaman, Liverpool ; Iris Kilson, able seaman,Norweglan ; B. M•Nielliable seaman, London; J. Jones, messroom steward, Clapham ; Patrick Darren, fire- man, Liverpool; R. D. Roberts, steward, Liverpool ; John Pugh, fireman, Birkenhead; Thomas Evans, fireman, Sea- combs ; Elias Evans' fireman, Birkenhead; Thomas Causton, cabin boy, London. List ol officers and crew drowned :—Mrs Connolly, stewardess, widow; William Long, cabin boy, Croydon; David Jones, second mate, Llanrystyd, near Aberystwith. •

div.head: FOREIGN NEWS.
div.p: FOREIGN NEWS.
ENGLAND AND RUSI[A.

mr.a, SerustaY.—The Afghan Boundary Commission is now encamped at Tunian, 17 miles distant from Herat. CALCUTTA, SUNDAY.—The telegrams received from Eng- land and from the Boundary Commission, stating that the Russians were reinforcing their troops along the frontier caused some anxiety, and had a slightly depressing effect on the Money Market last week. Confidence has not, how- ever, revived. It is generally believed that the motions of the Russians were mainly precautionary measures in view of the recent change of Ministry, and that the danger of col- lision is now over. The Afghans are said to be busily en- gaged strengthening the fortifications of Herat, and it was doubtless with the object of assisting in this work that the Commission approached that city. Sir J. Ridgeway when last heard of was about to leave the Zarmast heights for Tunian,l7 miles from Herat. The Russians are reported to be strengthening Penjdeh, and to have appointed a new governor of that place.—Tones. VIENNA, Morenay.—M. Lesser declares to everyone who likes to listen to him that the possession of Herat has be- come a necessity for Russia, and endeavours to show that its occupation would not justify complaint, still less war. Some people therefore affect to fear that Russia will occupy Herat by surprise before England can succeed in fortifying it. The St. Petersburg correspondent gives an abstract of the Havas Agency's statement of Lord Salisbury's inten- tions respecting the new Afghan frontier line, and says that the Russian Government contest. England's right to nego- tiate with Afghanistan upon the subject. If England be entitled to meddle with Russo-Afghan affairs on the northern frontier, Russia claims the same right on the southern. _ _

THITERDAY —lt is currently reported that Rus- sian officers have been granted permission to drill the Coreans, and, further, that Russian troops have been authorised to occupy temporarily Quelpart Island. Ili and Kaskgaria continue in a disturbed state, and the Chinese Government is sending reidforzements thither.

div.head: ENGLAND AND EGYPT.
div.p: ENGLAND AND EGYPT.

BERLIN, MONDAY.—According toe telegram received by the Kolnische Zeitung from Constantinople' Lord SalisbnrV has informed Musurus Pasha, the Turkish Ambassador to England, that it is his intention to continue in Egypt the policy of his predecessors, and to evacuate the country when the time for doing so is favourable. He will, however, decide upon nothing without the assent of the rest of the European Powers, including that of the Sultan. ATTACK ON KASSALA.-3,000 REBELS KILLED. CAIRO, TUESDAY.—Capt. Chermside telegraphs that the rebels attacked the suburbs of Kassala in great force on June 15th and Mb. After severe fightini, they were re- pulsed by the garrison, who killed 3,000 of the rebels and captured 1,000 oxen, 1,000 sheep, and 700 rises. CAIRO, TUESDAY.—It is understood here that the British Government is in hopes of an arrangement being made with King John of Abyssinia for the relief of the Kassala Gar- rison by Ras Aloula. the Abyssinian General. M. OLIVIER PAIN REPORTED TO BE LIVING.

CAIRO, TVESDAY.—The Bosphore Egyptien publishes a letter from an engineer named Berti, who escaped from Berber. He declares that M. Olivier Pain is living and at Berber. THE REPORTED DEATH OF THE MAHDI.—

_ FURTHER CONFIRMAIIO 4. CAIRO, WEDNESDAY.—Major.General•Grenfell telegraphs from Assonan to-day that messengers who have arrived from Gabra report the death of the Mandi from smallpox on Jane 29. . .

CAIRO, THRIISDAY.—A telegram received tonlay from Major General Grenfell states that the Handak merchant, who, on the 6th inst., reported the Mabdi's death, has seen several shieks from Khartoum, Ivhe affirm positively that the Mandi died of smallpox on June 22. One of the shies asserted that he witnessed the Mandi'e funeral. MILITARY AC TIVITY IN INDIA.

Catarrra, MONDAY.—Two great camps of exercise will probably aseemble for their manoeuvres early in December. Forces composed af 20,000 men each will be formed at Delhi and Umballa, and will move on each other. A na- tive contingent of 5,000 troops will be attached to each force.

div.head: EARTHQUAKE IN INDIA.
div.p: THE EARTHQUAKE IN INDIA.

CALCUTTA, MONDAY.—According to the latest reports, the earthquake on Tuesday last caused altogether 70 deaths in Bengal. Of these 40 occurred at Sherpore, near Bogree, and 11 near Rajbari. Four Mahometans were killed by the fall of a mosque at Gorindpore, and four Hindoos lost their lives at Dumdum. Considerable damage was done to property at Mymensing and elsewhere. SIMLA, TUESDAY.—TweIve shocks of earthquake—one very severe—were felt in Cashmere on the 16th inst. TRAGEDY IN INDIA.—SEVERAL NATIVE OFFICERS SHOT.

BOMBAY TUESDAY.—A. soldier in the Madras Native In- fantry, incited, it is supposed, by having been reduced to to the ranks, shot dead several of the native officers and fired at Lieut. Carnegy, the adjutant of the regiment, who, however, escaped unhurt. -

div.head: 1,000 PERSONS FOR HUMAN SACRIFICES.
div.p: 1,000 PERSONS FOR HUMAN SACRIFICES.

, PARIS. MONDAY.—The journal Le Malin today publishes intelligence from Lagos, dated May 15th, stating that the troops of the King of Dahomey made a sodden descent on May 10th on the village in the a eighbourbood of Porto Novo, which are under French protection, and massacred many of the inhabitants. They also carried away 1,000 prisoners for human sacrifice% STRANGE SrREET SCENE.

PARIS TrEsnex.—An extraordinary and tragic accident has occurred near Paris. A horse was seen running wildly along the road to St. Germain, the vehicle to which the animal was attached being enveloped in flames. Several persons having succeeded in catching the horse, a dreadful sight presented itself. In the bottom of the burning vehicle the body of the driver was found reduced to an almost in- distinguishable heap of cinders. It is supposed that the man, having lit his pipe, fell asleep, and that the burning ashes set fire to the old woodwork. GREAT FIRE IN
F RANCE.

ROTTEN, MOM:ay.—A seridus fire broke out here this naorninK in Rue d'Amiens. Six houses, some of which are very old and of considerable interest, have been completely destroyed. FRIGHTFUL EXPLOSION IN FRANCE.

Pants, TUESDAY, 645 P m.—A telegram from the Mayor of Aides (Puy de Dome) announces that an alarming ex- plosion has occurred among some cases of gunpowder and come barrels of petroleum. The number of killed and injured is not yet known, but several persons are mis- sing.

div.head: PIOHTING IN CAMBODIA.
div.p: PIOHTING IN CAMBODIA.

PARIS, WRDNFSDAY.—A ccording to letter=s from Cambo- dia to the 15th ult., published this evening by the Temps, a French detachment of 110 men captured Fort Angko on June 5 at the point of the bayonet, after four unsuccessful attacks. The enemy fled, leaving 30 men killed and a con- siderable quantity of stores. The French loss Was four men wounded. The rebels subsequently retired in the direction of the Gulf of Siam to the province of Rampot, pursued by the French troops. It is also announced that some agita- tion prevailed in Northern Cochin China, and that flying columns of French troops were scouring the district, and had already received the submission of several of the rebel bands. The Temps also publishes a letter from Saigon stat- ing that the revolt was not serious, but had done immense harm to commerce in that district.

div.head: DISASTROUS FIRE IN FRANCE.
div.p: DISASTROUS FIRE IN FRANCE.

PARIS, THURSDAY.—Another c-a-la-mit.;:i;-"r"eportecl this morning to be added to the lone list of those which have recently occurred in France. A fire broke out yesterday at Claraford, near Aix, and sixteen houses were destroyed. Several of the inhabitants were burned to death. SOUTH. AFRICA.

DURBAN, MONDAY.--It is stated that there are grounds for beiieving that many of the titles to farms in SteDeland were obtained by fraud. The native chiefs and people have applied for a land settlement, and the burghers of Stellaland have asked for is formal inquiry before a final settlement is sanctioned. 'lle Secretary of State some months ago pledged himself that a settlement should be made by a British officer. If now by a hasty annexation an alteration be made in the relationship of t'e.e Imperial officers to the land question, that pledge will be endangered and other complications will ensue. General Warren has returned to Ste'!eland, and he was to proceed to Vryburg to-day. Mont- so has submitted to Sir C. Warren a letter to the Queen conveying an urgent appeal that the direct rule of England over the country may be continued. THE REBELLION IN CANADA.

TORONTO, MONDAY.—The volunteers returning here from the scene cf the recent rebellion in the North-west have met with an enthusiastic reception. A banquet has also been arranged in their honour. The trial of Louis Hiel, the leader of the rebellion, commenced here to-day. General Middleton was summoned as a witness.

OTTAWA., MONDAY.—Tha Dominion Parliament was pro- rogued by the Marquis of Lansdowne. His Excellency con- gratulated the members on the suppression of the recent rebellion in the North-west, and praised the bravery and good conduct of the Canadian troops. He also referred to
r the tidal capacity to the extent of 180,000 cubic yards.— The opponents refrained from commenting on the new plans and clauses at the present stage.

THE ROYAL MARRIAGE. POEM BY LORD TENNYSON. TO H. R. H. PRINCESS IiEA.TRICE. Two Suns of Love make day of human life. Whit* else with all its pains and griefs and deaths Were utter darkness—one, the Sun of dawn That brightens thro' the Mother's tender eyes, And warms the child's awakening world and one The later-rising Sun of spousal Love • Which from her household orbit draws the child To move in other spheres. The Mother weeps At that white funeral of the single life. Her maiden daughter's marriage; and her tears Are half of pleasure, half of pain—the child Is happy—ev'n in leaving lur ! but Thou, True daughter' whose all-faithful, filial eyes Have seen the loneliness of earthly thrones, Wilt neither quit the widow'd Crown, nor let This later light of Love have risen in vain, But moving thro' the Mother's home, between The two that love thee, lead a summer life, Swayed by each Love, and swaying to each Love Like some conjectured planet in mid heaven Between two Sans, and drawing down from both The light and genial warmth of doable day. July, 1885 TENNYSON.

div.head: PREPARATIONS.
div.p: THE PREPARATIONS.

The preparations for the wedding of the Princess Beatrice with Prince Henry Maurice of Rattenberg were completed on Wednesday. Her Majesty t',le Queen has superintended all the arrangements, and on Wednesday visited the church at Whippingham, with her daughter and Prince Henry, to finally inspect the decorations that had been designed by the ladies of Bast and West Cowes. Wreaths abound, fes- toons of flowers intermingled with evergreens hang at all points, the monotony of every arch is broken by coils of exotics, and the communion table presents the appearance of a bed of flowers. In the centre of the church, on either side, at the junction of the aisle and the Vanscept, where the pulpit and reading desk stood, two marble columns have been placed, garlanded with rare ferns and blossoms. The entrance to the church is approached thraugh an avenue of shrubs and flowers, behind which are arranged three tiers of crimson-covered seats for the fortunate few holding tickets of admission. Her Majesty on her visit to the church ex- pressed her approval of the work done, and thanked the ladies who had given their services for the purpose. The Lord Chamberlain. accompanied by his several assistants, was present at the Royal inspection, and the concluding arrangements respecting the disposition of visitors in the church was subsequently made. From Whippingbam Church to Osborne House through a winding country lane —the distance is about a mile—and in the fields bordering the road stands have been erected capable of accom- modating a thousand people. A large proportion of the seats have already been secured. Venetian masts are erected at frequent intervals along the route to be taken by the Royal procession, and the crimson coverings of the stands add to the gaiety of the scene. In- side the Royal demesnes marquees of visions colours have been raised, one of them being reserved for the use of the Royal party. Near these stands tents have been provided for the bands of the Royal Marines and the 93rd High- landers. Several other tents for the accommodation of

The guests not of royal blood left at five o'clock, travelling from Cowes in the yacht Osborne to Portsmouth, from whence by special train they were conveyed to London. Her Majesty expressed herself much pleased at the efficient manner in which the Lord Chamberlain's department had carried out the arrange. inents of the ceremony, and personify thanked many offio cials of that office. In the evening there was a farther illti. mination of the grounds at Osborne and a display of fire. works, organised by Mr. James Pain, of London. . The Princess Beatrice is the youngest child of the Quells' and was born 14th April, 1857. THE BRIDE'S DRESSES. It appears to be one of our unwritten social laws that cur Royal brides shall wear nothing but white upon their wed. dint day. The Queen's "going-away " dress was white satin trimmed with swansdown. Part of Her Majesty's wedding dress reappears in the bridal toilette of her young. est daughter, whose sumptuously soft and rich white satin is trimmed with the 136 W historical Honiton lace that was manufactured specially for the youthful sovereign to wear upon her wedding day. The design of this lace was of bush elaborate beauty that it made quite a sensation in the world. of lace-workers forty-five years ago. To its primal beauty is now added the mellowing touch of all those forty-five long years, which have brought to beings sentient so much of grief and change that it seems anomalous that those dainty meshes and delicate stitches should be left by them unharmed.

On Princess Beatrice's wedding gown this lace is beauti. fully draped upon the satin, and at the left side two very' large cheaters of orange-blossems serve as trimming. The front of the skirt is edged with a satin flounce, and over this fall drooping sprays of orange-blossoms, the Honfton hiding the top of the flowers. A panel at either side of the skirt. consisting entirely of orange-blossoms, marks where the hoe draperies terminate. The long and perfectly plain train is made of white satin, and the low bodice has a trimming of lace and a berthe of orange-blossoms. Tee very small sleeves are made entirely of lace, with a cluster of the bridal flowers 0/1 each.

Surely an admirably simple dress for a princess. There are none of the pearl fringes or the gold lace, nor the silver embroideries, nor the self-reliant brocades of which we have heard so much of late, nor any stirfe of war- ring flounces, puffings, headings, and fringes. One OM but appreciate the tasteful contrast with so much ostenta• Lions over-elaboration.

The dress in which our youngest Princess is to drive to Quarr Abbey for her abbreviated honeymoon of eight-and- forty hours is made of pure white cripe-de-chine, embroie dered in the same snowy tint. The froint Is covered with fine old Irish point, which forms a tablier that is caught up at one side; the other ending under a graceful trivet...in made entirely of loops of white watered ribbon. This panel has an effect as of falling water, and in its shade of clear, cold white contrasts with the softer tint of the crêpe- de-chine. The back of the dress, which is draped with finest art, has also its trimmings of crepe-de-chine. A mantle of the same material and trimmed with lace to match the gown accompanies this original and artistic 4. going-away " dress, The trousseau dresses are by no means immoderate in number, comprising more walking costumes and tailor-made gowns, Redfern alone baying made eight, than toilets do- signed for more ceremonious occasions. One of the even• ing dresses is made of very pals blue satin, the front of the skirt being arranged in two large revers, one being placed on either aide of some plain folds of satin. These revers are trimmed al! over with cord and tinsel in yew soft, eale shades of different colours, all graduated rows, with small pendant tassels of cord relieved with gold. The bodice and train are made of striped pale blue satin and silk, the latter being starred with satin dots. The bodice is cut square back and front, and is trimmed with similar faint colours to those upon the revers of the skirt. The elbow sleeves terminate in small dainty folds of pale teue crepe, tied with a festive little satin bow and trimmed with a piece of gold cord. Another evening dress is of printed silk muslin. A very lovely dinner dress is of the palest reAda or mignonette green, the material being the soft, rich faille franeaise, which is in so much favour this season. THE WEDDING PRESENTS. Among the most interesting of the, wedding presents is the gift of the mothers and daughters of the diocese of Winchester—the diocese in which Osborne House is situated. This consists of a handsome bookcase of carved oak, con- taining a complete series of standard English poets. Mrs. Harold Browne, the wife of the Bishop, presented this some time ago on behalf of the donors, whose contributiona ranged from one penny to five shillings, and who repree tented all classes of the people. East Cowes gave four volumes of classical music, handsomely bound in white calf, and embossed with the Royal Arms. Newport also made a presentation of books, consisting of a fine edition of Staunton's Illustrated Shakepere, enclosed in an oak cabinet surmounted by the Newport Arms. Liverpool has given a wedding cake, and it need hardly be said that a very fine cake it is. The ladies of Kent have also subscribed for another cake, said to be a noble affair. It stands in three tiers and is supported by a wreath of lilies and adorned by jessamine, roses, ivy, and passion flowers. There are, we understand, several other cakes presented. The ladiels of Somersetshire have presented a beautiful embroidered eitilt and an album filled with watercolour drawings by members of the Royal Institute; and the ladies of Bristol have eert a linen chest. Windsor, of course, has been to the free. as becomes it. Two of the wedding cakes wete made here. Toe two cakes referred to are six feet high, tier above tier, marvellous elaborations of sugar and satin, pearls and Royal arms, orange-blossoms, and monograms, cupids, angels, and true-lovers' knots. The townsfolk have made several pre. senrations. The ladies of Windsor have subscribed for a massive silver-guilt toilet service and a pair ef candlesticks bearing the monogram and coronet of the Princess, and en- closed in a case of morocco and maroon velvet. A bracelet also is part of the present, and this is set with some 12 or 14 fine brilliants, and is valued at .£3OO. The gentlemen of Windsor and its vicinity have subscribed for the purchase of a diamond bracelet. Eton also has clubbed together. end the Head Master and his assistants have given a magnifirent diamond locket with a sapphire centre ; and the Eton beys, who are always very cordial in their sentiments towards the Royal Family, have also subscribed for a bracelet of dia- monds and pearls. Of course these, like all the rest, were graciously received and gracefully acknowledged. The Princess Beatrice a short time since distributed the certifi- cates to the successful pupils of the No. 3 District Mira- politan Centre of the St. John's Ambulance Association, and was on that occasion presented with a handsome mirror that had been subscribed for by the members of the Associrte tion. The ladies of Kensington have contributed to the costly treasure-gathering a magnificent p;ano, and the stu- dents of Queen's-square have sent a fan exquisitely painted with orange blossoms. All we have said, presents are still pouring in, and even of those which have been received for some time our list, it will be seen, does not profess to be complete. It does not, it will be observed, comprise any article presented by the friends and relatives of the bride, but merely some of those which may be described as indica- tions of cordial regard by the public at large. The jewellery given by several of the royal families of the Continent, and by a larg,e circle of friends and relatives, is said to be no- usually extensive and costly. The members of the Royal household have marked their interest in the marriage of the Princess Beatrice by very liberal and numerous gifts.

The prisoner, who was a omaker, tool: the child out, stating that she was conveying It toits father's, at IVarrington. She returned to her lodgings Without it, and its dead body wasshortly afterwards found in the canal. The jury recom- mended the prisoner to mercy.

THE WESLEYAN CONFERENCE. ELECTION OF PREM. DENT.—The Wesleyan Conference conamencel its annual sessions at Brunswick-place Chapel, Newcastle-on-Tyne, at ball-past nine o'clock on Tuesday morning. About 600 ministers were present, the Rev. D. Greeves, the retiring president occupied the chair, and the following ex-presi- dents were on the platform :—Revs. Dr. James, Birnsicg- harn ; Dr. Osborn, Richmond College; Dr. Rigg, Lon- don; Thomas WCullagh, Liverpool ; Alxonder Macau. ley, London; Ebenezer E. Jenkins, London ; and Cnarles Garrett, Liverpool. after devotional exercises, the Con- ference proceeded to the formal constitution of the Legal Hundred, two vacancies in which have been esue-d by death. The Conference then proceeded to the election of president. There was considerable quiet excitement on the votes being counted. The following was the result :—The Rev. Richard Roberts, 215 (elected) ; Rev. Robert NewtOn young, 136 ; Rev. Benjamin 14ilier, 26. Dr. Young was appointed secretary. Ibis year nearly 700 ministers are exchanging their circuits. The Conference at Newcamte_ on-Tyne resumed business on Wednesday, the newly slee- ted President (Rev. Richard Roberts) in the chair. A con- versation took place on the Criminal Law Amendment 8,11, And a commute' was appointed to draw up a petition to the House of Commons, urging that the measure should be pissed into law forthwith. The strong and unanimous opinion was expressed that the legal age of Protection ought to be raised to 18, but that in no case would prattle opinion t sitisbedif the age were not at least raised to 18. On Thersday an animated discussion took plaze on the sub- ject of the Criminal Law Amendment Bill, and after the Recs. Dr. Rigz, Dr. Stephenson, and others had spoken, a petition to the House of Commons was unanimously adopted, urgently praying that the ago of protection be raised to 18. kr. MUNDELLA made an interesting speech „134 education at Wolverhampton on Monday, , ;11 the occasion of the opening of new School ! •noard offices and a School of Art. He speaks ' Ifith wide and varied knowledge; he has for a generation taken great interest in education, 1 While for the past five years, as the working head of the Education Department, he has gained a reputation of which any Minister nxight well be proud. The report of the past Year of the Committee of Council upon Edu- Cation has just been issued, and, as it bears tile signatures of Lord CARLINGFORD and r. MUNDELLA, it may safely be assumed that this document, which gives such a faith- record of faithful work, was completed before the present Government came into °face. It is satisfactory to observe that there a notable increase in the number of "tesnnols ; in the number of children on the .cgisters ; and in the average attendance. It true that the highest results attainable have is't yet been reached. The report says— ., 'or every too children of school age, for Wilotn 89 seats have been provided, we have o scholars on the registers, and 60 in itt'lY average attendance." The word "only" p, this connection is suggestive; *Part • but for our We cannot but express surprise at the ett. bis.lia.ordmary progress which has been made th,'lni the past fifteen years It is obvious Ike the running is close when. taking one WTOI with another throughout England and th,Les, there are as many as 8o scholars on 511 e registers to every 89 seats provided. It (1i:4.4_1d be remembered that in agricultutal e",.‘ricts where School Boards have had to be th`ablished, and Board Schools built to meet lee requirements of wide areas', it has been , 46'eSsary, or at any rate desirable,"to be in school accommodation of the tta,„'"rig Population. In Berkshire, for in- thrb,ce, there are 4.3,000 places for 36,000 diferen. Then in large towns there is the ~.culty Which results from sectarianism. If bok;hurch school is full to overflowing, it is tet; th sufficient that there is a Roman Catholic P o°l in the neighbourhood that can take - 8- pt urplus. There must be an enlargement, tie another school built, and thus it is that inationalism tends to produce in- .lre-g"tv in school accommodation. The Orav,,.M. SANGAE, in backing up the Giy"genien, who were backing up Sir td e "s 1 UREENALL the other day, is repor- hea) have spoken of Roman Catholicism as uf 6ruisnl ; and if these are the sentiments the qUrchmen we need not be surprised that lic,re is a dividing line in education. Catho- oly„and Dissenters also prefer to send their the `4 children to their own schools, though '„,.re not in the habit, we trust, of speak- tstit;`, those who differ from them as heathens. Sarct"le result as to accommodation is the •theze.--the denominational system tends to SChooling in particular districts.

I Reverting to the speech of Mr. MUNDELLA at Wolverhampton, he made a statement which ought to stagger those who are in the habit of magnifying what the various sects have done in the past for the educa- tion of the masses. He broadly stated that fourteen years ago the majority of the people were without religious and secular education. But he did more than make the statement—he proved it. "In 1869," he said, "the children in average attendance at all the secular schools in the country was 1,063,000 ; in 1879 the number had risen to 2,559,000 ; in 1884_ the number had risen to nearly 4,000,000. On the registers in 1869 there were a little over We million children ; the number at this moment (July) had risen to 5,215,000, which was 167 of the population, or exactly one-sixth." Simi- lar progress has also been made in religious education, Mr. MUNDELLA remarking that he spoke as Chairman of the Sunday School Union when he said he "could testify that about 5,000,000 Sunday School children, mostly more or less educated, were now to be found in the country." It will be seen, therefore, that the parrot-cry as to " Godless education" is not supported by the facts of the case ; but it will continue to be made all the same, facts being altogether at a discount with those who raise parrot-cries in lieu of argument. Another important matter that Mr. MUNDELLA dwelt upon was the need to do "something more for interme- diate education." He added that it was for the middle classes to make the demand, and he was sure that if they made it they would I get it. This is good advice and should be acted upon. At present the lower middle class are being badly treated in the matter of education. The small shopkeeper has no choice in most cases between the ordin- ary elementary school, and a private school, or Grammar School, -where the cost of tuition is from four to ten times that of the National elementary school. He is called upon locally and imperially to pay for education, but he is offered nothing in return. Hitherto the middle-class man simply grumbled at this injustice; it is time he did something more than grumble. Accepting the inevitable as to our system of National Education, he I should demand that something shall be done for him—that provision shall be T.:ad& whereby he can receive his mone...Ys worth for his money. A Way has alrey been made if he will only follow on., The law already permits of School B.oards establishing Higher Grade Schools where, with a fee not exceed- ing ninepence per week, a boy or girl can obtain a, high-class education. But School Boards are apathetic where they are not stimulated by public opinion, and some places—Warrington and St. Helens for in- stance—have yet to be convinced that there is any need even for a School Board. They will probably have their wits sharpened by the next Parliament, which will, we venture to predict, be a go-ahead Parliament in the matter of education. What we should like to see, and what we shall have ultimately, is a system of National Schools so graded that an apt scholar may pass from one to another, going up step by step by means of scholar- ships until, if he be clever arid diligent, he may reach the University without impos - ing any burden upon his parents. Our elementary schools are excellent; and, there are plenty of scholarships in connection with ! our high-class endowed schools. But there I is a gap—a gap which requires filling by pro- vision for intermediate education. Mr. MUN- DELLA not only admits this—he deplores it; but practically tells us that those who ask may have. It is now for the middle classes throughout the country to make themselves heard in this matter.

SIR GILBERT GREENALL Will be disposeL to cry out, "Save me from my friends! " when he sees how the Tory prints have made bad worse by their defence of him in the matter of the stoppage of the footpath lead- ing to Morley Common. A hand-bill on the subject, which has been circulated, has been subjected to the sort of abuse which Tories call criticism. Professing to quote from it, a Liverpool daily paper says--“ Of course, the hackneyed phrases, Tory tyranny,' "Poor working-man,' and robbing him- of his right to breath,' are freely made use of." We have read, and re-read the hand-bill in question; and find that the statements as to the so- called "hackneyed phrases" are so man); " Salisburys ; " not one of the phrases which are unblushingly given as quotations is to be found in it. Unable to face the facts of the case as stated in the leaflet, the shallow defenders of the indefensible have resorted to wilful misrepresentation. "It is as easy as lying," as " Haml-t " has it, and, we may add, as disreputable. From the letters which appear, and have appeared, in our columns, it will be seen that the question of right of way across the strip of land lead- ing from Walton Arches to Morley Common is not disposed of by the assertion of Mr. WHITE, Sir GILBERT GREENALL'S agent, that "it is not, and never has been, a public footpath." We have reason to believe that the footpath in question may fairly be described as an ancient footpath, and it will be noticed that one of our correspondents speaks of having been in the habit of using it for 26 years. It is suggested that the Railway Company per- mitted Mr. GEORGE CROSEIELD, as a direc- tor, "to use this footpath for a short cut to Bank Quay" when he was living at Walton. Such a statement carries its answer with it; the footpath was there or he could not have used it. •But apart from the issue we have raised as to the footpath being an ancient Company pitnlya.s may be be pointed out that the Railway an dedicated it to the public by allowing continued use. Referring to a calste, Lord ELLENBortouox on one occasion laid the law down as follows :---" If the owner of soil throws open a passage, and neither marks by any visible distinction that he means to preserve all his rights over it, nor excludes persons from passing over it by positive prohibition, he shall be presumed to have dedicated it to the public." " Once a road always a road" ; it is not for the Railway Company now, at the bid- ding of Sir GILBERT GREENALL, to close a path which has been used by the public without let or hindrance for so many years. It is idle to say that Sir GILBERT has nothing to do with it. Flow comes it that his -agent writes to say that "there is not and never has been a public foot- :path ? " How comes it that his game- keeper blocks the way and turns those , back who are intimidated by his empty threats of prosecution? Why not let the Railway Company's servants take care of the Railway Company's land ? Is it be- cause snipe are in the eyes of the Autocrat of Wilderspool of more value than men? These are questions which the working- men of Warrington are putting to them- selves, and they will require better answers

THE compact between the Government and the Parnellites seems to be demoralising both parties. It is an unnaturil alliance ; it is of evil origin, and therefore no good can came of it. There are not a few Conserva- tives who are ashamed of the way in which • their leaders on Friday night turned their backs upon Earl SPENCER, and kissed the rod which Mr. PARNELL held over them. Some of them have been loud in the expres- sion of their opinion, and others have avenged themselves by applying for tickets to the banquet in honour of the late VICEROY of IRELAND. In the early hours of Wednesday morning it was the turn of the Parnellites to "go under." The Medical Relief Bill was being discussed, and Sir SYDNEY WATER- LOW, with the approval of the Liberals in the House, moved an amendment declaring that no kind of medical relief should dis- franchise an otherwise qualified elector. As the Bill stands, though it is intended to free the agricultural labourer from the burden of disfranchisement upon his obtaining medical relief, it still leaves him disqualified in case a doctor orders a certain "kind of food or stimulants. The object of the amendment was to remove the bar entirely, and the justice of this will be apparent when we state that it would simply put the English labourer on a footing with the Irish peasant. Between fifteen and twenty of the Parnellites were present, and it really rested with them to say whether justice should be done in this matter. Their votes were sufficient to turn the scale • but, instead of voting for the amendment as they ought to have done, they allowed it to be lost by walking out of the House. and thus gave the Government the victory. They stand, there- fore, in the position of men who, having secured justice to labourers in Ireland, refuse to lend a hand to put the English labourer on tile same level. Indeed, by their deliberate abstention, they will have been the means of denying the vote to suffering Irishmen in this country who may obtain medical relief under the conditions pro3cribed. This is part of the penalty they are called upon to pay for allying themselves with the Tories—a penalty so great that we are quite sure Irishmen on both sides of St. George's Channel will eros, long protest against it.—We are glad to be able to add that on Thursday night the Liberals were more successful. An amend- ment of the bill moved by Mr. JESSE COL- LINGS was carried, despite Tory opposition; the Government were defeated, there being a majority of so against them. The Parnel- lites seem to have repented, for they voted on this occasion in favour of justice being done in England as well as in Ireland.

OUR "neutral " c Dntemporary seems to have had a particularly smart "own correspon- dent" at the wedding of Princess BEATRICE; for he gives an item of intelligence which, so far as we have observed, no other reporter has recorded. Describing "the scene in church," he says : . " The Archbishop of Canterbury officiated, and Keogh, of the Boar's Head Hotel, Macclesfield. The health of the bride and bridegroom was proposed. He was assisted by the Bishop of Winchester, the Dean of Windsor, and the Rector of Whippingliam." Who is " KRoGH of the Boar's Head Hotel, Macclesfield ? " And how did it happen , that he was brought in —at the last moment—to assist the Archbishop of CANTERBURY? Perhaps it was because he was well up in proposing toasts to the health of ttie bide and bridegroom " ; and it needed, may be, a "boar's head" man with a nerve equal to proposing a toast in church. It is a pity the correspondent, having told so much of this extraordinary "Scene in church," doesn't tell us something more. It looks queer, and just a little suspicious. Can it be that the " special " has been drawing on his imagination—and "double X "—at the Boar's Head ? Or has the "P.D." been ,at it again ? The imp troubled us last week; but he is never so happy as when he is roguishly employed in trying to make our contemporary miserable.

AN OLD OPYRNDER.—The Runcorn magistrates on Wed- nesday sentenced Mary O'Neil, who made her 18th ap- pearance before them, to a month's hard labour for being drunk and disorderly in Fryer-street on the previous day. FAJINWORTH ORWMAR Bcmoor--At the recent examin- ations of the College of INceptors, held in Manchester, L. W. Linuell, cf this school, was plsced in the wet of the second class. The governrrs are arranging for the school to be made a centre for the Christmas examina- tions. TONIC SOLANI CHOIR, Rusecing.—A choral society to be known as the Runcorn Tunic SA-fa Choir, has been estab- lished. Members must have obtained the elementary or higher certificate of the Tonic Sol-f& College. Mr. John' Holford, who has been very successful as a teacher Of the new no'ation, is the conductor, and Mr. W. Wright is the secretary.

WIDNES SECOND' STARR BDWILETT BUILDING SOCIETY. —The first appropriation of this society took place on Mon- day evening, in the Lacey-street schoolroom. Mr. H. Wade Deacon presided and delivered an address. Mr. Mart gave a lecture upon the principles and advantages of the society. The appropriation resulted in Mr..J'ob Clarke being entitled to £2OO. free of interest, for 12 years. SCHOOL TREAT AT WIDNES.—To the number of about 1,200, the children attending the National Day and Sunday Schools, and St. Paul's and Simm's Cross branches,assem- bled in Waterloo-road School, and then headed by the IC.E.T.S. Brass Band, marched in processional order to a I field at Atipleton, kindly lent by Mrs. Deacon. The weather was beautifully fine, and a pleasant Urns was spent. Tea was provided. WIDNES &nom. BOARD.-0a Wednesday the following persons were summoned to Mines Petty Sessions to answer a charge of neglecting to send their children regularly to school :—William Smith, John Fenny, James Currie, John McCormack, Joon McCann, John Martin, Patrick Cair (two cases), John Farlington, Charles McKenna (two cases). They were each fined 51 on the evidence of attemiance offi- cers; Messrs. Davies. Joynson, and Rowe. Mr. G. H. Denby, olerk to the School Board, prosecuted.

A WIDNES GENTLEMAN DROVekED.—Amongst the list of thee drowned through the collision of H. M. torpedo ship Heela and the steamer Cheerful, on Tuesday, appears the name of Mr. Phillip Bernard, 24 years of age, who was em- ployed at the Whines branch of Parr's Bank. He was well known in the town, and his sad death was the them.* of sympathetic conversation. Mr: Herbert ,White, sou of Mr. Richard White, of Dittos, was also a passenger On the Cheerful. Although he could not swim he was fortu nately rescued from the water. Mr. Bernard was a good swimmer. .

ROBBERY FROM A RI:MOORE INN.—Samuel Mason, a tramp, was brought before the Runcorn magistrates on Wednesday charged with stealing a flute from the Rose and Shamrock Inn, Mersey-street, -cept by Tnomas Finegan. On the 31st May the prisoner was in the house, and after' Isle 'departure the flute was missed. On Monday he was re- ceived from the custody of the Shrewsbury police by Con- stable Smith, after serving 21 days hard labour for a felony. He stated that he had bought the flute from e min he did not know, who was working at the gasometer in Hilton- road.—He was committed to gaol for 14 days with• htrd labour.

BREACKES OF TICE CANAL BOLTS ACT AT BUNCORY.—On Monday, at Runcorn Petty Sessions, Messrs. FeHowes, Morton, and Co., carriers; Wolverhampton, were charged with an infringement of the Canal Boats Act.—Mr. Farring- ton, inspector to the Rural Sanitary Authority, proved find- ing one of the defendant's boats which was not marked, lettered, and numbered, as required by the Act of 1884. Mr. F. A. Lake, who defended, said this boat was being used in place of one which had gone to the dock for repairs, and it WAS an Oversight that it was not marked. It was registered. A line of ffe and Costs was imposed.—Andrew Humphreys, Carrier, Wolverhampton, was dealt with in a like manner for a similar offence, and so also 'was John Wood Gandy, of Derby. Mr. Lake defended Humphreys. A WESTON POIN/ POACNEE.--.At RIIECOCE natty Seeeione, On Monday, John Talbot, labourer, Weston Point, was ,chargod with being in possession of a gun unler circum- stances to raise reasonable suspicions that he had been tres- passing in pursuit of game.—At 3-15 on the merning of the 11th July Constables Dale sod Coopea saw the defendant walking down the wagon road belonging to Mr. Jeffs. Hisl trousers and clogs were very wet, as though be had been upon the grass, audio his pocket he had a double-bevelled gun. In answer to the officers he said he had a large family and was hard up, and that he had laaeft "after rabbits."— The Bench imposed a fine Of It/3 and costs, 12s 61, and ordered the gun to be forfeited.—The defendant excitedly protested against the forfeiture of the gun, and stated he would spend Ir...oati money in recovering possession. A FEROCIOUS Doti AT WIDNES.—At Widnes Petty Ses- sions, on Wednesday, before Mr H. N. Heald and Mr. John Brock, Patrick Cain, an elderly man, was cherged with having a dapgerous and ferocious dog, which was not under proper control. P.C. Chambers stated that at 12 o'clock on Monday night be was going along Carolimestreet when the defendant's dog, a large black retriever, sprang out of a gate- way and attempted to bite him. He had to beat it off with his knife. P.S. McGreger said he had received many com- plaints about the defendant's dog which was a very danger. one one. About a fortnight ago one of thh postmen made a strong complaint. A witness was called who said he had known the dog for four years, and it had a " wild playful way " with it when it got out, but it had never injured a child in its life.—The Bench were of opinion the dog was dangerous, and made an order that it should not be at large, defendant to pay costs, 15e. ATTEMPT TO DROWN A WIFE AT BUNCORN.—Before Mr. W. Bankes and Mr. J. Handley, at Runcorn Police Court, on Wednesday, Edward Littler' captain of two boats be- longing to Messrs. Verdi°, of Northwich, was charged with assaulting his wife Margaret. It appeared that at half-past eleven an the previous night Conatab es Brieme and Harper were en duty at Top Locks, when they heard screams pro- ceeding from the prisoner's boats which were lying in the canal. They went there and discovered the wife was bleed- ing profusely from wounds in the face indicted by her hus- band. The prisoner, upon the arrival of the officers, knocked his wife down the hatchways of the boat, then seizing her by the legs, threw her into the canal. Harper was attempting to pall her out but the prisoner prevented him, and a boatman named Foster jumped into the water and with some difficulty rescued the drowning woman.— The wife now told the magistrates she wished to eXCLISo her husband for what be had done as she struck him first. She also alleged that it was by accident she went into the canal. —The Bench declined to believe thie statement, and sen- tenced the prisoner to 14 days' hard labour without the Option of a fine. A CHAPTER OF ACCIDENTS AT WIDNES.—George Rat- cliffe, labourer, Duke-street, Ditto; on Saturday broke both bones of his left leg and otherwise injured himself under the following circumstances. A horse, drawing several waggons along the railway metals which run through Widnes Foun- dry Company's yard, fell down, and Ratcliffe went to the assistance of the driver, in releasing the animal from its entanglement. He knelt upon the horee's head, but the animal gave a plunge and threw Ratcliffe a censiderable , distance, causing the injuries mentioned. He is under the I care of Dr. McCambridge.—A married woman named Mularkev, who lives in New-street, Siinm's Cress, while cleaning the windows of her dwelling broke a pane of glass, and severely cut her right band. She lost an immense quantity of blood, and it wee for some time thoneht she had cut an artery and was bleeding to deatl3.—A. man named McNeven, formerly one of the Papal Zouaves, who is em- ployed at Messrs. Snape's Chemical Works, was carrying some metal pipirg across a tank, when he fell to the ground, a distance of 13 feet. His back was seriously in- jured by the fall.—We are sorry to state that Joseph, the eon of Mr. Swale, Victoria-road, met with an accident a few days ago and broke his arm. MASONIC INSTALLATION AT BUNCORN..--The members of the Ellesmere Lodge of Freemasons celebrated the festival of St. John on Wednesday evening. The retiring W.M., Brother Richard Oldbury, opened the lodge in due form, and afterwards performed the ceremony of the installation of Brother George Bell, J.W., as W.M., in a most impressive manner. He was assisted by Brother E. Marwood, P.M. The W.M. then elected his officers as follows t—Brother R. Oldbury, ',P.M.. Brother Joseph Torking,ton, S.W.; Brother J. H. Salkeld, J.W.; Brother Rev. R. Edwards, chaplain ; Brother E. Marwood, treasurer ; Brother G. Summerfield, secretary ; Brother J. Coxhill, P.M., D.C.; Brother Ft A. Lake, S.D.; Brother Thomas Wright, J.D.; Brother L. Rosenberg, ; Brother John Cooper, organist; Brother S. H. Annett, S.S.; and Brother Richard Clarke, jun., J.S. Subsequently the usual banquet took place. amongst the brethren present being Brother R.Clarke, sen. P.M.; Brotter W. R. Wass, P.M.; Brother James White, P.M.; Brother W. Mellor, P.M.; Brother George Moss, P.M. ; Brother S. Orme, J.W.; and Brother Harrington. The retiring W.M., was presented with a pest master's jewel, and was also made a life governor of the Cheshire Masonic Educational Fund. It was arranged that the annual pic-nic should take place on the 301 h inst, when the members will visit Stoke and Trentham Park. ROBBERY y now WIDNES CRICKET CLUB.—A Sr. HELENS PAWNBROKER CENSURED.—Before Mr. H. N. Heald. and Mr. J. Brock, at Widnes Petty Sessions on Wednesday, Wm. Tarleton (13), Joseph Tarleton (11), Thomas Dann (12), and James Kelly (12), were brought up on remand charged with having broken into the Pavilion of the Widnes Cricket Club, Lower House-lane. and stolen a silver watch, a silver guard, and a seal, werth lOs,. the property of James Briggs, professional cricketer, of 30 Frederick-street, aced 9 cricket balls, 12 tennis balls, trousers, jerseys, caps, &c., to the value of £5 2s 61, the property of members of the club. On Wednesday night, the 15th inst., Mr. Briggs securely fastened up the pavilion and saw that everything was safe. Next morning at eight o'cleck he discovered that the door of the pavilion had been smashed open, and the articles mentioned in the charge abstracted. Subsequently P.S. Strickland discovered that the watch and guard had been Pawned at the shop of Mr. Birchall, Market-place. St. Helene, by the prisoner Dunn, and also a quantity of the clothing for 4s, and, the money had been divided between the Tarletons and Dunn. They were apprehended in Widnes, and afterwards Kelly, who had received a cricket ball and sold it for 4d, was taken into custody. When charged they made statements showing that Dunn and William Tarleton had smashed open the dour, the younger Tarleton having I kept watch outside. The boxes in the pavilion had been ' broke open with a pick.—Mr. Birchall, the pawnbroker, gave evidence that Dunn pledged the articles in the name of Kenyon, stating that they had trouble in the house. But for this statement he should not have taken them in.—Mr. Heald said the Bench were of opinion that he was to blame in this matter. He had acted very incautiously and very improperly, and they warned him to be more careful in fletnre.—The prisoners pleaded guilty. William Tarleton and Dunn were sentenced to receive twelve strokes with the 'birch rod, and Joseph and Kelly six strokes each.

ativennvansw AT BunCOns.--Under the presidency of the Rev. J. Lockwood. vicar of the paish, a meeting of Con- servatives was held at Halton on Tuesday evening. There wail a good attendance. On the motion of Mr. T. F. Acton, wooded by Mr. T W. Verdin is a fit and proper person ro ,reorisent this divihion of the county in the House of Com- mons, and pledgee itself to do all in its power to ensare his return at the general election." Mr. Thomas Fielding, of Manchester, a representative of the National Consarvative Union, delivered a lecture, entitled 'Radical Fallacies." On Thursday morning the Local Conservative Committee met in the smaN hall of the Public Hall, Runcorn, to discuss quer,- lions of organisation. Mr. W. H. Verdin, the candidate, wee present. It was decided to hold a series of meetings in the neighbourhood, to conclude with a mean meeting. Mr. , Charles Wigg occupied the chair. HOUNDEIts : Page-lam .e.ielelphi. v.. Warrington.— These clubs met on Saturday, on the ground of the latter, but owing to the unpropitious state of the , weather, theplay had to be suspended at the close of the first innings.—Scores -: Widnes. 56; War- rington, 31. • THE LORD Mixon's BALL.—Amongst the guests who were present at the ball given to the provin- cial mayors and mayoresses at the Mansion House on Friday were Mr. Alderman Harrison, the Mayor of Warrington, and Mrs. Harrison. Amongst those who accepted the invitation of the Lady Mayoress were the mayors and mayoresses of 115• English cities and boroughs, 11 provosts of Scotland, and their ladies, and of the 11 mayors of Ireland four were present on the occasion. MUTINY IN THE CONSERVATIVE BANJUL—Under the head "Sops to Law-breakers," the St. lames's Gazette" (Conservative) writes :—The bulk of the English people, both Liberals and Conservatives, will read Friday night's debate in the Commons with a common feeling—a feeling of profound re- gret not unmixed with humiliation, We have dif- ferences of opinion, very real and bitter differences. But, since constitutional Government reached its full development among us, it has been the con- tinuous tradition of public life that certain subjects should be placed high above party controversy; and first amongst those subjects has been the ad- ministration of the law. The administration of ' Lord Spencer was on its trial in Parliament, and. the Constitutional party coldly refused to defend. it. We believe their action will be condemned by thousands and tens of thousands of their own. sup- porters. The Conservative chiefs, have allowed. themselves to be forced into a totally false position, from which they cannot escape without humiliations and loss. •

A RIVER PORT. —ln certain provincial daily newspapers it is the custom (the Globe remarks) to. encourage the reader to ask all sorts of questions on the most variety of subjects. The newspaper reader in the provincial city is able, at twenty-four ' hours' notice, to.secure by 'a very modest expendi- ture, more or less valuable opinion upon any sub-- ject ranging from the ethics of the Platonic philo- sophy to the proper method of repairing the parish pump. There is one vexed question, the solution of' which is probably associated not remotely with bets made in public-houses, in regard to which the. typical newspaper reader in the north has a peren,- nial thirst for information. Scarcely a day passes in which he does not ask :—" Is Liverpool a sea- port ? " Innumerable quarts of ale must hs.ve been lost and won in the northern counties on the. settle- ment of this subtle dialectical point, the issue. being whether a port which really stands on a river can be properly described as a seaport. In this matter the lekicographers.are on the side of commonsense. The ceremony, therefore, which was performed by the Prince of iVales yesterday in laying the founda- tion stone of the new docks at Preston, really im- plies the establishment of an augmented claim, on the part of that busy Lancashire borough, to be re- garded as a seaport, even although the bar at the entrance to the Ribble is sixteen miles distant.- The enterprise which Preston is showing in creating the conditions whereby such a sea-borne commodity as foreign timber shall be delivered from the ship's. side, close to the spot where it is required for min- ing and other industrial purposes, points to the fact that we are 'only beginning to realise the lxissible. extent to which our rivers may yet be utilised for heavy traffic.

WIDNES WELSH WESLEYAN CHAPEL. The Rey. John Hugh Evans on Sunday preached three sermons in aid of the funds for erecting a new chapel for the Welsh Wes• leyans in the town. APPROPRIATION AT WIDNES.—At a meeting of the first Widnes Starr Bowkett Building Society on Wednesday, an appropriation took place. and Mr. J. Barton was successful in obtaining £4OO for 14 years free of interest. ST. Bo's SCHOOL, APPLETON.—The scholars had their annual treat on Thursday, when they engaged in various games in a field belonging to Mr. Lengton, and were regaled with refreshments. Ditton Brass Band was present. WIDNES C.E.T.S. An open air meeting was held at Anderson'. Corner, on Thursday evening, when addresses were delivered by the Rev. J. Hamilton Wilson, the toy. C. Rumfitt, and others. There was a fair attendance. RUNCORN VOLUNTEERS.—The Runcorn Volunteers of the 2nd C.R.V. on Sunday attended, divine service at All Saints', Runcorn, under the command of Captain ffazlehurst The Rev. R. Edwards preached. A week hence the volunteer" will go into camp. ACTION FOR LIBEL AGAINST DR. MCDOUGALL, OF RUN. CORN.—An action for libel, brought by Mr. R. Seaw chair- man of the Board of Commissioners, against Dr. McDougall, will be heard at Chester Assizes on Wednesday next. It is alleged that the libel took place at a ratepayers' meeting held in the spring with regard to the Ship Canal. Counsel have been engaged on both eides, and the trial is awaited amongst the townspeople with feelings of lively interest. ROBBERY AT RUNCORN.—Yesterday, before Mr. C. W. Hazlehurst, at Runcorn Police Court, George Spruce and John Wilkinson were committed to Chester ASSiZeB for trial on a charge of stealing and receiving a trowel, a hammer, and a plumb bob, the property of William Herbert, and a hammer and chisel, the property of JAMSS Wilson, contrac- tor, on the 15th July. The circumstances have been re- corded. Superintendent Leah said he had been unable to obtain any farther information with regard to the prisoners since they were remanded. FOUND DEAD IN THE MERSEY.— At the Weaver Hotel, Weston Point, on Monday, an inquest was held before Mr. T. J. Ridgway, upon the body of Rabert Cook, late captein of the steamer Lord Marpeth, Liverpool.- On Saturday afternoon the crew of the steamer Hawarden Castle found the body floating in the Mersey, near Eastham Lightship, and towed it up to Weston Point. The deceased had been missing since Saturday, the 11th, when he was seen sculling from New Ferry to Liverpool in a small boat. A verdict of "found dead" was returned PRESENTATION TO A WIDNES CURATE—The Rev. J. Holden, curate of Farnworth Parish Church, having ac- cepted the curacy of St. Clement's Church, Salford, the parishioners met in the school-room, on Saturday evening, for the purpose of testifying their appreciation of his char- acter and services during the five years he had resided amongst them. The meeting was presided over by the Rev. George Bond, vicar, who on behalf of the subscribers pre- sented Mr. Holden with an Illuminated addrese, and a ca'anet containing a purse of £l7 10s.—The Rev. J. Holden replied in feeling terms, and Dr. Hurter, Dr. Booth, Messrs. Carey, Watts, and Kidd bore testimony to the recipient's energetic and valuable services in the parish. A vote of thanks was accorded to Mr. Kidd for his kindness in collect- ing sabscriptions. SUICIDE NEAR WIDNES.-11r. S. Brighouse, the county coroner, on Monday, held an inquest at the Crown Inn, Farnworth, touching the death of Joseph Bowett, aged 59, formerly a night watchman in the employ of the Bridge- water Navigation Company. The evidence showed that the deceased had lived with his son, Jonas Bowett, signalman on the Cheshire Linea Railway, Farnworth, sod bad re- cently complained of acute pains, and had seemed distressed in his mind. About noon on Saturday, Mr. Arthur Kidd, coal merchant, Farnworth, found the deceased lying on his back in the railway company's stables. He had a great gash in his throat, and was quite dead. A razor and a hat filled with blood were in the manger.—A verdict to the effect that the deceased committed suicide during a fit of temporary insanity EU returned.

THREE WEEKS WITHOUT WATER AT WESTON. Mr. Aaron said the Runcorn. Weston, and Halton Water- works had to supply Weston with water, belt for the past three weeks the inhabitmts have been unable to get water between the hours of five o'clock in the morning and sine o'clock in the evening. He had seen the directors ef the company, and they came to the conclusion that Weston Point was so much lower than Weston that they took all the water, lie wished to know what the Board could do about the matter.—The Chairman questioned whether the Authority hal anything to do with it.—Mr. Aaron said the Authority compelled every man to have a good supply of water in his house before they would allow him to occupy it, and he was of opinion they could interfere.—The Deputy Clerk said it was the Authority's duty to see that

The Water Company had the exclusive right to supply Runcorn, Weston, and flagon with water, and if Mr. Aaron I could show that they were oot finding water for the ac• comnsodation of Weston on the-ground that the property was • to some extent above the level of their reservoir, he could no doubt compel them to provide a reservoir at Weston of sufficient height to supply the inhabitants. SUFFOCATED N • SEWER AT WIDNES. GALLANT ATTEMPT AT RESCUB.
