div.head: OUR LONDON LETTER.
div.p: OUR LONDON LETTER.

LONDON, TERMSDAY. When the wisdom of the resignation of the Gov- ernment regarded as a matter of tactics was being discussed a well-known Liberal cynically, re- marked.: "Let Lord Salisbury and Lord Randolph Churchill come in by all means. It will be only for five months and the people will have a practical taste of &Conservative Administration. g Liberals e

on now and come in again at the General Elec- tion there will always be people who will imagine that the Conservatives would have done better. Let them try them now.' This remark indicated a cer- tainty that even within five months a Conservative Administration would have so managed affairs as to complete the discredit born of the six years rule of Kr. Disraeli. The discredit has come, but in a quite unexpected'form. With the Liberal majority look- ing on. Lord Salisbury has not presumed to make any strikingly new departure in foreign policy. The Ministry in the House of Lords lead' equable lives and have on the whole quite a comfortable time. It is in the Commons where things have gone wrong and where the Administration is weakened through the operation of the most powerful instru- ment. All Governments can with more or less suc- cess withstand the attacks of their political opponents. What is fatal to any Administration is ,revolt within its own camp and attacks on its own 'followers.

The -condition of the Ministerialists at the present moment is as creditable to the honour of the rank and file of the party as it is humiliating to the leaders. On Friday last Sir M. H. Beach added another episode to a political career which promises to be exceedingly striking. To desert his friend and leader in a moment of peril, going over openly to the camp of the rebels, might be thought to be of itself sufficient for one session. On Friday Sir Michael capped this by concluding what his own followers call "a shameless alliance," joining in an unmanly and unpatriotic attack upon Earl Spencer. In both cases there was a prize in view. Sir Michael sold Sir Stafford iN orthcote for the re- version of his office. He bartered all the traditions of honour and patriotism of which the Conservative party are proud for the support of the Parnellites through what remains of the present session, and for the Irish vote at the general election. What the Conservatives acutely feel is that this was worse than a crime. It was a blunder. The loyal attitude assumed by the Liberal Opposition in the House of Commons would have made ineffective the obstructive tactics of the Parnellites, supposing they had been set in action. The session might have been lengthened by a; few days, but that is surely an immaterial sacrifice compared with the price paid by Sir Michael Beach. As to the vote at the general election, that was Already assured. Under no conceivable circumstances would the Irish vote, as far as it can be controlled by Mr. Parnell, have been given to the Liberal candidates. Thus Sir Michael Beach has given everything and gets no- thing in return. The Parliamentary reports feebly indicate,the personal position of Ministers in rela- tion with their followers. The spectacle of the Home Secretary having his nose rubbed with a newspaper held by an irate Conservative is one of the signs of the times. This happened on Monday night when Sir R. Cross attempted to put aside with a few choice platitudes the searching question of Mr. Stavely Hill as to his intentions with respect to the sale of " filthy literature " in the streets. When he sat down Mr. Onslow produced a copy of an illustrated number of Town Talk and pressed it upon his acceptance. As he would not take it, the irate member for Guildford, standing over him, shook it in his face and finally, with the assistance of the ChancelfOr of the Exchequer, played battle- dore and shuttlecock with it. ThiS instance of contemptuous insubordination rose upon a side issue, but it is indicative of the general condition of affairs. On the Medical Relief Disqualification Bill, the principal opposition came from, the Conservative benches, the Government being twitted here, as in the case of the Irish Gov- ernment, with having eaten their own words, and steering in office a course directly opposed to that , they had laid down to themselves in opposition. There will be. more trouble from the same quarter on the Criminal Law Amendment Bill, and if the Government manage to get to the end of the session without being forced to resign, they will love reached the limit of probabilities. The incident ' taking place at half-past three in the morning has escaped general notice; but it is a fact that the Government defeated Sir Sydney Waterlow's amendment to the Medical Relief Bill only by threatening to resign, and then they were saved by a bare majority of three. ." The din of political controversy is to-day hushed if not entirely silenced by the Royal ceremony at Osborne, which absorbs the attention and engages the interest of every subject of the Queen." So, this morning, writes the Times, emulous of the daily fare of the Daily Telegraph. The sentence is a good one, its single failing being that it is not only not true, but is conspicuously the reverse of the truth. Of the long series of Royal weddings known to England during the last fifty years, none has excited less attention than that of Princess Beatrice. This is partly because it is capriciously held in a remote corner of the kingdom, but principally because the country shares the well-known view, of the Prince of Wales on the matter. The quiet self- sacrificing life of the Princess Beatrice has earned for her the sympathy and esteem ef the nation,

which does not like to see her thrown away upon an obscure Gern,`an Princeling, who to secure the advantages of the, match is content hereafter to live is mother-in-law's household. as an appanage in Amongst the workiers of the week a new tele- phone may perhaps clia.;n2 precedence if only for the boldness of the idea up' which it is based. This new invention is entirelr_independent of electricity, and has nothing to do with .batteries and the gene- ral paraphanalia of electet.tkdephonee,. It is sim- plicity itself, and consists only of a small wooden case containing a diaphragm,. tor sounding board, made of small slips of willow wood interlaced to- gether and varnished. In the ce);tre of this dia- phragm is fixed a metal disc to bokl te wire which is then ready to be conveyed to any distance re- quired up to two miles. At the other end a similar apparatus is fixed to the wire, the teiephOne hoeing a transmitter and receiver in one. In some experi- ments which took:place a few days ago, the new telephone showed to greater advantage, and every test that was applied was fully responded to. -All kinds of sounds were sent across the wires, and ti‘e slightest noise was easily transmitted, the ticking' of a watch being heard witlrthe greatest distinct-. nes&

Five ots six years ago I hadloccasion to visit Wok- ing prison in connection with', an inquiry into the. -state of female prisoners. Walking through. the 'common room, the matron pointed out a rather short, stout,. sullen-looking woman whom she whispered was Constance Rent,- With her hail-cat sltert and her ungainly prison dress, she did not look more thateseventeen, though as she was but sixteen at the time of the memorable mnrderat, Road she could'not have been less,than thirty-sik. The matron told'me that there were few of the prte- soners who gave more trouble thanlConstance Kent' . though she had oflate years shownea disposition lei-, tone down. She displayed extraordinary ingenuity and daring in communicating with the outer world, writing letters and getting them pissed out with surprising success. She was of a mutinous disposi- tion and was in frequent trouble under the disci- plinary rules. This made it all the insere surprising to hear that the woman had been "discharged ' earlier than was expected on account of geed con- duct." Possibly she had mended her ways during , later years. It will be. remembered That she was convicted upon her own; confession, and WAS sen- tenced to death, the 'sentence being subsequently ' commuted to penal Servitude. It is just a quarter of acentury ago, on the 29th of June, 1860, that the country was first shocked and then puzzled by: the announcement of what since became famous all over the world as-the Road murder. The victim was a little boy named. Francis Saville Kent, who was three- years and ten months old. He was Constance Kent's step-brother; and was put quietly to bed in the nursery on the night of the murder. At five o'clock in the morning- he was missed by the nurse. But the alarm was not raised for two hours later, when the boey of the child was found thrust down a water closet, wrapped in a blanket taken from the nursery; and its throat cut in the most determined manner. It was evident that the crime had been committed' by some one in the house, and suspicion at first fell upon the nursemaid, who was twice arrested.. Mr. Kent himself came under suspicion, though it never reached a stage at which he was taken into cus- tody. Whicher (the "Inspector Bucket" of Charles Dickens's fancy) had from the first fixed his medi- tative eye upon Constance Kent, whom after tabrief interval he charged with the murder. But nsrthing , could be made of it. The young girl was as cool and collected as if the matter at issue were a broken dish. She was discharged, and for five years the affair remained shrouded in mystery. At the end of that time, Constance Kent electrified the country by confessing that she had murdered the little bey, giving, always in the same calm unemotionable manner, details of the crime, which showed that it had been accomplished with remarkable delibera- tion and determination. The motive was jealousy as between the children of her mother and the little family born of the second wife. It would be interesting to know by what means a convict sentenced for life is allowed his liberty, who sets the matter going or starts the movement which ends in the Home Secretary's interference. I assume that in every' case the remission of sentence is an act of wise and considered clemency. But has interest influence even within prison walls, or is the prison chaplain in every instance the ori- ginator? Of course it is Constance Kent's case that suggests the question. Many such criminals have been from time to time liberated and,no harm has ever resulted to the community. Still one would be glad to know the procedure, and the mere so because the public are never informed till the convict is actually at large. There has been a marked peculiarity abcnit the season which is now almost at an end. hints, in its 'amusements, followed the programme of the Mid- land Railway, and discouraged second class. rdo not know whether it is that people have had more sense, or only that they have less money, but the result has been very serious to the caterers of amßBe- ment. Concert givers and theatrical managers are in a bad way. Generally the month of July is given up to complimentary concerts. They are adduct of return which fashionable people give for the. ser- vices of the musical profession at their houses in.the winter. The annual benefit is largely supported. This year there has been a re-action against music. ,People have shown a preference to laugh'rather than to. be bored. Comic reciters—Grossmith ancbCerney Grain—have had their hands full of " work, each asking and getting £l5 for an afternoon, and the difficulty being to secure them; but the " executioners " on the piano or the violin ' have fared badly. Theatrical experience has run in parallel lines. Comic opera is, dead and I buried; the sacred lamp of burlesque has gone out, and no one seems anxious to light it. At-nearly all the houses there have been "frosts," There•ha.s'beert a decided taste for the Palais Royal farce, It is the only thing that has prospered, but that kind of thing can't support more than a couple of theatres, and engagements must now be made for the, winter months. Londoners seem to be forsaking the theatre, just as they have revolted against the, opera. The truth is, and the sooner it is faced' the better, salaries must come down, and the ten shilling stall be reduced to the familiar three half- crowns, It is all very well where expenses are great and the piece a success; but it is miserable to see stalls lined with paper or only half full. I hear that- when some gf the theatres re-open the price liSts wile be found. , revised.

LANCASHIRE AND CriESIIIRE FARMERS: The Warrington Farmers' Club isined a circular not long ; since to landlords asking them to take into consideration the I desirability of reducing farm rents. It is satiafactory to I know that, on the whale, the request is beginning to bear : fruit. Sir John Chetwood has informed his tenants on the Agden and Whitley estate that a reduction of ten per cent has been made upon their rents. Mrs Banks, of Winstan- : ley, has informed the secretary of the Farmers' Club, !through her solicitors. that she is about to make a general I reduction in farm rents. Concessions Hies these contrast I very favourably with the action of a neighbouring landlord, who cast the communications of the Farmer,' Club into tbe wastepaper basket, and asked that he might be spared , the receipt of any more such trash. The Mark Lane Express says :—The following question& have been adopted by the Chester, Wirral, Wigan and War-. rins,eton Farmers' Clubs, to be put to the Parliamentary candidates 1. Will You vote for the main roads ef the county te be maintained out of the Imperial Fund? 2. Will you vote for the election of County Government- Boards ? • i 3. Will you vote for an Amendment to the Agricultural. Holdings Act, 1853, to give to the sitting tenant prorntricpetnisaon. from having his rent raised on his own improvements ; 4. Will you vote for a Bill to Amend the Agricultural ;Holdings Act, 1883, by securing to tenant farmer,,fraeuom, I of cultivation and absolute certainty of adequate co tion for all unexhausted improvements?

5. Will you vote for a Bill to compel Railway Com- panies to carry farm produce at rates net exceeding the of Other. rates charged by them for the carriage of goods. industries? 6. Are you in favour of all local rates being esuallv Larne by owner and occupier? 7. Will you support the present 'regulations as to the exclusion of live stock from all countries infected with die- ; ease? S. Will you vote for the abolition of tithe ? 9. Will you vote for the above Programme. whether brought forward by your own party or otherwise? Mary members of the Warriugton -Claab live in the M- k trincharn division of Cheshire„for which. Mr. I S. Leadam, an old and valued member of the Farmers' Alliance and a sound agricultural reformer, is a candidate. His opponent is a landlord. Mr. Leatiam miy be trusted, not only to answer all or nearly all three questions in the affirmative, j but also to work energetically and with great ability te ' carry out the objects indicited. The members of the • clubs need to bear what the candidates have to say on each question, and should not be satisfied with a general answer.

t We may add that a public meeting is announced to be held on Monday evening next, in the Congregational ;Schoolroom, Bucklow•hill, in the Altrinoham and Knots - ford Division. when addresi,,a will be delivered by the Liberal candidate, M. L S. LaaAam, and Mr. G. Ee !Barlow,

div.p: fOLICE _INTELLIGENCE.
WARRINGTON BOROUGH. POLICE COURT. MornaY.—Before the Mayor (Alderman Harrison). Coun- cillor Greening, Mr. John Fairclongb, and Mr. R.

Garoett. A NCISANCE.—Edward Connor was summoned for keep- ing pigs in Connor's-yard, Sankey-street, in such a state as to be a nuisance, He expressed his entire willingness to remove the pigs, and the Banco adOurned the case for a week for that to be done. TEMPORARY Avrnourrs.—Mr. Fox applied on behalf of George Brooks for temporary authority to sell at the Ring o' Bells beerhouse. It transpired that Mr. Brooks had been convicted recently of an assault, and the Bench. In granting the application, advised him to keep better control over his

temper. MISCELLANEOUS.—The following were fined for drunken- ness :—Peter Cartledge, in Turner-street, on Saturday night, fined lOs and costs; Emma Richardson, in Horsemarket- street, fined 10s and costs; Daniel Crosby, in Market Place, on Saturday midnight, 43rd appearance, fined 20s and costs; Mary Balmer, in Academy-street, on the 9th inst., fined 58 and costs; Sarah Riley, on the 11th inst.,fined 103 and coats; Annie Barnes, in Smith-street, on the 11th inst., fined 5s and costs; Edward Sauce, in Winwick-street, on the 11th inst., fined 10s and costs; John Kearns, on Fin- nets-brow, on the 11th inst., sent to prison for a month.— Thomas Brown (12), for plucking a flower in Bank Park on the 12th inst. was fined 2s 6d and costs.—Joian Hart, for allowing two 'horses to stray in Knutsford-road, was fiee.di 53 and costs. Scnoot. ATTENDANCE Casys.—The following persons were fined 5s each for neglecting to send their children to school :—William Lawrenson, forgeman ; Richard Stockton, labourer ; James Joyce, labourer; William Latimer, file cutter; James Bibby, hamper maker; and James Backhonse, forgeman. Michael Cryan was fint;fi 10a for not sending two children to school; and Kate Owen was fined 2s 6d in respect to one child. Mr. G.Riley, school attendance officer, proved the cases. FIGHTING.—WiIIiam Stokes, for being drunk and dis- orderly in Froghall-lane, on the 11th inst., was fined 5s and costs; and Walter Gourke, charged with committing a breach of the peace at the same time and place, was hound ' over to be of good br,hayioar. The two defendants had a pitched battle, which was interrupted by Market Inspector Place. The circumstances of the case have been previoasly given. WEDNESDAY.—Before Mr. John Fairclough and Alderman Chandley. NEGLECT CF FAMILY.—John Plunkett, labourer, was charged with neglecting to maintain his wife and family. who were admitted to the Workhoase on Monday. The case was adjourned for a month to enable prisoner to make pro- vision for his family. STEALING TIMBER —Jane Monks was charged with steal- ing train old buildings in course of demolition in Bridge- street. a portion of firewood, value 2.1, the property of John E. Wright. A conviction only was recorded. VAGRANCY.—Jane Runcorn, of no fixed abode, charged with sleeping out in Chesbyres-lane, was dismissed en pro- mising to go to the Workhouse. TRIIRSDAY.—Before NiAjor Litton and Alderman Webster. MISCELLINEOCS.—WiiIiarn Holt, charged with refusing to work whilst an inmate of the vagrant ward at the Work- house, was dis missed on promising to leave the town.— Thomas Ellison was cautioned for sleeping out in a coal yard in Tanners-lane. FRlDAY—Before Captain Reynolds and Dr. Gornall. MISCELLANEOCS.—Peter Clough, for being drunk and dis- orderly in Whowick-street and assaultinv John Mannion, the previous evening, wis sent to prison for a William Hunt Hunt was bound over to keep the peace, he having assaulted his brother, Matthew Hunt.--William Webb, charged with assaulting Hannah Harcourt on the 19th July, was dismissed.--Margaret Clark was summoned for as- *malting ElizabAh Cassy. Mr. A. Browne defended. There was a cross-summons charging Casey with using threats to Clark:—The Bench ordered both to be bound over to be bound over to los of good behaviour.--Ellen McCormack was fined 23 61, including costs, for throwing stones in Museum-street on the 21st inst.—Sarab Kilcourse was summoned by William Hockenhall for neglecting her work So an apprentice to fustian cutting. She was ordered to pay the compensation claimed, 123, at the rate of 6d a week.-- Frederick Gosling was similarly summoned by Joseph Wil- kinson.—Adjourned for a month.--A similar case against Matthew Little was adjourned for a week.--Michael Flynn was summoned to show cause why he should not be com- mitted te prison for disobeying a magistrate's order to re- turn to work as an apprentice to Mr. Wilkinson.—He said he was afraid of:the foreman under whom he worked.—Ad- journed for a fortnight on defendant's promise to return to work.

WIDNES POLICE COURT. MONDAT.—Before Mr. John Brock. DEVSICRITNESq.—Francis Livingstone and Martin Nugent, young men, pleaded guilty to being drunk in the Vine Inn, , Waterloo-read, on Saturday night, and on the evidence of P.C. Murray, Livingstone was fined 7s 61, and costs 6s 6d or ten days; and Nugent, who had been before the magis- trates previously this month, was fined lOs and costs. or 14 days.—George Woodruff, of Halewood, was fined 7s 6d and costs 64 6d, for being drunk in chargé of a horse in Warring- ton road Co Saturday. Martin Finn, James Finn, James Brewan, James Green (9th appearance), William Henry Jones_ (Liverpool), Thomas Parry (Liverpool) were each

fined for drunkenness. ABSENT WITHOUT Lnave.—Jno Barrett and Charles Vaughan, young men, were charged with being absent with- out leave from the Bth King's Own Regiment. P.C's Tim. perky and Gamble proved meeting the prisoners in Deacon- road, on Sunday morning, and they adtnitted their passes expired at a quarter to twelve on Saturday night. They were committed to gaol to await an escort. BREACH OF THE PEACE.—Patrick Tarleton, a young man, was charged with committing a breach of the peace. On Saturday night P.S. Clarksun and P.C. Savory were searching the prisoner's father's house in connection with the cricket club robbery. The prisoner behaved ma very noisy and violent manner, and the officers were compelled to take him into custody. lie was ordered to find sureties himself in £lO and two in £5, or go to gaol for 14 days.

WIDNES PETTY SESSIONS. WEDICESDAT.—Hefore Mr. H. N. Heald and Mr. F. H. GOSSaLIS. DRUNKEN:4EBI.—Rn* this offence the following parsons 'were fined :—Sarah Massey, Ralph Atherton, Ellen Carney, Charles Rotherham. DESTRUCTIVE &M.—James Matthews, a boy, living in Caroline-street, was charged with throwing stones.—P.S. McGregor stated that on the 14th inst. he saw the defend- ant and a number of other boys throwing stones in Sutton- lane. He saw three boys smash windows, and then the de- fendant threw a stone and also broke a window. The police only succeeded in capturing the defendant, who was now fined 5s and costs. BREACH OF TIIE PEAcz.—Felix Evans and John Evans, brothers, living in Pitt-street, were charged with commit- ting a breach of the peace in West Bank•street, on the 12th inst —P.C's Thompson and Bowlebank gave evidence in support of the charge, and Mr. Knowles, who defended, gave it a complete denial.—The defendants were bound over to keep the peace for a month. HIGHWAY OFFENCES.—Henry Jackson, for leaving his horse and cart an unreasonable time in Alforde-street, on the oth inst., was fined 2s 6d and costs. For a like-offence committed in Lugsdate-road, John Parsonage was fined , 25 61 and cors.—John Finnightv, a young man, was fined' 21 gd and costs for furiously driving in ilale-road, on the lOtla inst. SavloE Wornr.—Mary Whalley, a mareied woman, was summoned by Bridget Carthy for an assault. A cross-1 summons fora like offence had been issued. Mr. Knowles appeared for Whalley,—Carthy allfged that on the 20th July she was walking along the street, when the defend- ant struck her on tha eye with the door key, knocked her to the floor, and abused her in a savage manner.—Whalley's case was a complete denial of the charge, and it was asserted that Carthy had l),ien the attackin4 party, and had seri- ously injured Whalley.-The Bench bound each over to keep the peace for two months.
RUNCORN PETTY SESSIONS. MoNDAY.—Bei ore Mr. John Brundrit and Captain C. W. . .

Hazlehurst. DIitNRENNESS.—Tbomas Smith, list) dealer,Church-street, i was fined 203 and costs for being drunk and disorderly n Church-street on the 11th inst. P.S. Neild and P.C. Wal- lace proved the case. Fur Leirig drunk in Howard-street on the same day John Brereton was fined 103 and costs. FIGHTING.—Edwin Cook was bound over to keep the peace in the usual sureties for fighting in Fryer-street on the 10th inst. UNREGISTERED LODGING HOrSES. Elizabeth Steven- son was fined lOs and costs £1 5s 6d, Eiizibeth Hart 103 and costs £l, Mary Wilson 103 and costs £l, and Hugh Yon 105 and cnsts £l, for keeping an unregistered lodging house. Mr. W. H. Linaker prosecuted on behalf of the Board of Commissioners, and evidence was given by Nuis. j ance Inspector Percival.

WARRINGTON COUNTY COURT. Taustswar.— Before his Honour Judge Ffoulkes. THE Cosiasormats' Dim:rm.—His Honour had again before him the case of James Stewart v. Joseph Penning- ton. At the last Court, when Mr. Riley appeared for the plaintiff and defendant was sot professionaity represented, judgment was given for the plaintiff for £lO. and £3 16s 4d costs. Mr. H. J. Longton, solicitor, now applied en be- half of the defendant that the payment might be delayed , 'until the 6th of August, when, he said, a claim by Mr. Pt heentgeten contractaga against Stewart woulde w abret enteredfor thatforcobuardawoorr,kin the alternative, that the £lO and costs might lie in court and not be paid out to Stewart without the further order of the Court. Mr. Longton said that his client thought that if Stewart now got hold of the £lO, there would not be much chance in getting it back in his cla nip Stewart's real posibion only being that of a labourer. As it was really all one matter, he should apply on the 6th of August to have the amount of any judgment given against Stewart set off against the £lo.—Mr. Riley appeared for Stewart, and op- posed the application.—His Honour ordered that the £lO remain in court until further order, but the £3 16s 4d id be paid over to Mr. Riley. DAMAGES FOR WOONDING.—John Gerachty, ash wheeler at a forge, sued John Bradbury, puddler, employed at the same place, on a claim of £2 damages, alleged to have been sustained in consequence of loss of work caused by injuries inflicted upon him by defendant. Plaintiff told the court that while working at the forge the defendant threw a lump of slagg at him, which hit him on the forehead, causing a wound. Plaintiff had the wound dressed by Dr. Adams, and was seven or eight days off work in consequence of his injuries.—James Donohue, puddler, deposed to seeing de- fendant throw the missile.—Dr. Adams spoke to dressing plaintiff's wound. Afterwards plaintiff was threatened with an attack of erysipelas, and witness ordered him to give up his work for eight or ten daya—Defendant did not deny throwing the slagg, but alleged that in the course of work the Dlailltiff bad needlessly annoyed him.—His Honour gave judgment for the plaintiff for the amount claimed, payment to be made at the rate of 5s per month. CONTEMPT OF COURT.—A case was heard in which Samuel Gough and Company, Tanners-lane, were Plaintiffs, and Frederick Lawton was def mdant. Phintiff claimed 163 4d for a load of coals supplied in March last, but the defendant's wife denied having raceived any coal from the plaintiffs. His Honour, haying heard the plaintiff's carter, made an order for payment by instalments of 6s. a month. The wife of the defendant, whilst leaving court, conducted herself in a very noisy manner, and his Honour ordered her to be brought before him. He said that he was surprised that a respectable-looking woman like she was should behave herself in such a manner. If she did not conduct herself properly while in court he should be obliged to take steps to compel her. He had the power to send her to prison for such conduct, and if it was repeated he should certainly do so. Sha then expressed sorrow at her conduct, and left the court. I COMMITTAL OF A BANICROPT.—Peter Clemo, of 37, Howard-street, Warrington, was summoned to show cause why he should not be committed to prison for disobeying an order made on November 27h, 1884, under section 122 of the Bankruptcy Act, 1883, for ties payment of 21s per month until his debts were paid off. Defendant did not appear, but had paid into court £3, leaving £2 15s in arre.r. —Mr. Gough, a creditor, gave evrAence as to defendant's means, and his Henour made an order that defendant should be committed to prison for 40 days.

div.head: WARRINGTON – BOARD OF GUARDIANS.
div.p: WARRINGTON - BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

The fortnightly meeting of this Board was held at the Workhouse on Wednesday morning. There were present the Rev. G. F. Roberts (chairman), Messrs. Derbyshire, Appleton, Brown Jolley, Wm. Houghton, John Houghton, Forster, Broselbent, Greening, Retcliffe, Blackhurst, Bat- harry, Gibson. and Humphries; J. C. Sutton (clerk), and S. Sutton, (assistant clerk). TRADESMEN'S ACCOUNTS. On the usual accounts being submitt.id it was mentioned by the Clerk that a bill had been sent in by a tradesman which could not legally be paid owing to its not having been sent in in proper time.—Mr. DARHYSIIIRE remarked that trades- men had been advised to send in their bills in proper time. —Mr. JOLLEY said thee s delayed accounts cost the Guar- dians three times more trouble than they gave the trades- men to make them out.-The CHAIRMAN thought the trades- men who did not send in their accounts in proper time had only themselves to blame.—The CLERK said the ac- count in qaestion had been sent for three times. The subject then dropped. SCHOOLS COMMITTFIE. At a meeting of this committee, on the 219 t met, there were present the Rev. G. F. Roberts (chairman). Messrs. Jolley, J. Houghton, Greening, Gibson, Ratcliffe, and Broadbent.—A letter was read from the Rev. Canon Dodd, of Stretton, and from the Warrington Band of Hope Union asking that the school band might attend their procession on July 31st and August let, and these reel/legs were ac- mead to. The past services of the band when leading similar processions were spoken of in high terms by the Rev Canon Dodd and Mr. F. Williams, secretary of the Band of Hope Union. The superintendent reported the children tube in excellent health, and that there was con- siderable improvement in the care and attention given by the officers to the children out of sehool hours, Mr. Naylor, Mr. Williams, Miss Wood, Mrs. Norman, and Mrs. Smith joining in the children's games and sports. The committee expressed their pleasure to hear of this improvement, and they trusted it would continue. The committee having read and carefully considered the applications for the office of assistant clerk at the schools, and the testimonials presented by the applicants, and having separately interviewed each boy and examined the test work of each as put to them by Mr. Mines, were very favour- ably impressed with the excellence of the candi- dates, any one of whom they considered to be well fitted for the duties of the office, and having also considered their respective ages and the circumstances connected with each boy's application, they finally agreed to recommend to the Board the name of Isaac Arthur Biddle for appointment. The names of the candidates before the committee were re- spectively William Grounds, Richard Jones, Isaac Arthur Biddle, Joseph W. Cavanagh, Henry Hay, and David H. Aitken.—The CHAIRMAN, in moving the confirmation of these minutes, spoke in high terms of the applicants for the assistant clerkship, and said that their difficulty had been rather in refusing so many eligible candidates than in mak- ing an efficient appointment to the post.—Mr. GEER/41RO seconded the proposal —Mr BLACKHURST remarked that it would have been well if the committee had fixed upon a Catholic to fill this post as they had had some difficnity in getting anyone to take charge of the Catholic school chil- dren on the Sunday.-The CHAIRMAN said they took that into consideration, an had gone thoroughly into all the merits of each case.—Mr. R&TCLIFFE said that the appli- cent Cavanagh was a Catholic, but as he was 18 years of age they thought be was rather too old for the post.—Mr. JOLLEY thought the committee had made a judicious choice. —Mr. BROADBENT said that in the selection they had made they had not taken the question of religion into considera- tion at all, at least they did not make it their business to learn the religious persuasion or convictions of the candi- dates that came before them. It had, as the chairman said, been very difficult to make a choice, and he believed any one of the applicante world have performed the duties very well. It was rather painful to find what a number of eligible young men there were willing to take that office at a salary of £l2 a year. It showed, he thought, that it was better for young men to be brought up to other professions or trades than that of clerk.— The minutes were then adopted.
SCHOOL FEES COMMITTEE. The committee reported that fees in nine new and 92 old cises bad been granted.—Mr. BLACIIIIIIIST moved, and Mr. JOLLEY eecended the adoption of these minutes.

THE CALLS. The CLERIC reported that the townships of Grappenball and Sonthworth-with-Croft were two calls in arrear, and that the Board was back at the bank about Mel.—lt was agreed that these townships sheu.d be requested to pay up their calls.

VACCINA.TION- The CLERK stated that the returns required by the Local Government Board from Mr. HoHord, vaccination officer of the Warrington district, and Mr. Cooper, of the Newton district, with regard to cases not vaccinated, and reports upon proceedings in consequence t'•lereof, had been sent up. —An explanatory letter was also read from Mr. Cooper, and it was agreed that it should be sent up to the Local Government Board; and also that the Clerk should inform that Board that Mr. Cooper was pursuing his duties very satisfactorily, considering the difficulties he had to contend with.

MR. JEANS' ACCOUNT. The queAtion of the costs incurred in the late litigation with the Newton Commissioners again came before the Board, and Mr. HARRISON proposed, and Mr. APPLETON seconded, that Mr. Jeans' account as presented to them be pail—This proposal was agreed to, Mr. Darbvshire being the only dissentient. This was all the business of public interest.

The Scotch Secretary bill is now regarded as safe, tnd the Marquis of Lothian has been selected as the first Sec- oetary for Scotland. PROTECTION FOR YOLINO GIRT.S.—A great meeting was held on Thursday evening in the Free Trade Hall, Manches- ter, under the presidency of Mr. C. E. Schwann, to urge upon Parliament the necessity of passing the Criminal Law Amendment Bill for the better protection of young girls. A resolution, moved by Mr. J. A. Beith, seconded by Dr. Peter Royle, and supported by the Rev. NV. A. O'Conor, the Rev. J. A. Macfadyen, and the Dean of Manchester, was unanimously passed. The Dean presided at an overflow meeting held in the Young Men's Christian Association Hall, at which the same resolution was adopted. KILLED AT DRILL —At the Riddlesdown Rifle Range on Saturday, James Caswell, a private in the Ist Battlion Scots Guards, was drilling with his company. The men were ordered to charge at the double, when the man on the I left of Caswell stumbled, with his rifle-butt on the ground and bayonet upwards. The deceased fell on the top of his comrade, whose bayonet entered the left side of his mouth and passed up into his brain. Caswell withdrew the weapon from his head, and expired within a quarter of an hour of the infliction of the injury. The man who caused the de- ceased to stumble is in custody. div.head: EXAMINER. SATURDAY, JULY 25, 1885.
div.p: THE EXAMINER. SATURDAY, JULY 25, 1885.
GENERU NEWS.
At noon on Sunday, an explosion occurred at a powder mill at Tunbridge. A man was blown across the river, and

he is not expected to live. It is stated that Mr. Michael Davitt has written to Mr. Chamberlain expressing his readiness to appear with him on any platform in Ireland during his tour through that country. THE RISING OF PARLIAMENT.—II ill expected that Par. Hai:milt will be enabled to rise, at the latest. on Thursday, August 6th. The promoters of temperance legislation in the House of Commons hope, by keeping their proposals upon the journals, to obtain an opportunity of snatching a

bill. CONFESSION or CANNIBILLISILL—A. Tyrolese has been arrested at San Dona, Venice, on a charge of kidnapping. The man admits the charge, and states that he has stolen a number of children and eaten them, having no other food. The account further states that the man appears to be mad. IMPRISONED FOR 25 YEARS.—Constance Kent, who was sentenced to penal servitude for life for the Road murder, which caused great sensation 25 years since, was liberated on Saturday on ticket-of-leave, owing to the convict's good conduct. She was released much sooner than was ex-

pected. CLUBS AND DRINK.—At Stratford, on Saturday, the trustees of the Prince Regent Working Men's Club snd In- stitute were summoned for selling beer without a license. Liquor was supplied on separate occasions to an inland revenue officer, who was accompanied by a member of the club. Fines amounting to £7O and costs were inflicted. The defendants gave notice of appeal. WRECK OF A LIFEBOAT AND LOSS OF EIGHT LIVES.—At an early hour on Wednesday morning, while the Caister yawl lifeboat Zephyr, with a crew of fifteen hands, was proceeding to the rescue of a brigantine which had gone on the Barber Sand, near Yarmouth, she struck upon a sunken wreck, and sank almost immediately. Seven of the men were saved by a shrimp boat, but eight were drowned. HORRIBLE DEATIL—At Aldershot, on Saturday night, two men of the Royal Artillery were intexiceted, and com- menced quarrelling about half-past ten on the verandah of the artillery barracks. After a desperate struggle, one threw the other over and was himself dragged over also, both falling heavily on the pevement. Tbe under- most was killed, and the other is lyibig in a very precarious state. CHESTER MUSICAL FESTIVAL —The three days' triennial musical festival opened at Chester on Wednesday with aounod's " Redemplon." Every seat was occupied at the opening performance. Dr. Bridge (Chester Cathedral) con- ducted, and Herr Straass led the band and chorus of 300 performers. The chorus is composed of picked voices from the Bradford Festival Choral Societ and the Chester festival chorus. 37, Charles Halle's choir, LORD GEORGE HAMILTON AT LIVERPOOL.— The First Lord of the Admiralty (Lord George Hamilton), in addres• sing a body of naval volunteers on Wednesday evening at Liverpool, said the Admiralty had come to the conclusion that we must for the future rely upoe local effort co-opera- ting with the military and naval forces of the Crown should there be any imminent danger. They were also of opinion that in order to increase the efficiency of naval volunteers some pecuniary aid ought to be given to them. He had now pleasure in announcing that it was the intention of the Government to grant that aid, which would in all probabil- ity take the shape of a capitation grant. SHOCKING SUICIDE OF A SOLDIER.—A private of the Royal Marines, named Wm. Hare, arrived at Chatham from the depot at Warner, on Saturday, and for some breach of discipline was sentenced by court-martial to five days in the cells. On returning from the orderly • oom, Hare managed to elude the vigilance of his guard, and started off at a rapid pace for the open country on the banks of the Med- way. After an exciting chase he was recaptured and con- veyed to the cells where, shortly after dinner on Monday he was discovered with his throat cut in a fearful manner, an earthenware plate having been used to inflict the wound. He was conveyed to the hospital, where he died. THE LAUDERDALE PEERAGE.—The Committee of Privi- leges of the House of Lord gave judgment on Wednealey in the Lauderdale peerage. Major Maitland claimed the title through Colonel Maitland, who died in New York in 1772. , The question turned solely upon the velidity of marriage of Colonel Maitland with Mary BPAelem two days before his death. Sir Gibson Maitland put in a counter claim, and argued by counsel that there was not sufficient evidence to establish the marriage in New York. Their lordships found that the marriage was valid and the previous offepring le- gitimated, and that even had there been neither banns nor license the marriage would not have been nullified, 1 but the contracting parties would have been liable to pun- ishment. THE MANCHESTER BETTING Can.—The principal case heard at the Manchester Assizes on Wednesday was that in which 29 men connected with the Ellesmere and Prince of Wales Clubs in Manchester were charged with having con- travened the Betting Act. Acting under the advice of coun- sel, 23 of the defendants pleaded guilty to a charge of using the clubs for betting purposes. The count charging them with conspiring to break the law was then withdrawn, and Prosecution did not offer any evidence against the six who pleaded net guilty. Mr. Justice Lopes said be had found it difficult to decide whether be should fine or imprison the defendants. The practice of betting at clubs was an evil and a nuisance, and must be put down. He ordered four of the defendants, who have previously been convicted of an offence against the Betting Act, to pay a fine of £lOO each ; four, in whose case mitigating circumstances were urged, were fined £10; and 12 were lined £75 each. The de- fendants were also ordered t 3 pay the costs of the prose- cution.. SUICIDE OF A LANCASHIRE MAGISTRATE.—Mr. Robert Whitaker, a magistrate, for the county of Lencaster for the last 15 years, and chairman of the Reyton Beach, commit- ted suicide on Tuesday morning at his residence, Brook- lands House, Royton. At eight o'clock he got up to dress, and when supposed to be washing himself cut his throat with a razor. The noise of a heavy fall alarmed the house. Medical aid was at once summoned, but he died an hour afterwards. Deceased should have appeared at the Man- chester Police Court at 11 to answer a charge of perjury preferred against him in swearing in two affidavits connec- ted with the floating of the Lancashire Spinning Company, which he was chairman of. He was also the defendant in an action for some thousands of pounds arising out of the same concern, and this case was to come on at the present Manchester Assizes. He was about 65 years of age. An inquest was held on Wednesday. The jury found that the deceased was of unsound mind at the time he committed i the act which cost him his life. MR. FORSTER AND THE BRADFORD LIBERAL ASSOCIA- TION.—Another phase has developed itself in the dispute of this aesociation with Mr. Forster. The senior member for Bradford asked the association to call a meeting of the elec- tors of the borough, to which he proposed to give a fare- well address prior to contesting the Central Division. Mr. Forster on Saturday received a resolution from the execu- tive committee stating that they did not think they would i be acting in harmony with their functions in undertaking ' arrangements for the meeting suggested by Mr. Forster. This resolution was arrived at at a private meeting of the executive committee held on Thursday night. The reeoln• tion was only passed after an animated and prolonged dis- cussion, in which several members who have hitherto been cpposed to Mr. Forster's line of action urged, for the sake of the unity of the party, an amicable end should be speedily put to the present relations between the association and the senior member. WIMBLEDON THE QUEEN'S PRIZE.—The Queen's Prize was won on Tuesday by Sergeant Bulmer, of the 2nd Lin- coln, with 307 points. Private Guy, 2nd Ayr, was second with 291 points; Private Newns, let Surrey, third with 288 points; and Private G. Watkins fourth with 287 points. The results of the Kirkham prize competition were issued on Tuesday. Lieut. Heap, 611 Lancashire, with 33 points, takes the piano, the second prize of £lO falling to Captain Godsal, 2nd Buck& who made 32. Private Thornton, sth Lancashire, wins r 2. There were 15 28'8 counted out. After the score of 68 in the Cambridge, the next best are a brace I of 66's made by Mr. Whitehead, of Bury, and Mr. Fraser, of 1 Edinburgh. On Wednesday the chief competition was that for the Kolapore Cup, between teams representing the mother country and her dependencies After a close struggle the first place was taken by England, with a grand total at the three ranges (200, 500, and 600 yards) of 650 points, Guernsey was second, with 1339; Jersey third, with 612; and Crnada last, with 597. A team of Indian marksmen had entered, but retired owing to having only six men present, against eight in the other squads. On Thursday Clifton won the Ashburton Challenge Shield, competed for by representatives of public schools. In the contest for the Elcho Shield England was victorious by a small majority. The scores were—England, 1,574; Scotland, 1,568; Ireland, 1,551. LIBERAL CONFERENCE.—Mr. John Morley, M.P., pre- sided on Wednesday afternoon at a conference held at Col- chester of the Liberal associations and clubs in the Eastern counties. There wore 57 associations represented. Earl Cowper sent a letter stating that he shculd have been glad had he been able to attend to bear public testimony to his adherence to the Liberal party. In opening the conference Mr. John Morley remarked that he did not think on the whole that what had happened during the past few weeks held out very encouraging prospects to thoir moderate friends, who were now seeing that they inieht go a great deal further and fare far worse than by remaining constant to those whom they had been denouncing as violent and immoderate. It had always been understood that it was a , very fine thing to have the courage of cne's opinions, but their Tory friends were showing them that it was a very tine thing to have the courage of other people's opinions. They were boasting of what a peace had fallen upon the House of Commons, but he wondered whether the staunch old country gentleman wouldthis time think it was "peace 1 with honour." The Liberal party would pursue the same I path as their forefathers, and in spite of all the nicknames 1 their opponents lavished upon them they would show them- selves while strenuous yet sober, while convinced yet tolerant, and while resolute and determined yet patient. A resolution was passed expressing satisfaction that the Fran- chise Act has been supplemented by the measure for the redistribution of seats, and congratulating eMr. Gladstone and his colleagues upon the complete success that has crowned their efforts to secure the enactment of these iin portent reforms. A resolution was passed urging the im- perative necessity of organisation, and another recognising the many eminent services rendered to his country by Mr. Gladstone during a political career of more than half a century. NOTES BY THE WAY.

The wet weather of Saturday proved very di appointing In the County Palatine, as it prevented a finish being made in the match at Liverpool, and almost entirely stopped club matches. The quality of the batting in county elevens seems to be improving greatly, and judging from the num- ber of matches which are left unfinished through want of time in the three days allotted to them, it seems as if some new departure will have to be taken. Many people think that the art of bowling is being neglected, while others see their way out of the difficulty by giving greater liberties to the bowlers, and use this as an argument against the recent action of Lord Harris and the Kent Executive. The meeting between Lancashire and Surrey was looked forward to in the north as the great event of the past week. There were wanting not a few who were inclined to think that the Southerners would prove the masters, but these were heartily glad when on Friday morning they saw that the formidable opponents had been got rid of for the small total of 117. The Surrey team was a full one with the ex- ception of Maurice Reaa, who is still disabled from the in- jury to his hand in the North and south match. The state of the wicket is in some measure to be blamed for the low scoring, but, apart from this, the play of the Lancastrians was admirable. The wicket produced 173 runs, the most remarkable stand on record in a first-class match. So pleased were the spectators with the treat afforded them that a subscription was opened and £.36 realised. In their second attempt Surrey fared much better, but when the time for drawing stumps came they were still 34 runs to the bad with five wickets to fall. Yorkshire, after their victory ever Notts, treated Glou- cestershire to a sound thrashing on Saturday. The Notts County Committee are carrying their crusade I against "imported Notts professionals to the utmost pos- sible limit. It is now reported at they have lodged an objection to two or three men at present playing for Sur- rey. In an hour and a quarter on Saturday the Middlesex and Notts match at Lord's was brought to a conclusion, Notts winning by an innings and 154 runs. The advantage gained by Notts on Monday at Brighton was so fully maintained on Tuesday that shortly after five o'clock the match terminated, Sussex sustaining a severe de- feat by an innings and 96 runs. In the match Lancashire v. M C.C. and Ground, Barlow and Mr. 0. P. Lancashire accomplished a remarkable batting performance for their county on Tuesday, when Lancashire, with one wicket down in their second innings, wanted 190

runs to win. The two men put on no fewer than 188 before they parted. Overnight the scores were—M.C.C., 122 and 108 for four wickets; Lancashire, 12; so that the Club, with six wickets to fall, had alrekdy 93 runs on. On resum- ing Marylebone completed their innings for 236. The county were left with 227 to get to win, and the runs were obtained for the loss of but two wickets, and Lancashire therefore obtained a brilliant victory by eight wickets.

The principal Dublin depositors of the Munster Bank have now signed the undertaking not to withdraw their deposits for six months. Edward Robert Teare, found guilty of having wilfully ' and with fraudulent intent to set fire to his drapery shop m Chester.road, Manchester. was sentenced to seven years' penal servitude. SENTENCED TO DEATH.—On Saturday, at Dur- ham, a domestic servant named Sarah Dunn. 17, was sen- tenced to be hung for having murdered her la mouths' old child by thrusting it into a drain a semi-liquid stream was flowing. She was convicted chiefly through the evidence of her father. _ . .

The fourth annual meeting of the International Arbitra- tion and Peace Association was held on Wednesday at the Westminster Palace Hotel. Sir George Campbell, M.P., pre. sided, and in addressing the meeting said that the principles of arbitration had lately succeeded in assuring the peace of England, of Europe, and of the entire world. SUPPOSED LOSS OF A SHIP AND 30 LIVES —All hops has been abandomd of the safety of the four-masted ship County of Aberdeen which, after landing a cargo of jute at Dundee, left Cardiff for Bombay on the 22nd December and has not since been reported. She was commanded by Captain Millar, of Aberdeen, no carried a crew of thirty hands, some of whom belonged to Fortarsitire. THE DOUBLE IVIURDER BY AN INSANE MOTHER.—At the Manchester Assizes, on Saturday, Margaret Hibbert was indicted for haying at Moss Side, Manchester, wilfully mur- tiered her two young boys. The prisoner, who had recently come out of a lunatic asylum, drowned the boys in a bath, and then tried to drown herself. Counsel for the defence submitted evidence that the prisoner .was not its a fit condi- tion to plead to the charge, and the gaol surgeon said the y omar. was perfectly insane, she entertaining the delusion that she bad only put the children to sleep. The jury found that she was unfit to plead. On Monday she was ordered to be detained in a lunatic asylum during Her Majesty's pleasure.

The most imposing booth was Total ,—Played on Saturday at I "Ghost exhibition," the expansive front of which was lavishly adorned with ghoul-like pictures, such • as the "Duel of Satan," in which " Auld Nickie Ben" is represented as achieving a very decided victory over a frail mortal, "Faust and Margaret," with Mephistopheles whispering his poisonous sug- gestions into the former's ear, and the sad" Death of poor Jim." Inside of this show there was a very creditable display ot dissolving views, most of the subjects of *Which seemed to be of that painfully sensational type which these itinerant showmen seem to find to " take " best with ' the British public, perhaps, as the scoffing French- man said, because they take their pleasures sadly. The visitor had the benefit of having connective explanations of these views, or rather was intended to have, as the reciter had to struggle unavailingly to make his voice heard above the ceaseless drone of the steam organs. The main at- 'traction of another booth was the" Great American • Beauty," whose beauty, however, was altogether dependent upon taste, as it was not of that kind which poets and painters love to delineate and sing. Of the greatness there could not be much question, for she was great in stature and circumference. The exhibition of this adipose prodigy was made de- cently and in order. She simply stepped from be- hind a curtain, and having staidly and deliberately wheeled round two or three times, again retired be- hind the curtain. "The Canadian Marvel " was to be seen in the adjoining erection. This was a man who, it was explained, had been born without arms, and who had in early lifebegan to use his feet in place of those invaluable members, and long practice, had certainly given him an astonishing proficiency in the use of his pedal extremities. The mallet and chisel, the saw, pen and paper, the concertina, and various other articles, were all " handled " and put to their proper uses in a way which left nothing to be desired. Outside the booths, the stalls, which were pretty well stocked with almost everything Which is most tempting to the immature tastes of juveniles, the swings, and the roundabouts were all apparently fairly well patronised. Taken altogether, it would seem that the fair, though it may be one Of those events which would be "more honoured in the breach than the observance," shows as yet no sign of decaying vitality. 'TILE ROYAL AGRICULTURAL SHOW., The showyard was opened at nine o'clock. The morning being doe, there again promises to be an exceptionally large attendance. The number at three o'clock on Thursday was over 9,000 larger than the total at Shrewsbury at the close of the seconeday. The special prizes for implements and the medals offered by the society have not yet been awarded. Excursions have again arrived in the town from all parts of the country, and crowds flock on to the ground to have the double privilege of seeing the Prince and the show. Miss Smithard, the demonstrator at the working dairy, which was visited by his Royal Highness on Thursday, delivered another lecture on Friday morning, and there are frequent illustrations of bee-driving at the

tent. I An enormous influx of visitors to the Royal Show at Preston on Saturday—the first "shilling day "—was natu- rally to be expected. Much, however, depended upon the weather, and unfortunately it happened to be of the worst character. Notwithstanding, however, the dull and un- promising morning, a steady stream of visitors began to pour into the Show Ground at an early hour. They were mostly from rural districts, and were evidently prepared to spend a profitable day at the show, come what would In the shape of rain or storm. Principally farmers, their wives, and dangliters were the early visitors, and the dogged m..an- ner in which they trudged through the mud, and the serious countenances, indicated a determination to learn something by the visit of the Royal Show. There was na sauntering aimlessly about in these early comers. They either com- menced a tour of the Showyard in a systematic way, or proceeded to some particular department which specially appealed to their tastes or pursuits, and there made a close and business-like study of the exhibits. This was the clans then on whom rain had no deterrent effect. The general Visitors came later on, and it must be said, taking into con- -1 . sideration the very unfavourable state of the weather, that they turned up in large numbers. By eleven o'clock the number that had passed through the turnstiles was 10,813. The record closed at seven o'clock with 34,302, the lowest attendance for the day that.the society has experienced for nine yeare. Notwithstanding the vast quantity of rain that fell during the day, the ground was not so sloppy as might , have been expected. and the only explanation that can be given of the comparative infrequency of mud puddles on Moor Park on Saturday is the thoroughness of the drainage operations which had been carried on by the Council. Tiled drains had been laid down throughout the grounds at intervals of six yards. Of course, remembering how the floodgates were opened on Sunday, the ground was in a much worse condition on the following Monday. Great In- terest was taken in the live stock, and large and critical par- ties, composed to a great extent of farmers, assembled, especially in the neighbourhood of the cattle sheds, and spent some time in examining the various classes. At eleven o'clock there was a parade of cattle in the large horse ring, and at half-past two the parade of agricultural and Cart horses commenced, and was succeeded by a display of the thoroughbreds, huntere, hackneys, and ponies. The usual exhibitions were made at the dairy, large crowds of persons tiking a•cleep interest in the various manipulations of the milk and butter. It was gratifying to note intently watching the dairy opsrations a large preponderance of people, generally farmers' wives and their daughters, who have a practical acquaintance with dairy work. This de- partment has been one of the principal attractions of the showyard, and the display of its resources was not wasted on Saturday. Bee-driving was another interesting feature, aud was not looked upon altogether in the light of a curious exhibition, as one would look upon a snake-charming sjance. Many of the country people, who still in the cultivation of bees stick to the old-fashioned straw skep and primitive methods of extracting honey, learned a great deal from Mr. Baldwin about bee-keeping appliances, and how to handle bees with impunity at.d drive them from one hive to another. The afternoon was miserably wet, and there was • not a sign the whole day of any clearing up in the weather. The heavy fall of rain on Sunday eight thoroughly satu- rated the stiff clayey soil of Moor Park, and the tramp of thousands of feet on Monday morning churned the ground In many places into a mass of viscous mud which clung to people's boots and rendered walking a difficult task. During the day 1490 S persons passed the turnstiles, bringing the total for the week up to 94,013, exclusive of about 400, the attendance at the implement show on Tuesday, and admis- sion of exhibitors, members, holders of season tickets, Sze., a hich must have been considerable. -.---arelse--- -

Late on Wedmesday night an ex-Guardsman amend Whiteley, who lived in one of the " mansions" near the Victoria Station, London, shot at his wife three times with a revolver, and then killed himself with the same weapon. The poor woman received three bullets in her head and neck. THE POST•OFFICE.—The annual report of the Post- master-General was issued on Saturday. It shows a con- siderable growth on several branches of the department, hut the telegraph business does not develop as largely as had been expected. The expenditure largely exceeds the revenue, and for two years no contribution has been made towards the payment of interest on the debt. The total number of persons in the employ of the Post-office is about 48,000. TErtuirmE EXPLOSION IN LIVERPOOL.—A terrible explo- sion, caused it is believed, by spontaneous combustion, took place on Thursday at the works of the Liverpool Sac- chsirne Company. The roof of the premises were blown otf and the place set on fire. One of the workmen was severely burned and remains in the hospital ; others bad narrow escapes. The lire brigade attended in strong force, and the fire was fortunately extimzuished though not before considerable damage had been done.

Secretaries of Cricket Clubs are requested to flak' that reports of matches played on Saturday must be sent tc the head office, Bewsey-street, Warrington, not later thaa ton o'clock on Wednesday morning.

EARLESTOWN. NEwrow Toww Her.m.—Considerable improvements have been effected in the Town Hall at Newton during the past week. It has undergone a thorough renovation, and its interior has been painted and dtcorated by Mr. William Windtanley, of Newton, who secured the contract for the I work.

SLEEPING IN A BAN.—Thomas Hallman, a striker, was brought before Mr. B. Houghton, at the Town Hall, New- ton, on Wednesday afternoon, on a charge of sleeping in an old barn in Wargrave New-road, owned by Mr. T. Chambers The case was proved by P.C. Hunt, and the prisoner was committed for 14 days. HELPLESSLY Dssusx.—Before 'Mr. W. F. Gooch, at the Earlestown Police Station, on Monday morning, John Connellan, A farm labourer, living at Bartonwood, was charged with being drank in Bridge-street at half-past one on Sunday naorning. P.S. Commins and P.C. McMullen found the prisoner lying helplessly drank across the foot- path is Bridge-street, and they conveyed him to the police station._ He was fined 5s and costs.

A Ilivsracx ON Flii.---AbOut nine o'clock on Tuesday morning a stack of Hay owned by Mr. Richard Morris, of the Sunbeam Inn, Wargrave Old-road, Earles- town, was damaged by fire. The stack was in a field near the Sunbeam, and about the time it was discovered to be on fire. Fortunately plenty of water was close at hand and by means of buckets water was poured on the flames. In a few minutes the fire was extinguished, but one end of the stack was serious y burnt. It is not known how the fire originated. DEATH OF MR. THOMAS Vrearts.—The death of Mr. Thomas Vicars, head of the firm of Messrs. T. and T. Vicars, engineers, &c., Liverpool and Earlestown, on Friday last, was publicly announced by the hoisting of the flag at half mast on the roof of the branch works at farlestovvn.
Mr. Vicars was highly respeCte-d-iii-Ei;;;;Olt 'where he was known to a large circle of friends. Re was. less known in . . . .

Earlestown and the immediate district, as the branch works there were more directly managed by and in charge of his two sons. His remains were interred in Antield Cemetery, Liverpool, on Tuesday afternoon.

ELECTION COMMISSIONERS,—The annual elec- tion of three Improvement Commissioners for the township of Newton has, as was last week expected, passed off with- out a contest. The retiring members of the Board were Colonel George McCorquodale, Mr. T. .1. Gillespie, and Mr. J. E. Pardey ; and these three gentlemen were again nominated. Messrs. George Ratcliffe, John Barr, and C. F. Borten were also nominated, but as the two lot named and Mr. Pardey declined to stand Colonel McCorquodale, Mr. Gillespie, and Mr. Ratcliffe have been elected without op- position. In case a poll had been necessary the voting would have taken place on Wednesday last in the District Infants' Schoolroom Market-street, Earlestown. On the evening of that day the annual township meeting was held, and a report of the proceedings appears elsewhere. Capra Pec-enc.—The choir and friends of the Pri- mitive Methodist Chapel, Legh-street, Earlestown, held their annual pic-nic on Wednesday, and speat a very 'pleasant day at Southport. The party, numbering about 50, left Earlestown station at 7-30, and arrived at their destination shortly after half-past nine. Their departure was amid a shower of rain, but before the end of the jour- ney was reached the weather cleared up and for the rest of I the day it was all that could have been desired. During the day the company visited the Botanical Gardens and other S' attractions" of the town, in addition to having an enjoyable sail upon the sea. Both dinner and tea were served at Kay's refreshment rooms. Tee return journey was commenced about seven o'clock, and the company arrived home shortly after eight. The arrangements had been satisfactorily carried out by Mr. W. Banton (leader of the choir), and Mr. E Dickens. THE WARGRAVE BIRTEMAY CLUB.—The first pic-nic of the season in connection with the Wargrave Birthday Club—a society formed for having periodical "Outs "to the principal places of interest in the district—was held on Sat- urday. The party, numbering about 30, assembled at the house of Mr. Peter White, the Victoria Inn, Wargrave, and took their seats in a waggonette supplied by Mr. J. T. Fletcher, and drawn by four " greys." The horses had been decorated with roses, mad as each member of the party wore a new white hat and had a red rose in the button- hole of has coat, the "turn-out" was a striking one. A start was made about half-past eight, and as the pleasure- seekers passed through the Vulcan their approach was heralded by notes from a bugle. The destination of the company was Halton Towers, and at this charming spot, notwithstanding the inclement weather in the afornoon, the day was pleasantly spent. The party arrived home about ten o'clock. A MAD DOG KILLED AT EARLESTOWN.—An exciting oc- currence was witnessed in Market-street, Earlestown, on Thursday afternoon. Abbut one o'clock a large dog, a cross between a retriever and Newfoundland, was noticed in the street, frothing at the mouth and manifesting other signs of suffering from rabies. It is stated that it 'eit another deg and then ran into the shop of Mr. Pollard, pork butcher. Here it lay down in a corner, but the assiAsiet, a man named Richard Cross Griffin, seized a lump of thick wood known as a "Gambreel " (an instrument for suspending the bodies of pigs) and drove out the unwelcome intruder. A number el people assembled with the cry of "Mad dog," and as the strange animal severely bit Mr. Pollard's terrier 'dog about the ear and legs, the man Griffin followed it. The dog ran through the shop of Mr. T. Molyneux into Cable-street, and thence into Lawrence-street, where the people, considerably alarmed, rushed into their houses in fear. As it made a rush at another dog in the street. Griffin ran I and dealt it a blow on the head which partially stunned it. The dog, however, again ran along Cable-street and round by the New Market Inn (Mr. W. Mailings), and it finally I lodged near the door of Mr. Boardman's shop in Market- street. Here Griffin again rushed at the animal and sue- ' needed in killing it with a heavy blow on the head with the " Gambreel." Griffin has been complimented for his bravery, and the large number of people who assembled displayed signs of relief when the dog had been killed. FOOTBALL CONTEST AT WIGAN.—A considerable number of persons from Earlestown visited Wigan on Saturday afternoon, to witness a six-a-side football contest in connec- tion with the annual sports promoted by the Wigan Cricket and Football Club. Among the teams competing were J. Duxbury's team (Earlestown), J. Whalley's team (Earles- town and Haydock St. James's). The other clubs entered and the matches played were as follows :—Wigan easily disposed of Weathoughton • Blackburn Rovers did not turn up, and New Springs had a bye; ll,ydock (St. James's) defeated Springs Branch : and Laith- waite's team (Elindley), had the better of Wigan Hornets. The two teams from Earlestown were drawn together in the first round, ond were composed as follows :—Duxbury's team: J. Duxbury, R. Bowker, J. Green, J. teim and A. W. Dagnall. Whallev's team : J. Whalley, R. Green, J. Ogden, J. Ellison, S. Williams, and J. Harrison. The game Wee limited to ten minutes.each way. The play Was ef a fast and exciting character, Whalley's team securing a victory by two goals to none. The winners of these ties met again Monday evening in the presence of a large concourse of spectators. The Wigan team beat Haydock St. James's by one goal and one touchdowl to one goal though the Havdock men had by far the best of the game. Earlestown and New Springs succeeded, Earlestown win- ning by two goals to one. Ilindley had a bye, and in the next round they were drawn against Wigan, Earlestown thus being "lucky "in securing the bye. The Wigan team defeated their opponents by four to none. Tte even- ing lead so far advanced when the last game was concluded that it was decided to postpone the final tie between Wigan and Whalley's team (Earlestown).
THE COMMISSIONERS AND RATEPAYERS. ANNUAL MEETING.

The annual joint meeting of the Improvement Commis- sioners and Ratepayers of the Township of Newton, for passing the accounts of the Board and transacting any other township business, was held in the District Infants' School, Market-street, Earlestown, on Wednesday afternom. The chair was occupied by Mr. W. F. Gooch, J.P. (chair- man of the Commissioners), and there were also present— Messrs. B. B. Glover, T. Forster, and G. Ratcliffa (Com- missioners) ; R. Brierley (surveyor), the Bev. T. H. Mat- thews, and Messrs. Burchall, M. Birkhead, N. Scott, Joseph Lythgoe, Whiteneld, and James Lyttgoe.
THE RECENT ELECTION.

The Chairman said he had to report and declare that 512ssrs. George McCoripodale, T. J. Gillespie, and George Ratcliffe had been elected Commissioners for the ensuing year with- mit opposition in place of those who retired.

AcCOLINTS —THE INCREASED IMPROVEMENT RATE. Printed copies of the accounts (a summary of which has appeared in these columns) were distributed among those present, and the Chairman asked if someone would more that they be passed.—Mr. B. B. Glover moved that the accounts be taken as read, and adopted.—The Rev. T. R. Matthews : I beg to second that.—Mr. Ratcliffe said he noticed they had an increase of 4d in the £on the Im- provement rate. Last year it was 93, and this year it was is ld.—The Chairman : That is to meet the new cemetery. —Mr. Ratcliffe asked if it was not possible to levy the rate as a cemetery rate, so that it would have gone over the en- tire district. The landed class only paid one-fourth of the Improvement tate, so that on it id they would only be pay- ing 31d.—The Chairman said the surveyor informed him that the Act clearly detined that the cemetery must be put on the Improvement rate. It was considered by the Com- missioners and they levied the rate in accordance with the Act—Mr. Glover rose to a point of order. Ile did not think that question ought to be raised at that meeting. The pro- position was that the accounts be taken as read, and the rate they were discussing refesred to the coming year. He suggested that Mr. Ratcliffe should raise the questitin at the first Board meeting he attended. The Commissioers were compelled by Act of Parliament to charge the, Cemetery rate on the General Improvement rate, though he had no doubt the Commissioners as a body would have been glad if they could have put the Cemetery rate upon the whole of the property of the district. It was a fact that land owners and railway companies simply paid upoa one-fourth of their assessments, so that cottages were paying more than they really should do in proportion.—The Chairman held that it was in the power of the Commissioners to alter any rate that'might be wrong or wrongly laid.—The matter then dropped, and the accounts were passed.

PIZESCOT. ANNUAL MARCH OUT OF THE VOLVItTEERS...—The local corps of volunteers, of whom the town may well be proud, on Thursday evening, at seven o'clock, assembled at their headquarters, the Assemblyloom for the purpose of their annual march ont, which should Wave taken place on Shrove Tuesday, but owing te the unpropitious weather was post- poned. They mustered 80-rank and file, with their band of 23 members, under the command of Captain J. C. Gamble, Lieutenant A. Hall, Colour-Sergeant Scotson, Sergeants Chorley and Jackson, Band-Sergeant J. Welsby. The route taken was through Huyton by Huyton-lane to Roby, where refreshments were partaken of at the Stanley Arms Hotel. On the way the men were put through their sections. They presented a clean and soldier-like appearance, and are now stronger in number and more efficient than ever they were, 160 being on the roll. The return was made shortly after 10 o'clock. PetashoT BOARD OF GFARDIANS.—The fortnightly meet- ing of this Board was held at the Whiston Workhouse on Thursday afternoon, when Mr. J. Leatherbarrow presided. There were also present the Rev. T. Chambers and Rev. J. Barnacle.—A splendid basket of flowers had been presented to the inmates of the Workhouse hospital by the Rev. T. Chambers (Guardian for Rainhill), and the Chairman said the Guardians would be wanting in courtesy if they did not accord to Mr. Chambers their cordial thanks.—On the mo- tion of Mr. Dobell, tne thanks of the Guardia, s were ten- dered to the Rev. T. Chambers, who, in acknowledging the compliment, said it had afforded him great pleasure to bring the flowers, and he hoped to be able to bring more during the season. (Applause.)—Mr. Hale (the Workhouse master) reported that there were 408 inmates in the Work- , house this week, against 409 last week, and 420 in the cor- responding week last year. There had been 48 vagrants relieved during the week against 54 in the corresponding week last vear.—Mr. Borchelt expressed the opinion that it was time there was another revision of the list of out-door paupers, and moved that a revision should take place as early as possible.—The Chairman maid it must be under- stood that the expense of an investigation of the out-door pauper list would have to be borne by the members them- selves.—Mr. Newsome seconded the motion, which was adopted. FUNERAL OF THE REV. B. VARLET.—A large number of friends assembled at the Wesleyan Chapel, Eccleston-street, at half-past two o'clock on Monday, and proceeded to the late residence of Mr. Varley, Ward-street, where the funeral procession was formed, and a hymn was sung. The coffin was covered with beautiful wreaths, and was followed by Mrs Vatley and her father, Rev. George Allen, Mr. and Mrs Kelly, brother-in-law and sister (Mr. Robert Varley, brother, arrived at the graveside before the conclusion of the service) the Revs. J. Shipham, superintendent St. Helens and Pres- cot circuit, James Johnston, congregational, Mr. S. H. Hartley, clerk of the union, Mr. T. P. Hewitt, Mr. J. B. Pratt, Mr. Molyneux, Whiston, Mr. Lawrenson, Mr. J. C. Leadbetter. The congregation, bible classes, and Sunday schools of the district were numerously represented. The cortege numbered about a hundred and fifty and the streets were lined through the town by hundreds of people. The vicar, the Rev. H. A. Macnaughten, placed the church at their diaposal, and he himself read the scripture portion of the service in this church, the concluding portion being conducted by the Rev. J. Shipham. while the choir sang " Give me the wings of faith to rise." The deceased dur- ing the short time he was in Prescot had endeared himself to a large circle of friends, and the visits of the " blind' preacher, as he was familiarly called, will be greatly

missed. HEAVY PENALTY FOR CRUELLY WORKING A HORSP.--At the Prescot Petty Sessions on Tuesday, before Mr. F. W. Earle, Mr. W. L. Evans, and Captain Willis, John Critchley, a master carrier, of St. Helens, was summoned for allowing his horse to be worked in an unfit state on the 11th inst. The defendant pleaded guilty.—P.S. Bull deposed that at half-past eight on the night of the 11th ult, he saw a horse drawing a waggon up the brow in Derby-street, Prescot, from the direction of Liverpool. A man named Cooper was in charge. He examined the horse, an old one in low condi- tion, and found a large raw wound, from which matter and blood was flowing beneath the saddle ; the whole of the shoulder was tender and very sore, while a portion of the shoulder was also raw. On the top of the head was another raw sore. The man Cooper said his master knew all about the wounds when he sent the horse out—William Cooper, employed by the defendant, said the latter was aware of the wounds on the horse.—Superintendent Barker stated that the defendant had been twice convicted on previous occa- sions for cruelty.—The Bench considered the case a very bad one, and though the defendant bad been twice previ- ously convicted, they would give him another chance and not send him to gaol. He would be fined £5 and costs. If he again came before them he would be sent to prison like a man named Robinson, who was committed to prison for three months for a similar offence.—The man named Cooper was summoned for working the horse in an unfit state, but the case was withdrawn on the application of Superintendent Barker.
