THE CLOSING OF MORLEY COMMON.

Sir,—The correspondent who first called attention to the above subject told us that Sir Gilbert's keeper was on the Common warning people off. This, so far has not been denied. If the Railway Company have closed the road, who authorised Sir Gilbert's keeper to turn folks back? May I also ask whether snipe is the only " shootable "article on Morley Common 7—Yours, drc., TOMMY ATKIN.

div.head: SM GILBERT GREENALL AND. HIS SNIPE.
div.p: SM GILBERT GREENALL AND. HIS SNIPE.

Sit.:;:-TII; amiable old gentleman who lives at Walbn and aspires to the favour of the Conservative electors of the Borough of Warrington is, I see by your columns, still figuring in practice as the determined enemy of the working- men, at whose hands he asks the distinction of becoming once more an ornament to the British House of Commons, I thank you for the exposure. Does the Tory candidate think that the working-men of Warrington, even such as are professedly Tory, will in spite of the notorious facts that stare them in the face, believe him when he tells them from the platform that he loves them as his own. Yea, that he loves them with a great and yearning affection. Bah! Eng- lish working-men have sense enough to judge a man by his deeds, and they know that if Sir Gilbert cares more for a few paltry snipe than for the pleasures of his poorer brethren, his love for them is a singular one. It may be said that the stoppage of a footpath is no great hard- ship and that the labouring-man can turn his steps in another direction, but these little things are straws that show the current of the stream. What I say is, let the working voters of this town leave Sir Gillant in the enjoy- ment of Walton fishing and snipe rearing, pursutts much more saitahle, one would think, to his taste and capacity, than sharing the deliberations of statesmen. If he will so despise the poor in small things, how much more so would he do it great things—if he had the chance. But be will no doubt be left sitting on that fence which you mention in in- glorious obscurity, yearning for the honours that he has lost and is not likely to regain.—Yours, dtc., July 23, 1885. ONts DISGUSTED. _

MORLEY COMMON AND SIR GILBERT GREENALL. Sir,—l am glad to find that this matter is being investi- gated. Let me tell you my experience. I have been a regular user for the past 26 years of the footpath now under discussion. Three weeks ago last Sunday afternoon I went -

as usual for a walk to Walton. I was Much surprised to find the old stile taken away, and some pailings nailed up to prevent people getting over. I got over, however, and when about half way across the Common I met a keeper of Sir Gilbert's, who eyed me over very sternly, but made no remark. I was returning some time later in the evening, and, after again climbing over the fence, I bad got about half way across the "snipe" ground, when a man ran down out of the railway signal box at Walton Junction and shouted to me to stop. When he got nearer, I saw that he was the man whom I had met in the afternoon, that is, a keeper of 'Sir Gilbert's. The keeper then told me I must tarn back and go round by Weir's farm, which would have taken me a good share of half a mile out of my way. I said I would not go back, and told him he had no authority to turn me back, and, in fact, that he had been trespassing himself on the railway. I offered to give him my name and . _ _ .

address, but he said " other people had done Let, and he had found that they hid misled him." I then said he *mild follow me home if he liked to see that my statement was true. This, of course, he refused to do. I had seen him, while I was coming across the Common, tarn two other "couples" back, and this made me all the more deter- mined to go straight on. He then told me that some years ago they had been able to get a dozen brace of snipe er so in a season off this marsh, but since those "low fellows and their dogs had been in the habit of coming across they never could get one, and they had determined to put a stop to the trespassing." I still refused to go back, and after keeping tee about half an hour I was allowed to go on. I consider it is a monstrous shame to attempt to deprive amrking-men especially of this pleasant path, and if it had not been that I did not wish to have a " row " on a Sunday lam not sure whether that " obstruction " would not have been speedily removed. I enclose my nams in proof of my statements, and am quite prepared to substantiate them before anybody. We working-men have, in my opinion, nobody but Sir Gilbert Greenili to thank for the footpath being close], and I Would willingly be one of a number to see if it needs to remain closed.--I am, Sir, yours truly, A WORKING-MAN FROM BANK QUAY.
A SAMPLE OF TORY EQUALITY.

- want a little of your help to spread abroad the Rae. J. M. Sangar's opinion respecting the religion of our Roman Catholic brethren. It would be a great pity if this new acquisition to the Tory party should have to depend Upon a halfpenny rushlight for driving out Catholic dark- more so as just at the present time there seems to be a determined yet spazmodfc effort to gain, not only place, but Power, by any means however unscrupulous, by these new fledget lovers of the people. The Rev. J. M. Sangar, pastor Of the Emmanuel Church, Bold-street, preached a special sermon to the brethren of the Orange Lodges in this district, and, mind you, Mr. Editor, the brethren wore their regalia in ciu-ch. Faecy the rev. gentleman looking around at his brethren, decked out in their sparkling regalia, the symbol of undying hatred, and the badge of darkness, belonging to a by-gone day. How the rev, gentleman must have felt stirring within him "the peace which passeth all under- standing "as he went on with his sermon, thanking God for deposing James 11, one of the kings who reigned in

England by Divine right, and bringing Over to this country a Dutchman, who also reigned by Di ine right! How he must have warmed to his subject at the thought that he, and those before him, were Protestants, and not schismatics, of the Church, yet not in the Chhrch. This is rather com- plex, Mr. Editor, but the rev. gentleman will understand it, and Irish Catholics and English Catholics must understand him; when speaking of their religion this rev, gentleman termed it" heathenism." Yes, this man dared to stand be- fore his fellowmen and stigmatise the religion of three- fourths of Irishmen as being nothing but heathenism. Fellow countrymen! I beg you will beware of these new-found friends, the Tories, ere it be too late. SHAMUS.

JOHN KING'S WIDOW.—FINAL APPEAL. Sir,—More than three months ago I made an appeal through the press on behalf of the widow of " Old John King,' who died on January 29th last, in his 90th year, and who was the first man in England who signed the pledge of total abstinence in 1832. His widow is now working as gatekeeper on the railway, on the scanty pittance of 35 6d per week. Site is required to be at her post 151 hours daily, and in all weathers. We want to raise money enough to , Place her in comfort. Her late husband was, throughout life, a comparatively poor elan; and in his later years a serious affection of the eyes entailed a large outlay for med- ical attendances and consultations, and for a long time pre- vented him from following his work. Consequently, at his death, his wife found herself in very straitened circum- stances. Her devotion to him was beyond all praise, and it Is, I think, but right that temperance people especially should be asked to subscribe to the fund now being raised. It is estimated that there are some 4,000,000 total abstainers in Great Britain and Ireland. I have, so far, received about £55. "What is this among so many ?" I have received subscriptions from (among others) Sir Wilfrid Lawson, M.P., and the Rev. Charles Garrett, and the latter has also kindly written an epitaph to be placed on the tombstone which we propose to place over .King's remains in South- port Cemetery. This we shall be quite unable to do unless a greater number of our friends come foward and help the fund. We ought to raise at least £2OO. This is the last ap- peal I shall make, and I trust it will be responded to in a way which will reflect credit upon the temperance commu- nity, who owe so mnch to John King, one of the staunchest pioneers of the great temperance reform movement. I will gladly send collecting cards to all applicants. Cheques and P.o.o's should be made payable to yours very truly, S. NORBURY WILLIAMS,
Hon. Sec. and Treasurer. Chorlton-cunepHardv, near Manchester, July 16, 1885.

THE "PALL MALL GAZETTE" REVELATIONS. Sir.—Allow me to thank you on behalf of many of your readers for the clear and spirited statement regarding the shocking revelations that have just thrilled the nation, which you gave in your last week's issue. It seems to be beyond doubt that the horrifying details published by the plucky London evening journal have their foundation on fact, incredible as it might seem, and that is surely excuse enough for their publication, especially when it is con- sidered that by no other means did it seem possible to gain ju.tice for the innocent children of the poor. It is a sad re&ction on our boas Led Christianity that such a state of things should have existed, but now that the exposure has come shall these enormities be allowed to continue? No, a thousand times no. There are yet left noble, pure-minded men and women, who would sacrifice life itself in the cause of innocent girlhood, and these will see that the agitation commenced shall not die; and SOMO Of the aristocratic, despots who have made a hell upon earth with their mis- spent wealth may learn this to their dismay. The Press, which, with a few honourable exceptions at first igeored by silence the bold move of the Pall Mall Gazette, can no longer remain silent, and the pressure of public opinion will tell. Now is the time for our ministers of religion to throw off the veil of false modesty which excludes from pulpit reference a subject so shameful, and to speak with no uncertain voice against these abominations. Let them do this for the sake of the religion they profess, and even deign to follow somewhat in this respect the noble example of the Salvation Army, and then ere long the reproach may be taken from us. But it must also be seen to, if laws are passed sufficiently stringent to make this notorious abduc- tion and seduction impossible, that they are rigidly enforced, or else for bread we shall receive a stone. What we want, and will have, is not only a law capable of suppressing thesa abominations, but the determined carrying out of such law. —Yours. dm., A FATHER OF DAUGHTERS. July 24th, 1885.
WORKING MEN AND THE FORTHCOMING GENERAL ELECTION.

Sir,—l have always found your paper an impartial organ for the free veptilation of public opinion. In fact, it is the only one in this district that ventures to advocate the cause of the people. I was much gratified in reading " Pedestrian's " letter, in which he exposes the folly of the working, men of Warrington putting any trust in Tory pro- mises. Now, it would be wrong to charge the late Conser- vative member for your town with acting contrary to his political creed, for his actions have been in strict accord with the Tory principle of curtailing the liberties of the many for the gratification of the few. But for all that, it comes with bad grace even from a Tory, after the great interest he pretended to have in the people. The working-man will have to be on his guard against such oily-tongued vote-catchers. He will find plenty just now that will appear to take a remark- able interest in his case. But let all enlightened voters put little trust in Tory candidates, for it is well to have in mind that a Tory is a Tory for all that. Underneath these fair words lies a determined opposition to the advancing liber- ties and enlightenment of the people, no matter how this is concealed—even if under garb in its latest form of "Tory Democracy." The old spirit of feudal tyranny is there, and if it was not kept down hy the weight of Radicalism it would Rot, I think, be long before Toryism would appear divested 9! the frail covering that now, in part, hides its deformitia The fact that the Tory patty have in a few instancett sanctioned what we may call Radical measures Veil for little in my mind, for in all stith Cates it has been forced from them, because they found thenasehres not strong enough to oppose the national demand, they knowing well if they attempted to do otherwise HON sweets of office would be a thing that they could not esjoy. Ido not say that we must believe all the tromises of the Liberals either. No, not half of them. The working-man must not be content with either; but he must get candidates from among his own class, pledged to his interests, and his alone.—l remain, yours, &c., SUB-ROSA. , Frodeham, July 21st.

div.head: CAUCUS AND ITS WORK.
div.p: THE CAUCUS AND ITS WORK.

Sir —Conservative phrase-mongers seem to 1:)e quite over- joyed at the success of their own coinage. In America caucus signified a small knot of unscrupulous political whe- t:milers ; if it ever means the same in Esglaod it will be the peoples' own fault. Do our ConserVative friends remember how candidates were selected, and elected, previous to the days of reform ? Let them look hick a little, and glance over the twenty odd years during which Sir Gilbert Greenall misrepresented this borough, and tell us how many times he appealed to the inhabitants as to what their wishes were. If they will be candid they must confess that it was at caucus meetings held at the Lion Hotel, meetings at which a few of the big wigs of the party decided, at once and for all, who should be the member. I don't blame the Tories for this. Before Liberal- ism was born, and only the Whig and Tory existed to divide the fat of the land between them, no other way was possible. _

With reform, a new word came into use; Liberalism asserted itself, and it is often sneered at as being more sel- fish than its predecessor, but there are few students of poli- tical history who will not ackrowledge that its tendency has been to knock off the fellers that bound the workman's life to the employer's wishes. True, it has not made itself famous as the giver of doles; tbe load of coals and the pair of blankets at Christmas are missing, but Liberal legislation has built up English trade; ninety per cent of the manu- facturers throughout England are Liberals to-day, and if working-men will stand by them, be true to their own in- terest, they will soon break the fetters which Toryism, in the guise of" landed interest," insists upon rivetting upon trade.

- Liberalism, since the borough suffrage and the ballot became law, has had to place itself more in conformity with the people's wishes. When a few only of the inhabitants had the right of voting, it was an easy matter to get at their wishes; not only this, bat the political machine was simple for carrying out their wishes. When the voters in boroughs like Birmingham, Manchester, or our own small town, counted their thousands, it was necessary something more than a snug little meeting in the chief hotel should be called. The Liberals felt that first of all a good education must be given to every child. This the Tories opposed. They knew also that justice demanded that where a people' were taxed they should have °the power of appointing their own representatives. This also the Tories opposed. Here we have two features that, hand in hand, have come to the present generation in consequence of the perseverance of the Liberal party. The amount of money now spent in ca acation proves its success. The question is, how shall full and complete representation be brought to a Success? We want a candi- date ; how shall we get at him? How shall we select him ? And when we have selected him, how shall we form our- selves into a solid body so that we may carry our mail? These are the questions that touch upon the much derided system called, by our Tory antediluvian friends "the Caucus." To accomplish our end we call a ward meeting; every Liberal in the ward has a right to be there, and a right to speak, and a right to vote, in the election ef a re- presentative to the Central Management Committee of the party, and here we have, without more trouble, and open to the eye of every man of the party, a system which, if each man does his duty, cannot fail to give satisfaction to each individal member of the party. Organise is the advice given to each political party. How do the Tories in- terpret the word? What Tory working-man has had any part in selecting the land-grabber to represent him ? If they have had any part in his selection, in what does it differ from caucus methods?

Well, Mr. Edit;;;;;; far as I see, the system of focusing the aggregate political opinion of the party depends but upon one thing to make it a complete success, and that is that each man does his duty, and does not leave it to others. The voters having put themselves in order and ran4ed themselves under their respective leaders, select their can- didate. This in the past has net been a very difficult job. In the future, if we intend to reap any advantage from lhe extension of the franchise, great care will have to be taken ; vested interests from all directions will crop up, alai each will want its representative. Hitherto land and capital have

div.head: EXAMINETI, SATURDAY. JULY 25. I'BBs.
div.p: THE EXAMINETI, SATURDAY. JULY 25. I'BBs.

absorbed the whole of the attention of legislators. Labour I will ask now for more attention, but before labour can have its due we must clear the way. Saint Michael and his Tory Democratic leader, Lord Randolph, are just on the verge of dishing the Tories. When this is done Whiggism will be absorbed; Radicalism can then shake itself free, and then the question will be—What will it do with its new found power? The land question will be one of the first to demand notice. .. He ties up hands That locks ap lands. Tie lands which can't be sold and bought Bring men and states to worse than nought; The lands which can't be freely sold Are worth a world of barren gold" _ .

Just now the Tories are bidding very high for the people's vote. Parnell and Lord Randolph seem to be hand And glove with each other, to the great consternation of the staid and ancient _fogy, the Tory county member. Raving promised to do a great deal for the people in the Fair Trade direction, we are to have an inquiry. Radicalism will soon settle this ; the land question forces the people to herd together like pigs in all our large towns. The land laws make the working-man's wages go into the lan owners' pockets. Rich Tory landed magnates are trying to persuade working-inen that if we keep foreigners out of our markets by some neat Fair Trade juggling, that is all we reqdire. Why don't they tell working-men that they have to pay, in the shape of reduced wages, to rich landowners a royalty for iron ore that would fully compensate the manufacturers without taking it from the workman. In Germany toe ore belongs to the State; here we pay per ton as follows :
Great Britain: Cleveland. Scotland. Cumberland. Gm•many. France, 3s. 63. 6s 6s 3d 6d. Bd.

No need to talk of Fair Trade if working-men will only open their eyes! If they want to make their trade better, they must look keenly after two points; the land from which the ore comes, and the railways that carry the ore. These two sources are making millionaires and turning large towns into modern Babylons.
CLIFFORD DIX.
ATTEMPTED FORGERY.

What Is supposed to have been an attempt at fraud upon Parr's Banking Company, Limited, was made at Warrington on Thursday forenoon. An advice had been received by the bank authorities purporting to be from the National Provincial Bank of England Establishment at Pwßell, in South Wales. It was apparently signed by the manager there, and asked the bank authorities at Warrington to pay to Mrs. Mary Taylor, ore account of John Taylor, the sum of £2OO. On Thursday forenoon a well-dressed lady called at the bank at Warrington had claimed the MOO as belong- ing to her. She was informed that the money could not te given to her, as their correspondent had not given them the means of identifying her as Mrs. Taylor, and that she would have to be introduced by some one known to them before business could be transacted. She went away, and - shortly afterwards returned with a gentlemanly man of military appearance, but as he also was unknown matters were not facilitated. The lady said she had come to live in Parker-street, Warrington, that the man who had paid in the money was John Taylor, her husband, who, she ex- pected, would join her on Saturday. She produced a leer frem him, in which he stated that he was coming to War- , rington, and then they would consult as to the disposition of the money, although he thought that it would be better that it should remain in the bank for the present. The bank authorities refused to pay the money, and telegraphed to their correspondents at Pwlleli, and a reply was received Ito the effect that they knew of no such advice. The lady, however, was asked to go away and return in an hour or so, when it was hoped a telegram would be received from South I Wales, but she did not put in an appearance. Yest,rday morning a telegram was received at the bank at Warrington stating that the advice, which had been sent by plat to Pwlleli, was a forgery. Neither the lady nor the gentleman have since been seen at the bank.

WARRINGTON. 'sT. JAIIES'S NATIONAL SctrooL.—The managers of St. James's National School, Latchford, have accep- ted the tender of Messrs. Gibson and Son for the erection of new schools, and the work will shortly be proceeded with.. _ .

ANNIVERSARY SERMONS.—On Sunday anniver- sary sermons were held in Bold-street Wesleyan Chapel, when sermons were preached, morning and evening, by the Rev. John Eglinton, of Ryde, Isle of Wight, formerly the superintendent of the Warring- ton circuit. There were good congregations. TILE HORSE FAIR.—On Saturday the usual July horse fair was held, and the animals on sale, though in quality up to the average of previous years, were rather smaller in number. The rain interfered greatly with business, which was very dull. From .E. 50 to £6O was obtained for some of the best animals.

OCCASIONAL COURT.-At an Occasional Court, held at the office of Messrs. Nicholson, White, and Nicholson, Bank-street, on Monday .morning, an agricultural labourer, named William Highfield, was brought up before Mr. James Marson charged with being a person of unsound mind, and was committed to ErptonAsylum._

Ti ANNUAL MILITIA TRAINING.—The men of the Liverpool (King's) Militia Regiment assembled at Orford barracks on Monday, where they received their arms and accoutrements preparatory to pro- ceeding to Altcar for their 27 days' training. About 483 men and 18 officers belonging to the 3rd bat- talion, and 400 men of the 4th battalion, marched from the barracks to Bank Quay Station in the afternoon, and left for their destination in special trains, the former contingent leaving at, about 4-15, and the latter soon after five o'clock. Colonels Garroway arid Bolton were in command. Each bat- talion was escorted by a band, and the route of march was by Winwick-street, Horsemarket-street, and Sankey-street. A RAID ON STONE THROWERS.—At the Borough Court, on Monday, the following boys, whose ages ranged from eight to twelve years, were each fined half-a-crown for stone-throwing, viz :—James Ap- pleton, Aaron Sherratt, William Taylor, John Todd, Thomas Knight, Edward Ashton, William Evans, Henry Newton, Henry Acton, Alfred Dunbobbin, Thomas Hallwood, Henry Corless, and Henry Lewis. The last four defendants committed the offence in Bold-street, and the remainder of the boys were charged with throwing stones in St. Mary's-street, Latchford. With respect to this the Rev. Father Thompson, of St. Mary's (R.C.) Church, attended court and informed the Bench that for some time there had been a considerable amount of stone- throwing at his church, Particularly at the door. When lie had gone to morning service, he had frequently had to remove a heap of stones and bricks that had been thrown at the door. He thought that was simply and solely done be- cause it was a Roman Catholic church. The Bench regretted if such was the case and expressed the determination to suppress the stone-throwing prac- tise as far as possible. , TRIP FROM DARESBUEV. The annual trip in connection with the Daresbury choir , was this year to Buxton. The choir and party were conveyed to th&Warrington Central Station by omnibus—one starting from Daresbury, and a second from Moore —for the better accommodation of those residing in 1 that quarter. On the arrival of the 81 train they were accommodated in saloon carriages, and after a most enjoyable ride Buxton was reached. In the course of the day visits were paid by the excur- sionists to the places of interest which abound in and around this popular Derbyshire spa. After tea, the Vicar spoke of the good feeling that existed to- wards the choir, and of the very ready willingness with which members of the congregation had pro- vided the necessary expenses of the day. Prizes of books—through the kit-Id:less of Mr. Rodger, of Newton Bank—were then made to six boys, who had been most regiilar and well-behaved at the church services and practices. After emery hearty vote of thanks to the Vicar for his kindness and company, the saloons were again occupied, and on arriving at Warrington the morning conveyances were in waiting to drive to Daresbury and Moore. Home was reached at 9-40, an enjoyable da,y having been spent. BRUTAL WrFE ASSAULT.—A man named Mains was charged at the Borough Court, on Monday, with committing a brutal assault on his wife on the • 6th of last December. The wife refused to offer any material evidence, but, as Chief Constable Hunt informed the Bench that he believed the assault to have been a most brutal one, the case was proceeded with on the evidence of the police.—Constable 23 I said that on the night of the day in question he was called to prisoner's house in Lythgoe's-lane, where he found Mrs. Mains on the floor and insensible. He ascertained that she had been assaulted by her husband.—P.S. Rowbotham said that it was thought that the woman would die on the day following the assault. Her eyes were swollen level with her nose, and she could not see the light of a candle held close to them. Her face was black, and wasi one mass of bruises, and she had also been kicked' about the body.—Prisoner alleged that his wife was of drunken habits, ftnd that on coming home on the 6th of December from his work he found her drinking in the house with a man. He and his wife had, however, been Hiring together in Man- 1 chester since the asssult, and were now comfortable with each other,—The magistrates sent him to prison for a month. A WALKING FgAt—On Tuesday morning. Joe Spencer, a long distande walker, of Shropshire, ar- rived in Warrington from Manchester, he having undertaken the task of walking 6,000 miles in 110 days, continued. Spencer has defeated Weston in two of his longest Walks, Weston walking 1,200 miles in 30 days vi,htle Spencer got over 1,326 miles • in 29 days, and on another occasion Spencer walked 5,306 miles in 100 days, against Weston's 5,000 miles in a like period. Spencer is 65 years of age. On the 16th June Spencer commenced his present task at Lillie Bridge Grounds, Thence he proceeded North, passing through Leighton Buzzard, North- ampton, Rugby, Coventry, -Birmingham, Notting- ham, Leicester, Derby, Newcastle-under-Lyne, and Manchester, where he arrived on Monday night,hav- ing completed 1,707 miles. Starting from Manches- ter at 6 a.m. on Tuesday, Spencer reached War- rington by eleven o'clock, having walked the 20 miles in five hours. By permission, he put in 35 miles on the square at Orford Barracks, starting at 12-40 and finishing about 8 o'clock, having rested an hour during the afternoon while the soldiers were on parade. Spencer left Warrington for fur- ther north, and will afterwards turn southward and walk to Penzance and along the South coast to London. CONSERVATIVE CLUB.—The annual ordinary general meeting of the Warrington Conservative Club Buildings Company, Limited, was held in the Assembly Room at the Club on Monday evening. Captain Reynolds (chairman of the company) pre- sided, and Sir Gilbert Greenall and a number of shareholders were present. The balance sheet was read as follows :—" Liabilities: To share capital— To amount paid up on 6,000 subscribed shares, £4,594 Os.; to Parr's Banking Company, Limited, £1,489 2s. Bd.; to sundry creditors, £4O 9s. lid.; rents received and accrued to date, £lBO lie. Bd.; £6,304 13s. 3d. Assets: By buildings—cost to date, £5,860 Bs. H. ; preliminary expenses, £253 17s. 3d.; insurance, £lO Os. 3d.; sundry debtors, £lBO Is. Bd.; total, £6,304 13s. 3d." The report of the directors stated that the whole of the shares had been taken up, and the money due thereon paid in except £905 us., most of which becomes due at varying periods from present date to end of 1886. The number of +shareholders was 656, upwards of 500 Tieing working-men. The whole of thelpremises were let except one shop, the present annual rent being £345. The shop vacant was valued at £3O, making total annual income £375. The bowling green had been completed and handed over to the Club Com- mittee. The total cost of buildings, including bowling green, street making, decoration, &c., would be about £6,600; and as the present share capital, exclusive of Lord Winmarleigh's 500 shares, only amounted to £5,500, the directors recommended that it should be increased by £1,500, in shares of one pound each. The revenue account showed a balance of profit of £l7O ss. 5d.; out of which the directors recommended payment of a dividend for the half year ending 30th June, 1885, after the rate of five per cent,. per annum.—The Chairman remarked that they were indebted to the amount of £1,014 ss. 4d., and it was for the shareholders to consider the wisdom of having 1,500 additional shares.—ln answer to Mr. Wm. Bennett, the Chair- man said that £BOO or £9OO was owing in shares.- 1 Sir Gilbert Greenall said that suppose all unpaid calls were paid, he was afraid they would still be £1,014 in debt. He supported the proposal to raise additional shares.—Aftet a discussion the report and balance sheet were' passed, and it was decided to raise the additional shares. —Major Litton, and lfessrs. William Carson, R. W. Francomb, John Peer, and Robert Pierpoint, were re-elected direc- tors; and Messrs. T. and J. L. Tanstall were re- elected auclitors.—lt was decided to declare a dividend at the rate of five per cent, per annum, and the meeting terminated with a 'vote of thanks to the Chairman. ' .
LADIES' SCHOOL OF INDUSTRY. - A meeting of the sub4cribers to this school, which is in Smith- . _ _ _

street, was held at the School yesterday afternoon, but the business was private. Mn. ALFRpD H. YOUNG, KB., F.R.C.S., lecturer on surgical pathology, surgeon to the Salford Royal Hospital, has been appointed by the Council of Owens College (Victoria University) to the impor- tant position of Professor of Anatomy, vacant by the death of Dr. Morison Watson. The newly-elected professor is the son of Mr. J. C. Young, of War- rington. Al

:CCIDENT.—A man named Peter Philips was drinking in a public-house at Fearnhead on Monpy night, when an altercation took place. Philips was turned out, and in going he fell, his head coming in contact, violently, with the paving stores. He was badly cut on the fore part of his head. When picked up he was insensible, and Dr. Joseph was sent for to attend to his injuries. FA.TA.L SWING BOAT ACCIDENT.—On Thursday evening Private John Lynch, of the Liverpool Regi- ment of Militia, was standing up in one of the swing boats on the Fair Ground, which was going to a considerable height, when he overbalanced and fell to the ground, alighting on his head. He was picked up unconscious and taken to the Infirmary, wkere he died yesterday morning, never having re-gained consciousness. A TICKETLESS TRAVELLER.—At the Borough Court, on Wednesday, Thomas Stevens, labourer, Ash-street, Oldham-road, Manchester, was brought up in custody, and fined lOs and costs, or an alterna- tive of 14 days' imprisonment, for riding from Liver- pool to Warrington in a railway carriage on the Cheshire Lines without a ticket. On the collection of tickets at Warrington station, he was found secreted under the seat of the carriage. A GAY LOVER'S ESCAPADE.—It is stated that the other night a man, whom rumour Boys is mar- ried, was treated rather unceremoniously in the neighbourhood of Golborne-street, where, it is said, he ivas in the habit of paying visits to one of the fair, which the neighbours seemed to resent. He had paid a visit, and was leaving, when he was roughly assailed, and at the conclusion a quantity of flour was thrown over him. He left the spot a sadder and a " whiter " man.

div.p: LATEST NEWS.

It is understood that arrangements have been made for re-opening the Munster Bank on August 4th. William James, 15, was found hanging dead at Hook- agate, near Shrewsbury, on Friday, by his master, Mr. Bromley. A Central News telegram, dated St. Petersburg, Thurs- day, states :—Extensive carriage works at Riga have been destroyed by fire. The damages are enormous. The Lancet states that Mr. Gladstone's illness is a slight but somewhat obstinate and chronic catarrh of the larynx. His physicians bar

physicians have enjoined entire rest of the voice, and already there is a decided improvement. An Exchange Company's telegram from Paris states :—A telegram to the Gazdois says that Prince Bismarck has sug- gested the neutralisation of Zulficar, and it is expected that England and Russia will act upon that suggestion. Duane, who was originally arrested for the Castle Roe e triple murder, confesses to having been an unwilling wit- ness of the crime which he states was committed by the prisoners Sheehan and Browne with a " griffaun," an in- strument resembling a cooper's adze. FATAL COLLAPSE OP A GRAND STAND.—During a friendly society's fete at Penrith on Thursday, a grand stand on which were many hundred spectators suddenly collapsed. Several persons were injured, one of whom died on Friday morning. The strength of the structure was guaranteed hy the contractors. Tux STRIKE IN THE Carrow TRADE.—The first strike money was paid at Oldham on Friday morning to the mem- bers of the union on strike. There are eight districts where men are paid. Owing to the time of paying being well paled out, there was not a very heavy crush. Each man on strike receives 12s, and Is for each child under ten years per week. Minders'working had a meeting this week, and agreed to pay Is per day of extra levy, making 8s per week contributions. THE ROYAL MARRIAGE.—The festivities in connection with the royal wedding were kept up at Osborne until an early hour on Friday morning, the yachts in the harbour baying been illuminated during the night. The Prince and Princess of Wales, the Duke of Edinburgh, the Duke of Cambridge, the Marquis and Marchioness of Lorne, and Lord Wolseley, and Lord Salisbury crossed limn the Isle of Wight on Friday morning. A Shanklin correspondent says that while on their way from Osborne House to Quarr Abbey, where they are to spend their honeymoon, Prince and Princess Henry of ,Battenberg had a narrow escape of being seriously Minted. MR. CRAMBRRLAIN AND. MR. BRADLAIIOII.—Mr. Brad- laugh has received the following letter, enclosing cheque for 20 guineas :—"4O, Prince's Gardens, S.W., July 22, 1885.—Dear Mr. Bradlaugh,—Hitherto my sympathy with you in your struggle for securing the constitutional rightq of the constituency which you represent has been confided to words. I had some doubt whether so ,long as I was a member of the Government I should be justified in going further, but this scruple is now out of place, and I have much pleasure in forwarding a donation in aid of the ex- penses to which you have been put —Believe me. yours truly, J. CRARBERLAIN.—C. Bradlaugh, Esq., M.P."
who has interested himself so much in the matter.
